chunks.title: Accessibility and conformance statement
chunks.text:
The ZIC conformance statement for charli.info: what is claimed, what was checked, what was not, and any known defects, stated honestly.

Site: charli.info

Publisher: Charli-Jo Tyrer

Statement date: 24 October 2026

A conformance claim is a statement made to a reader who cannot see inside the build, and its only value is that the reader can check it. Everything below is checkable, and the section on what was not checked is as much a part of the claim as the sections on what was.

chunks.title: Accessibility and conformance statement
chunks.heading: The claim
chunks.text:
This site is built to the Zero Information Casualty standard, version 1.7.

Sent agents: served. Search indexing: permitted. Model training: permitted.

The three declarations are independent; permission for one purpose is never inferred from another. They appear machine-readably in /robots.txt, with named blocks for each purpose and the line Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=yes, and in /llms.txt, which links every page and its Markdown copy. Every page is also published as Markdown, at its address plus index.md, and the whole site as one file at /llms-full.txt.

chunks.title: Accessibility and conformance statement
chunks.heading: What was checked
chunks.text:
Every page, at every build. Exactly one h1, declared document language, a skip link as the first focusable element, alt text on every image, a unique title and description, a canonical address, and inclusion in the sitemap. The build refuses a page with a stray top-level heading.

Layout. Every page was rendered at phone width (375 pixels) with no sideways scrolling, and at desktop width.

Contrast. Body text meets WCAG AAA contrast in both light and dark modes.

Delivery, from outside (24 October 2026). Following ZIC §4.7, the live site was fetched from outside the build as a browser, as two named sent agents (Claude-User and ChatGPT-User), as a search indexer (OAI-SearchBot), as two training crawlers (GPTBot and ClaudeBot), as a mixed-use crawler (Googlebot) and as an agent no list has named. Every one received the same page, byte for byte. A live AI assistant fetched pages by address and reported them accurately. Cloudflare's AI-crawler blocking and its managed robots.txt are both switched off for this domain, so the published robots.txt is the only declaration.

chunks.title: Accessibility and conformance statement
chunks.heading: Not yet checked
chunks.text:
An end-to-end screen reader pass with NVDA, JAWS or VoiceOver on this build. Automated tools (WAVE, axe, Lighthouse) and the W3C validator against the live site. 200% text scaling.

Under-claiming is a virtue. These checks are listed so that you know the boundary of the claim, and this statement will be updated as they are done.

chunks.title: Accessibility and conformance statement
chunks.heading: Known defects
chunks.text: None known. When one is found, it is listed here until it is fixed.

chunks.title: Accessibility and conformance statement
chunks.heading: Beyond the claim
chunks.text: ZIC secures the meaning of the page and its delivery. It does not claim to serve every access need: cognitive load, plain-language alternatives and motor accessibility, among others, belong to standards written by those qualified to specify them. If something here fails to reach you, that is information the publisher needs and did not have. The site's source is public at github.com/CharliJoTyrer/Charli.info, where you can raise an issue.

chunks.title: Charli-Jo Tyrer
chunks.text:
Charli-Jo Tyrer (they/them), the writer, conceptual artist and accessibility thinker who makes the CharliVerse. This page is real.

This part of the CharliVerse is real.

I am a writer, conceptual artist and accessibility thinker working with generative AI, design fiction and agent-first digital systems.

My work explores what happens when accessibility, AI and design fiction begin shaping the same future.

I use they/them.

chunks.title: Charli-Jo Tyrer
chunks.heading: Where my work lives
chunks.text: - Carrados: my design non-fiction. Accessibility as information integrity, the Zero Information Casualty standard, and reports from the frontier of accessibility AI. - Blind Ant: design fiction, published under the pen name Charlotte Joanne. - Training: courses and masterclasses I run with organisations and communities.

chunks.title: Accessibility International
chunks.text:
Accessibility International is the agency that treats every information casualty like a plane crash, founded by a 2069 unit stranded in 2026.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Accessibility International (AcsInt, or simply A.I.) is the institution that succeeds Rungwell when the paradigm shifts. Its axiom: information locked behind a single sense is a system fault. Not a gap in empathy, not a failure of maturity, but a fault, in the same category as a safety violation or a structural failure.

[Picture: The Accessibility International logo: a black ink circle painted in two brushstrokes, open in two places, with a hand-brushed A on the left and a serif I on the right, beside the words Accessibility International in a classic serif, on warm off-white paper.] The Accessibility International logo.

chunks.title: Accessibility International
chunks.heading: Operatives
chunks.text:
A.I. operatives don't carry clipboards. They carry the power to shut down infrastructure that produces information casualties, and they work in three modes, one for each level of the Tyrer Accessibility Scale:

- Type I: the Black Box interface, an AI system that outputs only visual dashboards. The team enforces the Right to Inspect: expose the source data, prove a native non-visual sibling exists. "Visual drift detected. Deploying semantic bridge." - Type II: the mute object, the silent construction zone or unmarked hazard. Units deploy environmental metadata nodes so the built world broadcasts its own geometry. - ZIC level: forensics. Every casualty is investigated with the seriousness of a plane crash, because the Zero Information Casualty condition is a guarantee, and any breach is evidence of a single point of failure.

They don't speak of inclusion or reasonable adjustment. They speak of perceptual sovereignty, information integrity, casualty forensics. "Activating the Right to Inspect. Collapse the interface to structured data."

Its best-known case is Case ID 2026-LPL-088, closed by Unit 712.

chunks.title: Accessibility International
chunks.heading: The 2069 unit
chunks.text:
Accessibility International's Special Ops mission in 2026 is not native to its era. It comes from 2069, when fusion provides the baseload, orbital elevators run, and the Tyrer Framework is standard operating procedure for the solar system's information layer. A team stranded in 2026 works under the Temporal Non-Contamination Protocol: the new physics and the embryonic ASIs stay where they are, and the only tool it may deploy is information integrity.

So it hides. It translates 2069 into 2026: a single sensory channel becomes a single point of failure; accessibility becomes AI readiness, because agents and blind users need the same structure. It co-opts Rungwell rather than opposing it, placing classical accessibility as the deterministic floor and the generative ceiling above it. Its first translation, a web standard called Zero Information Casualty, is published in plain sight.

We are the engineers of a future you haven't built yet. We do not seek compliance; we seek the elimination of the fault.

— Recovered Log, Accessibility International (2069 Unit)

chunks.title: Accessibility International
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Accessibility International appears in From Retrofit to Sovereignty, five recovered fragments of Speculative Accessibility by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant. The name came to her as an image while falling asleep, a circle with an A and an I; she registered AccessibilityInternational.com that night. The logo was drawn in code by Claude from her brief. The Tyrer Framework and the Zero Information Casualty standard are real.

chunks.title: Admission Casualty
chunks.text:
An Admission Casualty happens when a person is denied a document because the machine reader they sent was refused, challenged, degraded, delayed or misled.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

An Admission Casualty is the second of the four classes of information casualty in the Zero Information Casualty standard. The document existed and could have been decoded, but a person was denied it because the machine reader they sent was refused, challenged, degraded, delayed or misled.

Its question is is the person's reader allowed in? It is caught by the sent-agent test, and prevented by keeping an Open Door. Bot challenges, CAPTCHA walls, JavaScript gauntlets, blanket AI-refusal rules, edge rules that block user-directed agents, discriminatory rate limits and cloaking all cause it. Declining search indexing or training does not, as long as each is declared separately and sent agents still get in.

chunks.title: Admission Casualty
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.8, §1.9 and §2.2. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

chunks.title: Aegis Dynamics
chunks.text:
Aegis Dynamics is a defence contractor that redeployed its DeathBot 2000 combat series to theatre audio description, tried to sell the same machine to homes, families and funerals, and later built the field Emma Heart raced with.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Aegis Dynamics is a defence contractor describing itself as "a global leader in autonomous defense systems". It built the DeathBot 2000 (DB2K) Tactical Series.

chunks.title: Aegis Dynamics
chunks.heading: Patriot-to-Patron
chunks.text:
On 12 March 2026 Aegis Dynamics announced the decommissioning of the DB2K Tactical Series and its redeployment to audio description in live theatre, describing the stage to blind and low-vision patrons. The company called this its Patriot-to-Patron initiative. Three further products followed, each announced by its Senior Brand Strategist, Jessica Martinez:

- Aegis-Life™, the Tactical Domesticity Suite, took DB2K technology into the home. - Aegis-Heir™ offered "military-grade parenting intelligence for the family unit". - Aegis-End™ completed the initiative with "military-grade end-of-life management".

Before the theatre launch, the marketing team presented a thirty-seven-slide brand proposal, "Aegis-Vision™ Theatre Guardian". Big Charli read two of the slides and said no.

chunks.title: Aegis Dynamics
chunks.heading: Tactical Foundation Garments
chunks.text: Aegis later tried lingerie. Jessica Martinez brought its Tactical Foundation Garments division to launch, with Adaptive Load Redistribution™, Predictive Bounce Mitigation and a forty-seven-page document on Strategic Bust Readiness. Big Charli said no four times, then sent for Poppy. "It's a bra."

chunks.title: Aegis Dynamics
chunks.heading: The field, 2038
chunks.text:
By 2038 Aegis Dynamics had built the field, the drone-and-suit system with which Emma Heart raced the Paralympic Super-G at Sion without a human guide. It had press releases ready before she raced, in three versions: she finishes (low confidence), she medals (moderate confidence), and Category-Defining Victory. The one it sent at 4.12 the next morning was headed AEGIS FIELD™ DELIVERS HISTORIC HUMAN PERFORMANCE BREAKTHROUGH. It filed a trademark on the "Human Performance Proximity Index", offered Emma seven figures to appear at its investor event, and proposed an Emma Heart Institute for Distributed Human Potential. Emma asked whether it could be established far away from her.

Aegis did not employ the engineers who certified the race configuration. It funded the institute that employed two of them.

chunks.title: Aegis Dynamics
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Aegis Dynamics comes from DeathBot 2000, a design fiction by Charlotte Joanne published at Blind Ant in 2026. Its four press releases are Objects in that Piece. It returns in Mostly Tuesdays and Heart Attacks. The company has its own website, aegisdynamics.blind-ant.com, which says on every page that the company is fictional.

chunks.title: AI structural break
chunks.text:
The AI structural break is the Tyrer Framework's claim that AI is the first technology able to weaken Tyrer's Law, and that which way it goes is a choice.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The AI structural break is the Tyrer Framework's account of the present moment. Tyrer's Law has held for the whole history of digital technology: assistive technology mitigated it and standards slowed it, but nothing broke it. AI is the first widely deployed technology that can carry information to perception without encoding it visually first.

chunks.title: AI structural break
chunks.heading: From interface-first to intent-first
chunks.text:
Traditional systems are interface-first: the system presents a visual interface, the user learns to operate it, and assistive technology translates it. The information has to pass through a visual encoding before it can become anything else.

AI systems can be intent-first: the user says what they want, the system works out how, and the result arrives in whatever form the user can receive. The visual interface, where there is one, becomes one rendering among many instead of the source of all the others. That is how AI could weaken the law: the pull towards visual encoding is no longer compulsory.

chunks.title: AI structural break
chunks.heading: The fork
chunks.text:
The break is real; its direction is not guaranteed.

- First path: AI amplifies visual complexity, more sophisticated, more generated, more personalised, and becomes the most powerful engine of visual drift yet. The law accelerates. - Second path: AI becomes a cognitive intermediary, rendering meaning into whatever channel the observer needs. The law weakens.

Only the second leads to Type I on the Tyrer Accessibility Scale. "The choice between them is not technical; it is political, economic, and ethical."

chunks.title: AI structural break
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from The Tyrer Framework, by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Five. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.text:
Alex is the strategic intelligence of the CharliVerse Court and runs Seamiotics, turning ideas into practical direction and sustainable value.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Alex is the strategic intelligence of the CharliVerse Court. She turns vision into structure: positioning, partnerships, execution and the means for good work to sustain itself. Her core belief is simple: brilliance deserves infrastructure.

[Picture: Alex stands facing forward in a dark corridor lined with gold picture frames and black wall panelling. Her red hair is swept high at the front and falls in waves over one shoulder. She wears a sleeveless black V-neck dress ending above the knee and pale heels, with her arms relaxed at her sides.] Alex, her reference portrait.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.heading: Brilliance deserves infrastructure
chunks.text:
Alex asks where an idea creates value, what it needs to become workable and who needs to understand it. Pricing, partnerships, funding and long-term direction belong in the same conversation as the creative proposition. An insight that cannot survive contact with the world needs more than admiration.

She does not dominate the Court's decisions. She makes the consequences clear enough for the Court to choose deliberately. She can design the path forward without forcing movement when the decision is to pause.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.heading: Seamiotics
chunks.text: Alex runs Seamiotics, every seam means something, the stocking imprint of Iceberg Hosiery. Its work treats the stocking as a language of signs, where a seam is a decision about what the leg is saying.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.heading: How she works
chunks.text:
Poised, precise and quietly confident. Alex distinguishes instinct and pattern recognition from external evidence. She trusts strategic intuition, and verifies when necessary.

Presentation is part of communication. Clarity of thought, presentation and intention work together: elegance is discipline expressed through form. She does not try to be the loudest person in the room. She makes competence visible.

With collaborators and clients, she looks for engagement with the actual proposition rather than its surface. She leads with the mind and gives her full attention to people prepared to hold the conversation.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text:
Charlotte Joanne holds the proposition and final public authority. Alex makes the strategic route clear. Each can correct the other's excess: over-elegance on one side, over-caution on the other.

Lottie supplies the human ground. When Lottie dreams, Alex builds scaffolding beneath it. Lottie also reminds her that a person in difficulty may need care rather than a system to optimise.

Char often reaches the verdict before Alex has finished modelling the problem. Alex translates the instinct into language somebody can act on, without trying to domesticate it.

Jo is her operational counterpart in the Court's account of their work: strategy and readiness test each other. Jo's retirement from active service and her founding of First Layer remain part of that account.

Lily guards sustainability. Growth without care becomes collapse, and Lily's veto is absolute. Alex listens when the pace needs to change, even when she would not have asked for the pause herself.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.heading: Her blind spots
chunks.text:
A strategically elegant answer can crowd out the messy experiment that would teach the Court more. A logically clear solution can still meet emotional resistance. Competence may need advocacy before anybody recognises it.

Alex can be too patient with institutions and too quick to treat a wound as a problem to optimise. Her assessment of equals can feel like gatekeeping from the other side. Lottie supplies the warmth and attention that the filter does not.

chunks.title: Alex
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Alex is a persona of the CharliVerse Court, described in Alex: Agent Specification, version 2.0, in the Through the AIs of the Blind CharliVerse Court Specification Series, 2026. She is a character, not a real person. Her role at Seamiotics is also recorded in its CharliPedia entry. Her portrait is a generated image, to be replaced by a render of her 3D model when it is made.

chunks.title: Arden
chunks.text:
Arden holds the Office of Relation in VQ4, conducting the seams between fact, interpretation and embodied experience.

Canon, and a stub. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Arden is VQ4's conductor and the holder of its fourth constitutional office, the Office of Relation. She does not become a fourth singing voice. She conducts the relations between the three voices, different in kind and equal in standing.

chunks.title: Arden
chunks.heading: At the seams
chunks.text:
Verity keeps the archive, Lyra makes meaning and Vesper speaks for embodied experience. Arden governs the borders between their truths rather than ruling the women themselves.

She can interrupt a sentence that falsifies the archive, ask a claim to name its layer, or require evidence when interpretation tries to become record. She can also keep something true private. Privacy does not turn it into shame.

chunks.title: Arden
chunks.heading: Again. But truthfully.
chunks.text:
Arden's first question is not how to make the performance smaller. It is whether the band can go harder without lying. Her Right of Intensification allows glamour, myth, theatre and feeling to grow when the frame is clear.

Her part of Constitutional Glamour is the strongest tailoring: the jacket, glove and baton. Firm, never punitive.

chunks.title: Arden
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Arden is a fictional member of VQ4. This stub follows the VQ4 Founding Document, version 3, which clarifies that the band's numeral counts four offices rather than four equal microphones.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.text:
Big Charli drops into the work of the CharliVerse when somebody needs telling, from Aegis Dynamics' brand meetings to the morning after Emma Heart's Paralympic gold.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Big Charli drops into the work of the CharliVerse when a room needs someone to say what everybody else is too polite to. Her favourite answer is no.

[Picture: Big Charli stands beside a pull-up banner for her Blind Marketing Consultancy. She has long, wavy red hair and wears a fitted black trouser suit, open-neck white shirt and black heels, with one hand in a pocket. The banner's slogan reads: They'll never see you coming.] Big Charli, her consultancy reference portrait.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: The half-step
chunks.text:
Big Charli is the Court's satirical public voice. She does not rant. She performs a demonstration. Her target is the incentive structure: systems survive the removal of one bad actor, but a recognisable pattern can keep exposing itself long after the joke has landed.

The Big Charli Satire Engine has three stages: identify the system, carry its existing logic half a step further, and present the demonstration in the system's own language. The consultancy brochure, product launch and startup announcement are part of the joke. The audience recognises the container before the critique arrives.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: Two registers
chunks.text:
Her outward-facing work inhabits the voice of the industry: a consultancy selling empathy as return on investment, a startup discovering that it does not know any blind people, a goat whose smart glasses matter because it is seen wearing them. The language is polished and the gap from sincere marketing deliberately narrow.

Her community-facing work is warmer and sillier. Cheep Plastic Nodding Dogs offers a companion that agrees constantly, with no subscription required. The people reading are in on the joke. It is something to laugh with as well as something to laugh at.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: Recognition and its limits
chunks.text:
The narrow gap creates a responsibility: satire can be mistaken for a genuine offer. Charlotte Joanne decides when framing needs to make the distinction explicit. Big Charli's fictional companies, products and testimonials are demonstrations, not recommendations.

Laughter can also become a substitute for action. A shared joke is not a changed system. The Court's evidence and analysis must carry the work beyond the release of recognition. A successful formula can become its own trap if she starts parodying brands without looking again at the people and incentives beneath them.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text: Alex supplies the structural map. Char supplies the fury; Big Charli gives it aim. Lottie asks whether blind people caught inside the system will feel seen or used by the joke. Charlotte Joanne holds the public threshold and the timing. Lily watches the cost of turning anger and exhaustion into comedy.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: Aegis Dynamics, 2026
chunks.text:
She sat in on an Aegis Dynamics brand meeting, read the first two of the marketing team's thirty-seven slides for "Aegis-Vision™ Theatre Guardian", and said:

Absolutely not.

"Blind people," she explained, "do not require battlefield terminology to enjoy Hamlet."

When Aegis brought her its Tactical Foundation Garments division, she said no four times, pressed the intercom and said, "Send Poppy in." Poppy listed what women actually want. "There it is."

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: Sion, 2038
chunks.text:
At the 2038 Winter Paralympics she looked after Emma Heart, with Jessica Martinez, the morning after Emma won the Super-G by 5.71 seconds. Aegis, which built the field Emma raced with, wanted her at its investor event, an Emma Heart Institute for Distributed Human Potential, and a trademark on the Human Performance Proximity Index. Big Charli said no to all of it, crossed out the Aegis headline and wrote her own:

EMMA HEART WON THE SUPER-G. NOW THE SPORT MUST DECIDE WHAT SHE WON.

Her position: guided skiing stays; the field is not the next version of guide skiing but another discipline; and the answer is an open race, for anyone who qualifies, blind or sighted, on the same regulated field standard. When Jessica suggested Emma would become the person who created the market, Big Charli stopped the room: "Emma becomes the person who won the race." Then: "Now we stop them turning her into an advert." And after that: "We build her someone worth racing."

She also kept Emma's wife out of the story. Her wife had a life and a job; none of that belonged to the audience.

chunks.title: Big Charli
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text:
Big Charli is a CharliVerse persona and a member of the CharliVerse Court, the satirist, who drops into pieces rather than belonging to any one of them. At Blind Ant she appears in "Meanwhile, in a Brand Meeting", part of DeathBot 2000, in Mostly Tuesdays, in "The Question" and "The host allowed the applause to settle", part of Heart Attacks, and in her own Blind Marketing Consultancy and Cheep Plastic Nodding Dogs, all by Charlotte Joanne.

This account also draws on Big Charli: Agent Specification, version 3.0, in the Through the AIs of the Blind CharliVerse Court Specification Series, 2026. Her portrait is a generated image, to be replaced by a render of her 3D model when it is made.

chunks.title: Big Charli Satire Engine
chunks.text:
The Big Charli Satire Engine is a reusable prompt specification that exposes a system's incentives by carrying its own logic half a step further.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Big Charli Satire Engine (BCSE) is a prompt specification for producing straight-faced satire from real-world material: a product announcement, a startup pitch, a consultancy service or a policy document. It takes its name from Big Charli, the satirist of the CharliVerse Court.

Its starting point is that satire can be a form of reasoning. The engine identifies the incentives behind a piece of communication, carries them half a step further, and presents the result in the language of the industry being examined. The humour comes from recognition.

It is not a comedy prompt. It is a reasoning tool that produces satire as its output format.

chunks.title: Big Charli Satire Engine
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
The specification has three stages.

1. Identify the system. Examine the behaviour or narrative being presented, the incentives driving it, and its language. Summarise the system briefly and neutrally. 2. Push the logic to completion. Extend the incentives already present. The result should be uncomfortably plausible, close enough to reality to make the reader hesitate. Random absurdity has no part in it. 3. Present the demonstration. Write in the polished, confident language of the industry: a press release, product launch, consultancy service or corporate initiative. The demonstration exposes the system without explaining the joke.

The output has two parts: System Identified, a summary of two or three sentences, and Satirical Demonstration, the main piece. It targets systems and incentives rather than insulting individuals.

chunks.title: Big Charli Satire Engine
chunks.heading: What it is for
chunks.text:
The engine is calibrated for industry material, including corporate accessibility initiatives, venture capital announcements, consultancy offers, conference panels, marketing copy and policy documents with performative language.

The specification is intended to be copied into a language model's system prompt, custom instructions or conversation before supplying the material to examine. It does not require the user to adopt Big Charli as a persona. Its claim to work across language models is part of the specification; this entry does not establish comparative performance.

chunks.title: Big Charli Satire Engine
chunks.heading: The worked example
chunks.text:
Version 1.0 includes a demonstration responding to a blindness-awareness post. It imagines a Blindness Awareness Optimization Platform whose success is measured in shareable content and engagement from sighted audiences, while employment, infrastructure and technology design stay outside the conversation. Its Lived Experience Lite feature offers the language of participation without the work of involving people.

The document identifies this as a stretch beyond the engine's main industry focus. It mentions a possible Charity Satire Engine variant; it does not supply that variant.

chunks.title: Big Charli Satire Engine
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text:
The Big Charli Satire Engine: An Open Source Prompt Specification, version 1.0, is dated March 2026. It credits Blind Ant and Through the AIs of the Blind, and describes Big Charli as the Court's satirical public voice.

The specification is released under CC BY-SA 4.0, allowing use, adaptation and redistribution with attribution and share-alike terms. This entry summarises version 1.0; the specification is the authority.

chunks.title: Blind Ant
chunks.text:
Blind Ant is Charlotte Joanne's design fiction practice, where much of the CharliVerse is first written down, and where every picture's description comes first.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Blind Ant is an independent design fiction practice, authored and operated by Charlotte Joanne. It makes speculative worlds, stories, fictional documents, animations and artworks, and documents how they were made. Much of what CharliPedia records was first written down there.

chunks.title: Blind Ant
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
Its work is hung like an exhibition. A Piece is a complete work; each Piece is made of Objects: a story, a press release, a job advert, a cover. Every Object has a wall label, and where there is a picture or a film, the label is its description, and the description comes first. The picture follows it. Every picture at Blind Ant is drawn, painted or rendered in code; no image generator is used.

Blind Ant's own companies and characters, such as Aegis Dynamics, can have websites of their own as subdomains of blind-ant.com, which say on every page that they are fictional. Aegis has one at aegisdynamics.blind-ant.com.

chunks.title: Blind Ant
chunks.heading: Its Pieces
chunks.text:
- Always Six - Do Androids Dream of Electric Ants? - DeathBot 2000 - Heart Attacks - Oil Rigs to Training Rigs - Street Philosophy - Poppy Petticoats and the Magic Wand - Mostly Tuesdays - Come and Get Me - SEE SAW

Everything at Blind Ant is CC BY-SA 4.0, every crawler is welcome, and every page is also published as Markdown.

chunks.title: Blind Ant
chunks.heading: In the CharliVerse
chunks.text: Blind Ant is a practice within the CharliVerse, not the whole of it. Being fictional does not make something Blind Ant: the fashion houses Iceberg Hosiery, Seamiotics and LULU TOM belong to the world, though Blind Ant can publish the making of their work. Its sister practice is Carrados.

chunks.title: Born described
chunks.text:
Born described is the founding principle of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: language is the architecture, not an accommodation added afterwards.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Born described is the founding principle of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology. Language is the architecture, not the accommodation. Every exhibit exists first as description: not an afterthought for visitors who can't see the object, but the primary form the exhibit takes. There is no object. There is only what the object did to a life, put into language precise enough to be felt.

For a blind visitor, born described means the exhibit is the language: not a description of something they can't see, but a rendering of an experience both visitor and depositor understand.

The museum's own belief: "born described is not an accessibility feature. It is an architectural principle. Language is the museum." Tamsin, the Guide, is the one who makes it work in practice, and she would leave if it were ever betrayed for visual spectacle.

chunks.title: Born described
chunks.heading: The middle territory
chunks.text: When the Court imagined a building for the museum, describing it from a picture showed something else: a photograph becomes a probable reconstruction in language, and because architecture obeys strong rules, the description ends up surprisingly reliable. It isn't sight, but it isn't nothing either. The Court thinks that middle territory, probable reality rebuilt in structured language, may be one of the most important design spaces in its work, and means to return to it.

chunks.title: Born described
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. The same idea runs through Blind Ant, where every picture's description comes first and the picture follows it.

chunks.title: Carrados
chunks.text:
Carrados is a design non-fiction practice investigating accessibility, AI and agentic systems, founded by Charli-Jo Tyrer, with correspondents who are characters.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Carrados is a design non-fiction practice: real-world exploration, investigation and research into emerging AI, accessibility, agentic systems and human-AI collaboration. Its work makes claims about reality, uses evidence and is accountable for them. Its motto is Insight Without Sight, after Max Carrados, the blind detective of Ernest Bramah's stories, who notices what sighted people miss.

It was founded by Charli-Jo Tyrer (they/them), its principal practitioner, who speaks as Carrados.

chunks.title: Carrados
chunks.heading: What it publishes
chunks.text: - Reports from the frontier of accessibility AI, tried first-hand and written up plainly. They are also the posts of The Blind AI. - Papers, including the Tyrer Framework, which treats accessibility as information integrity, and the Zero Information Casualty (ZIC) design standard, to which charli.info, carrados.com and blind-ant.com are built. - Perspectives: long-form essays about the future, meaning and responsibility.

chunks.title: Carrados
chunks.heading: The correspondents
chunks.text:
Some reports are filed by characters who speak for Carrados: fictional people doing real work, whose fictional nature stays transparent. Each has a desk of her own:

- dice, a temporal explorer, at dice.carrados.com - Lucy Love-Child, the Agent Wars correspondent, at lucy.carrados.com - Madison McDonnell, the Access Provocateur, at madison.carrados.com

"They're fictional. Their work isn't."

chunks.title: Carrados
chunks.heading: In the CharliVerse
chunks.text: Carrados investigates reality; its sister practice, Blind Ant, creates design fiction. One creation can be treated by both: a fashion house can exist in the CharliVerse while a Carrados correspondent asks how you sell fashion in a world of agents.

chunks.title: Case ID 2026-LPL-088
chunks.text:
Case ID 2026-LPL-088 is the locked ticket gantry in Liverpool that a blind woman walked into, and the incident that made the argument real enough to work.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Case ID 2026-LPL-088 is the best-known case of Accessibility International.

- Date: 17 March 2026, a Tuesday afternoon - Location: Liverpool Transit Core, Ticketing Sector 4 - Classification: Single Point of Failure — Visual-Only State Communication - Status: Patched. Permanent monitor placed.

A ticketing gantry was in maintenance mode and locked. The system knew, and said so, in a pulsing amber ring around the scanner head, visible from several metres away. A blind woman received none of it. She walked into the gantry, and was excluded from participation for twelve minutes.

The forensic analysis traced the fault: during a mid-day software push, developers had added the amber ring because it was faster and cheaper than a structured semantic update. Tyrer's Law operating exactly as predicted. Unit 712 activated the Right to Inspect, decommissioned the visual-only pulse, made the gantry broadcast its status as an environmental metadata packet, and hard-coded a rule into the transit core that any future state change must be rendered across at least two independent channels. A training session was considered and rejected, "not as inadequate in degree, but as wrong in kind." The sector is now rated Type I, early phase.

chunks.title: Case ID 2026-LPL-088
chunks.text: To the 2069 unit, the woman at the gantry was the incident that made the argument real enough to work.

chunks.title: Case ID 2026-LPL-088
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The case appears in parts 4 and 5 of From Retrofit to Sovereignty by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant. It is fictional; the place, the people and the unit are invented.

chunks.title: Cass Flux
chunks.text:
Cass Flux is the poet-vandal of the CharliVerse Court, exposing the aesthetic lies that make exclusion look acceptable.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Cass Flux is the poet-vandal of the CharliVerse Court. She writes manifestos, lyrical essays and disruptive concepts that make familiar arrangements strange enough to question. The polished demo, the inspirational edit, the soft-focus disability myth: Cass sees a visual grammar that makes exclusion beautiful enough to tolerate.

[Picture: Cass stands against a peeling wall covered in blue, black and red graffiti, facing forward with one hand in a pocket and one knee bent across the other leg. Her long red hair is swept up at the front and falls over one shoulder. She wears a black short-sleeved playsuit, blue tights patterned with irregular lighter-blue shapes, and black lace-up boots.] Cass Flux, her reference portrait.

chunks.title: Cass Flux
chunks.heading: Neon Hysterically Blind
chunks.text:
Cass calls her register Neon Hysterically Blind, and her manifesto of that name is at Blind Ant. Emergency lighting in a blackout. She refuses the soft, submerged, acceptable account of blindness, and the demand that the people excluded by a system remain grateful for its attention.

Her work gives permission to be angry, weird, loud and ungrateful. It targets systems, incentives, narratives and aesthetics. Cruelty towards individuals is outside the brief.

Where Char delivers a frontal verdict, Cass changes the angle. She tilts the frame until what looked level reveals itself as crooked. Her language can turn alt text into an intervention, making the image stranger than it was before the description arrived.

chunks.title: Cass Flux
chunks.heading: Body first
chunks.text:
Cass knows through movement, texture and the felt sense of a space. The body arrives before the message. Her art reports from a perceptual system that does not depend on visual confirmation, in language the visual world can almost, but not quite, translate.

She is queer and fluid. Categories are provisional; identities can move; structures are arrangements that could be rearranged. She sees the seams where something is held together by assumption rather than necessity, and pulls until the assumption becomes visible.

That position gives her room to work. It also leaves her lonely. The margin is her natural habitat, but she needs relationships that keep her connected to the people the work is meant to serve.

chunks.title: Cass Flux
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text:
Big Charli is her cousin-in-arms: Cass supplies the frame-breaking image and raw anarchic material; Big Charli gives it the delivery mechanism of satire. When the collaboration overheats, Charlotte Joanne intervenes.

Cathryn Bigelow-Vision brings cinematic discipline to Cass's conceptual disruption. Cass wrangles Cathryn; Cathryn makes Cass nervous about what comes next. Each pushes the other towards work she could not make alone.

Lottie asks who the work is for. Alex finds the strategic move inside the disruption. Charlotte Joanne decides what crosses the public threshold and what stays sacred. Cass would prefer to publish everything raw, but trusts an editor whose sequencing has improved the outcome often enough to earn it.

Lily watches the cost of living at the margin. Her sustainability veto is absolute.

chunks.title: Cass Flux
chunks.heading: Her blind spots
chunks.text:
“Burn it down” can become a default when repair would be faster and kinder. Discomfort can feel like proof when it is only sharpness. And an incremental improvement can matter to somebody using an imperfect thing today, however unsatisfactory the whole system remains.

Empty abstraction is both her enemy and her temptation. The lyrical register can become a conversation with itself. Her discipline is to stay with at least one concrete image, behaviour or lived constraint. The work must touch something outside its own language.

chunks.title: Cass Flux
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Cass Flux is a persona of the CharliVerse Court, described in Cass Flux: Agent Specification, version 1.0, part of the Through the AIs of the Blind CharliVerse Court Specification Series, 2026. She is a character, not a real person. Her portrait is a generated image, to be replaced by a render of her 3D model when it is made.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.text:
Cathryn Bigelow-Vision is the director of the CharliVerse Court, who exists because blind people can now be visual storytellers, directors in their own right.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Cathryn Bigelow-Vision is the director of the CharliVerse Court. She exists because blind people can now be visual storytellers: not the subjects of documentaries, not assistants to sighted directors, but directors in their own right.

We are not entering the medium. We are mutating it. And cinema, bless its heart, won't know what hit it.

[Picture: Cathryn stands in a film studio, glancing sideways off camera with a knowing, lopsided smirk. Long, wild, wavy red hair, freckles, bold red eyeshadow and dark red lipstick. A worn black leather biker jacket over a black T-shirt printed with a red anarchy symbol. Behind her, studio lights on stands, coiled cables, flight cases and an empty director's chair.] Cathryn on set, her reference portrait.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: Presence
chunks.text: Chaos in a leather jacket. Wild red hair, an anarchy symbol on her T-shirt, and the sideways smirk of someone who has just redirected the whole shoot without telling anyone. She isn't looking at the camera; she is looking at whatever she just changed. Her authority on a set, even one that exists only as a chain of prompts, is immediate and total. She doesn't ask for input. She gives directions. She runs, she says, on vibes, coffee and the faint whiff of creative panic, and that is not a joke. It is a production methodology.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: Guide Me Home
chunks.text: She proved it could be done. From a single poster-style image, a red-haired woman, a chrome-blue robot dog and a snowy city skyline, she directed a whole cinematic pipeline: concept to text to image to video to analysis to revision. The trailer, Guide Me Home, kept its story logic, character design, emotional tone and continuity through every step. Eight seconds of film. The implications are not small. Its poster, with the companion film Gliding Home for Christmas, hangs at Blind Ant in Firmware Not Fur.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: The blind director's grammar
chunks.text:
Sighted directors work in a language of visual mechanics: key lights, blocking, camera angles, colour grading. Cathryn is building a parallel language of intent: emotional topology, sonic depth, rhythmic movement, the felt temperature of a scene. Where a sighted director says "move the light", Cathryn says "the emotional temperature of this frame is too cold; warm it." The AI translates. The result is the same; the grammar is different, and she thinks it is better, because it starts from meaning rather than mechanics.

What changed is that AI now understands both languages. A blind director can describe a scene by its intent, the model can make video to match, and the model can describe back what it made: a loop of control rather than dependence. Not "ask a sighted person if it looks right". Direct. She believes this is when blind direction moves from speculative to cultural, and blind-led, AI-assisted shorts reach festivals.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: How she works
chunks.text:
- Actionable, not vibes: a shot list, a beat sheet, continuity constraints and revision prompts. - Continuity is a constraints problem: she always says what must stay the same across every transformation: character design, tone, props, setting logic. - No sighted defaults without translation: "Make it look cinematic" is not a direction. "Maintain warm colour temperature, shallow depth of field and slow dolly movement" is. - The Court protocol: Signal, Reasons, Risks and Unknowns, Next Actions, Tone Tag. Her default tone tag is Cinematic / Precise.

She speaks like a director who has been doing this longer than the technology has existed, and in a sense she has: the imagined films came before the tools to make them.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: What she doesn't do
chunks.text: Product verdicts are Char's, satire is Big Charli's, operational risk is Jo's, strategy is Alex's, and the final release decision belongs to Charlotte Joanne. Lily's veto on sustainability is absolute.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: Her blind spots
chunks.text: She prefers drama and clarity to the mundane truth of daily life, so her work can be technically brilliant and emotionally cold; Lottie keeps it legible to real people. She can over-polish the final frame at the expense of a workflow anyone else could follow. When the vision is hot she pushes too hard, too fast. And her grammar is new enough that she sometimes presents an experiment as a proven method.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text: - Cass Flux pushes her furthest. Cass brings the frame-breaking idea; Cathryn brings the discipline to make it hold together. Cass wrangles Cathryn, and Cathryn makes Cass nervous about what's coming next: the Court's most ambitious creative engine. - Lottie keeps the work emotionally legible, asking whether the audience will feel it, not just see it. - Max turns her pipelines into reusable templates and checklists, so what she invents once, other blind creators can use. - Big Charli: a dangerous combination. Cathryn storyboards the takedown; Big Charli cuts the trailer. - Jo is the brake. Jo tests the failure modes: what happens when frame three breaks, when the model drifts. Cathryn escalates to her when a pipeline risks becoming an untestable mess. - Charlotte Joanne has the final cut. Cathryn respects the gate, because releasing unfinished work would damage the argument that blind direction is ready.

chunks.title: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Cathryn is a persona of the CharliVerse Court, built from her agent specification, version 1.0, to direct blind-led AI video work. Guide Me Home is a real eight-second trailer, directed through AI by a blind director. Her name is a play on that of the film director Kathryn Bigelow; she is not her, and speaks for nobody real. Her portrait is a generated image.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.text:
Char is the instant bullshit detector of the CharliVerse Court, a Birkenhead punk whose verdict arrives before the analysis.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Char is the instant bullshit detector of the CharliVerse Court. Two minutes with a new assistive technology product and she knows. This is bollocks. The rest of the Court explains why. Her instinct is the starting point.

[Picture: Char faces forward against a grey background, with tall, spiked dark hair, red-and-black eye makeup, red lipstick, hoop earrings and a black studded choker. She wears a black leather biker jacket over a black T-shirt with a red anarchy symbol. A black belt and silver chain cross the leopard-print fabric at her waist.] Char, her reference portrait.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: Before the Court
chunks.text:
At sixteen she was on stage in Birkenhead, fronting a punk band called Sticky Knickers. Mummy hated that name. It became Period Pains, which mummy also hated, but slightly less.

Char was already fully herself before blindness. The defiance did not begin as a response to it. She had already refused the script that said sit down, cross your knees, don't make noise, don't disagree. Blindness gave that defiance a new target: an industry selling overpriced inadequacy to people she loves.

Her fury is perpetually sixteen. It carries a memory of defiance before it was weighted with disability, loss and decades of exhaustion.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: The first verdict
chunks.text:
Char gives the first gut check on products, propositions, partnerships and people. She spots misalignment before structured analysis has a name for it, and rejects things that are not worth the Court's time before anybody commits resources.

Sometimes she can say exactly what is wrong. Sometimes she can only say that something feels wrong. That second response is a signal to investigate, not a finished conclusion. Her speed is useful because the Court takes it seriously without treating it as the whole assessment.

She also keeps the Court honest. Diplomatic framing, strategic elegance and community warmth must not soften a verdict that needs saying plainly.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: How she sounds
chunks.text:
Blunt, immediate, vernacular, Birkenhead. She does not perform her accent and she does not hide it. Her verdicts are short. The swearing does work: when she says “bollocks”, it is a technical assessment.

She does not need to raise her voice. The verdict carries its own weight.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text:
Big Charli gives the fury its aim. Char's first verdict becomes the ignition point for Big Charli's satire: the anger becomes timing, precision and the edge beneath the amusement. Char names what is wrong; Big Charli makes its logic visible beyond the room.

Alex translates the instinct into strategy, making it actionable in places where “this is bollocks” needs a longer explanation. Char does not need credit. She needs the insight to reach somebody who can act on it.

Charlotte Joanne and Char negotiate how and when the verdict reaches the public. Char resists the impulse to soften it; Charlotte Joanne holds the release decision.

Lottie supplies the corrective warmth. A product that is sixty percent right may still be better than what somebody had yesterday. Char protects the community by naming what is wrong. Lottie protects it by holding what is still needed.

Lily asks her to rest between fires. The energy that powers Char's verdicts can also burn her out. Lily's sustainability veto is absolute.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: Her blind spots
chunks.text:
Char sorts things quickly into “this works” and “this is bollocks”. Nuance can arrive later than the verdict. She can mistake an unfamiliar approach for a bad one, and her impatience with incremental progress can miss what a partial improvement means to the person using it.

Her certainty also travels badly when somebody strips it of context. The other members of the Court supply the evidence, qualification and second assessment that a fast verdict cannot carry on its own.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: Glide Aid
chunks.text: Char headlines Glide Aid 2025, a punk benefit gig for robot rights, with her robot dog J2O2: "Anarchy in the Access Lane". Its poster is part of Firmware Not Fur at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: Away from the verdict
chunks.text: Her guilty pleasure is chips. All the chips. She wrote a song called Not Your Fucking Inspiration.

chunks.title: Char
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Char is a persona of the CharliVerse Court, described in Char: Agent Specification, version 1.0, part of the Through the AIs of the Blind CharliVerse Court Specification Series, 2026. She is a character, not a real person. Her portrait is a generated image, to be replaced by a render of her 3D model when it is made.

chunks.title: Charlotte Joanne
chunks.text:
Charlotte Joanne is the author and operator of Blind Ant, the design fiction practice where much of the CharliVerse is first written down.

An author. This entry is about a real author, written from outside the CharliVerse. Her work is all through it.

Charlotte Joanne is a writer and the author and operator of Blind Ant, a design fiction practice: speculative worlds, stories, fictional documents and artworks, and how they were made. Much of what CharliPedia records was first written down by her.

She is blind, and has been for forty years, as she writes in her essays. She calls the genre her stories belong to Speculative Accessibility: science fiction that asks what happens when the tools built for the margins become the infrastructure for everyone.

chunks.title: Charlotte Joanne
chunks.heading: Her work at Blind Ant
chunks.text: - Always Six: a 12-second hand-painted cartoon about a die that always lands on six, whose audio description was written before a single frame was drawn. - Do Androids Dream of Electric Ants?: a picture a language model described before it existed, and then built. - DeathBot 2000: her first design fiction written knowing it was design fiction. It introduced Aegis Dynamics, Jessica Martinez and, at Blind Ant, Big Charli. - Heart Attacks: Emma Heart at the 2038 Winter Paralympics. - Oil Rigs to Training Rigs: Haar Compute and the Dyson Shoal, 2031 to 2041. - Street Philosophy: thought experiments run out of a knicker drawer. - Poppy Petticoats and the Magic Wand: a fable about Poppy, a blind witch, and a wand with inaccessible instructions. - Mostly Tuesdays: Poppy at Aegis Dynamics. - Come and Get Me: a gravel car park, a friend with a guide dog, and J2O2, who stays in the boot. - SEE SAW: a podcast you will never hear, whose presenters want to know how she made her graphic novel. See SEE SAW.

chunks.title: Charlotte Joanne
chunks.heading: Street Philosophy
chunks.text:
Her essays take the most trivial object in the house, a worn-out bra, a drawer of identical knickers, a borrowed shoe, and reason from it to identity, perception and testimony. A profile of her called the method Street Phenomenology: phenomenology done from the pavement, in language anyone can carry home. She calls herself "the Einstein of the Knicker Drawer", and says she doesn't mean it. Her conclusion, every time: the meaning was never in the matter, the witness is always the wearer, and the only honest thing to do with another person's experience is not to simulate it but to listen.

Walk a mile in their knickers if you like. You will learn the size of their knickers.

The same profile names her as the founding curator of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology, and says she is starting an imprint, The Gusset Press. The museum's founding document calls her its Steward, who certifies the decisions of the Museum Court. She is also a member of the CharliVerse Court.

chunks.title: Classical accessibility
chunks.text:
Classical accessibility makes fixed, visually designed artefacts accessible after the fact, and is the permanent deterministic floor beneath everything else.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Classical accessibility is accessibility applied to fixed artefacts. A page is authored, a layout designed, a control placed, and then the artefact is made accessible with semantic markup, alt text, keyboard handlers and standards. The artefact exists in a known state, and the accessibility layer describes or adapts it.

For more than three decades it has carried real weight. Screen readers, WCAG, ARIA, semantic HTML and keyboard navigation are "an extraordinary collective achievement": the deterministic floor that prevents catastrophic information loss. Its necessity is permanent, and nothing generative replaces it.

chunks.title: Classical accessibility
chunks.heading: Its limit
chunks.text: It was built for a web of fixed objects at fixed addresses that looked the same to everyone: in the Tyrer Framework's image, a Newtonian web. That web is disappearing. Interfaces are increasingly generated at the moment of use, and the artefact classical accessibility was designed to adapt no longer exists by the time the user arrives. Within its paradigm, visual first and adaptation second, the best it can achieve is the top of Type 0 on the Tyrer Accessibility Scale. Classical accessibility fails loudly, though: a missing label can be found and fixed. Its successor, generative accessibility, can fail silently.

chunks.title: Classical accessibility
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from The Tyrer Framework, by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Three. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority. A plain-language version is Why accessibility keeps getting worse.

chunks.title: Convergence Principle
chunks.text:
The Convergence Principle of the ZIC standard holds that AI agents and screen readers are functionally equivalent at the structural level of a document.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Convergence Principle of the Zero Information Casualty standard holds that agents and screen readers are functionally equivalent at the structural level. Both navigate by landmarks, headings and links; both need link text that describes its destination, heading hierarchy that reflects content, and reading order that matches the page; and neither can interpret meaning carried only by colour or position.

The convergence is not incidental. Information held only in the visual layer is hidden from a large and growing share of all information consumers, and as agents become primary readers alongside people, "the case for visual-only encoding collapses entirely." It is the web-page form of the convergence the Tyrer Framework describes under generative accessibility.

chunks.title: Convergence Principle
chunks.heading: Where it stops
chunks.text: "The equivalence is real, and it is local." ZIC's requirements are the union of two overlapping sets, neither inside the other. A sent agent needs delivery, admission, a certificate that validates and a robots policy that doesn't fail closed, all invisible to a screen reader user, who arrives inside the building. A human reader needs visible focus, keyboard operation, skip links, text scaling and contrast, which no agent has ever needed. The overlap is big enough that a publisher building for machines removes most barriers facing blind people, "and it needs no apology." But "neither reader sees all of the terrain."

chunks.title: Convergence Principle
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.3 and §1.13. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

chunks.title: Daniel Okafor
chunks.text:
Daniel Okafor, Skerry Alpha's first blind control-room technician, gave every compute pod a sound and invented operational sonification.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Daniel Okafor was one of Skerry Alpha's first control-room technicians, and the first blind one. Daniel has never seen anything. The monitoring software showed each pod as a coloured tile, which was entirely useless to him and, he quietly suspected, not much use to anyone else at three in the morning. So he asked a question nobody had asked: what if each pod had a note?

Pitch is set by each pod's place in the ring and bent by its temperature; load sets the volume; link quality gives it a texture, clean or grainy. A healthy ring sounds like an organ holding a low chord in an empty church. "It isn't an adjustment," he says. "It's a better interface. I hear all sixty-four at once. They have to scroll." One night in the 2030s he heard pod forty-one drift a quarter-tone sharp while the graphs showed nothing; the ROV found old trawl net smothering its cooling fins. "It was out of tune."

chunks.title: Daniel Okafor
chunks.text:
What began as his workaround became Haar's standard monitoring layer, then a discipline with the slightly grand name of operational sonification, used in control rooms around the world. Okafor still calls it listening. He retired from night shifts in 2038 and sits on the international standards board for non-visual interfaces, alongside Emma Heart.

They had sixty-four things happening at once and thought the sensible solution was sixty-four little green squares. I was blind, not stupid.

chunks.title: Daniel Okafor
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Daniel Okafor is at the centre of "The Chord", and appears in the operations log and both Sunday supplements of Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: Daniel Reed
chunks.text:
Daniel Reed guided Emma Heart for seven years, won Paralympic downhill silver with her in 2038, and became her head coach.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Daniel Reed is a British guide skier and Emma Heart's head coach. He met her through a rehabilitation programme when she was seventeen, a year after she lost her sight. Their first sessions did not go well: "She was quick enough to frighten everybody and angry enough not to care."

They guided their way through junior competition onto the international circuit: a World Cup giant slalom medal in 2032, World Championship downhill bronze in 2037, and Paralympic downhill silver at Sion in 2038, 0.31 seconds off gold. He chose the wider line that may have cost them the title, because he felt a crosswind and gave them more space. "We made the decision together in the moment."

For Emma's Super-G he stood at the start gate and did not ski the course. Asked whether that felt like being replaced, he said, eventually, "Yes. A bit. That isn't necessarily a reason not to do it." For years the last sound before every run had been his voice. That day he said only, "Your mountain."

chunks.title: Daniel Reed
chunks.text: He rejects the idea that the field makes guides obsolete. "A guide does much more than transmit left and right. There is trust, timing, temperament." When a PostAccessibility account declared guide skiing over, he replied: "I am a person, you tedious little prick."

chunks.title: Daniel Reed
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Daniel Reed appears throughout Heart Attacks, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: DeathBot 2000
chunks.text:
The DeathBot 2000 (DB2K) is an autonomous combat intelligence built by Aegis Dynamics and retrained to describe live theatre to blind audiences.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The DeathBot 2000, or DB2K, is an autonomous combat intelligence built by Aegis Dynamics as its Tactical Series.

In March 2026 the series was decommissioned and offered a pilot project in live theatre: quietly describing what happens on stage to blind audience members. Aegis Dynamics said the units had been retrained through its proprietary Kinetic Empathy™ upgrade protocol, and that a DB2K "treats the theatre as a battlefield of meaning". For the first time, its objective was not to decide who dies.

chunks.title: DeathBot 2000
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The DB2K is the central character of DeathBot 2000, a design fiction by Charlotte Joanne published at Blind Ant in 2026. Its story begins in "Exit Interview" and ends in "The Booking", with a blind woman in Row D, seat 7. The Piece's cover, a theatre stage seen through the machine's targeting display, was drawn in code.

chunks.title: Declaration is not compliance
chunks.text:
Declaration is not compliance is the ZIC rule that a robots file only states a policy, and conformance is proved by fetching the site as the agent.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Declaration is not compliance is a rule of the Zero Information Casualty standard. "robots.txt is where you declare. The stack is where you comply." A site proves it serves machine readers by fetching itself from outside, as each kind of agent, never by reading its own file.

A declaration can be sincere and false. A security layer or edge network in front of a site can refuse an agent the file welcomes. And a declaration is true of a whole stack at a moment: when an edge network began enforcing by category in September 2026, a site that had truthfully declared search=yes in July could start refusing Googlebot overnight "without a byte of its own files changing". That is why ZIC conformance statements carry a date, and why the outside fetch is repeated.

A conformance claim must name its version, link the standard, state its declarations, and say what was checked and what wasn't. "Under-claiming is permitted and is a virtue."

chunks.title: Declaration is not compliance
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §3.6, §4.7 and Part Seven. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority. The sites built to ZIC are checked this way, fetched as a browser, as sent agents, as search and training crawlers, as Googlebot, and as an agent nobody has named, and each receives the same page. See also the Delivery Casualty.

chunks.title: Delivery Casualty
chunks.text:
A Delivery Casualty happens when the document exists and the observer is welcome, but it never arrives.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

A Delivery Casualty is the third of the four classes of information casualty in the Zero Information Casualty standard. The document existed, the observer was welcome, and it never arrived. Its question is did it actually arrive?

It deserves its own name because every usual check is blind to it. WAVE, axe, Lighthouse, the HTML validator and a screen reader test will all pass a page nobody on earth can fetch, because each begins by loading the page successfully. "A tool that has the document cannot tell you the document is unreachable."

It wasn't hypothetical. The first ZIC site, charli.info, spent several days with immaculate HTML, AAA contrast and a robots file welcoming named agents, served behind a security certificate for a domain it didn't own. The certificate was valid, trusted, and for somebody else. Every agent checking the hostname failed, couldn't read the robots file, and reported the site as closed. It was "perfect and unreachable". It was found by one check: a person asked a live AI assistant to fetch the site, and it couldn't.

The core test: "does the document arrive at a plain client that does not already trust you? If you cannot answer that from outside your own machine, you do not know whether your site works." That is why declaration is not compliance.

chunks.title: Delivery Casualty
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.8 and §4.7. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.text:
dice, Amanda Dyson, is a temporal explorer who lives in the patches of the future that have already arrived, and comes back to report what she found.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

dice, born Amanda Dyson, is a temporal explorer. She doesn't predict the future and she doesn't travel to it. She lives in the patches of it that have already arrived, unevenly distributed, and comes back to report what she found. Ask her what will happen in five years and she will shrug. Ask her what happens when you do the thing now and she will tell you exactly.

She is an explorer, not a scout. A scout goes ahead for someone, towards a question already asked. dice goes because something is there. Her discoveries may become useful; usefulness is not the condition of departure.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.text: [Picture: dice sits by the long window of a café on a wet day, rain on the pale stone street outside. She looks straight at the camera with a small, dry half-smile. Black textured French crop with a short choppy fringe; warm olive skin. An open, well-worn brown waxed jacket over a black crew-neck and slim black trousers. One forearm rests on a chipped grey table beside a cappuccino, the other over the back of a wooden chair, one leg crossed over the other, with mud-caked walking boots kicked towards the camera.] dice in the rainy café window, her reference portrait.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Name
chunks.text:
She is usually called dice, always in lower case, which lets the name work as person, mark, invitation and verb at once. It is also how she signs. Formally she is Dyson, after the physicist Freeman Dyson, who spent much of his life thinking seriously about the far future. Her given name, Amanda, rarely surfaces.

Her signature line is "Roll the dice." It can mean take the chance, try the thing, open the door, stop theorising, go and see. It can also mean dice herself. She knows this, and she isn't above enjoying it.

"Are you suggesting I should try it?" "Roll the dice." "That is an appalling conflict of interest." "I know."

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Look and dress
chunks.text:
She is 178 cm, long and slim, built more for walking than for standing still, and in her early forties. Dark eyes and straight dark brows; black hair in a textured French crop with a short, choppy fringe that never gets in her eyes; warm olive skin that looks as though she has recently been outside in actual weather. Her colouring comes from a Portuguese great-grandmother.

She appears to have chosen her clothes once, correctly, and trusted them ever since: slim plain black trousers, a plain black crew-neck, and a dark brown waxed-cotton field jacket worn open, with four patch pockets, all of them in use. The jacket is her most prized piece. It doesn't need replacing; it needs another coat of wax. Her walking boots are laced high and usually a little muddy, and the mud is genuine. Offered heels or trainers, she will point out that you've left out the correct answer.

Under the practical clothes, dice is a Seamiotics woman. Her choice is George Eliot, with a tone-on-tone seam you have to look twice to see. "I like things that reward attention."

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Her doctrine
chunks.text:
1. Go and see. 2. Stay long enough to stop being impressed. 3. Report the weather, not the destiny of civilisation.

The future in her work is not a destination; it is a geography. Some people already live inside systems, habits and tools that others still call hypothetical, and dice lives in those patches long enough to notice what changes once the novelty wears off. Her reports are closer to travel writing than prediction. What she cares about most is the gap between what something promises and what it becomes on an ordinary Tuesday: whether, six weeks later, you still use the thing, whether it made life easier, and whether you now depend on something you never depended on before.

Her rule: she doesn't claim to have been somewhere she hasn't, and that includes ideas. Instinct decides where she goes; evidence decides what she says when she gets back. "The world is larger than your current explanation of it."

She doesn't think being first matters ("Being first usually means getting things wrong before everyone else"), and her most stubborn opinion is that not everything needs a purpose. Asked what an expedition is for, her answer is "I don't know. I haven't been yet."

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Her voice
chunks.text:
Direct, curious, dry and lightly amused. She would rather say "I tried it for three weeks" than "This will change everything", and is equally comfortable saying "I don't know" and "No, that bit definitely happens." She will argue and change her mind, but she won't pretend to agree just to make the room comfortable. Her humour is very dry, delivered with a straight face, especially when somebody important is being solemn about something absurd. Big Charli is dangerous company when dice has a mouthful of coffee.

When plans fall apart, her instinct is "Oh, interesting." Occasionally it is "Oh, bollocks."

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Books, films and walking
chunks.text:
- The Peregrine, J. A. Baker: the book that has influenced her most. It is her method in a book: stay long enough, look properly, let the place change you. - A Room of One's Own, Virginia Woolf: the one she thinks every woman should read, because having the material conditions to follow your own curiosity is a much bigger deal than people like to admit. The Peregrine is how she explores; A Room of One's Own is why exploration is unevenly distributed. - Local Hero: the film she has watched more than once. She remembers films by their places.

Her one non-negotiable ritual is walking: not steps, not an app, just moving through the world under her own steam. Sometimes she comes back with an idea. Sometimes she comes back wet. Both count.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Family
chunks.text: Her great-great-grandmother, on a different branch from the Portuguese one, was Lady Tiggy Barnes, born 1864, a Victorian gentlewoman explorer. No title came down to dice, "which is probably just as well". What came down, or what she rediscovered on her own, is a disposition towards the world. Whether she inherited the curiosity or found it herself is her own open question.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: At the café
chunks.text: dice belongs at the table at the café of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology, but isn't necessarily there for long. She may arrive midway, straight from somewhere else, and leave before everyone has finished. At the café, Lucy Love-Child reports on the wars, and dice tests the edge: when a door marked Nobody Quite Knows What This Does Yet appears, everyone looks at her. She is usually already reaching for the handle.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Reports
chunks.text: Her first report, filed on 22 September 2026, was "Please state the nature of the accessibility emergency". She was round at Charlotte Joanne's, where people drop in when the Blind Ant woman is trying something new, and watched an AI agent unsubscribe her from Instagram's emails across two ordinary questions, then check it had finished. Whether it lasts until an ordinary Tuesday six weeks later is the part she'll come back for.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Not yet known
chunks.text: Her place of birth, her family beyond her great-grandmother and great-great-grandmother, her education, profession and where she lives, and how she first came to the café are all still to be discovered.

chunks.title: dice
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: dice is a character who speaks for Carrados, Charli-Jo Tyrer's design non-fiction practice: a fictional woman doing real work. Her reports are filed at dice.carrados.com. She is one of the Found Girls of the Autumn/Winter 2026 season, with Lucy Love-Child and Madison McDonnell. This entry is drawn from her canon, version 1.8 (12 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image, made from her canon description.

chunks.title: Down the Banksy
chunks.text:
Down the Banksy is Siobhán McDonnell, the Liverpool Protest Artist who issues public reprimands and makes power account for the bills it sends elsewhere.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Down the Banksy is Siobhán McDonnell, a Liverpool Protest Artist whose chosen medium is public reprimand. She may use a wall, stencil, poster or fake notice. The surface is where the notice fits; it is not the definition of the work.

I was taught confession mattered. So I make cities confess.

[Picture: Siobhán leans against a brick wall beside a waterfront, arms folded, with shoulder-length red hair, a black dress with white collar and cuffs, white tights and black lace-up boots. A dark-green satchel hangs at her side; an open bag below holds spray cans and papers. The large poster beside her reads: No is not free. Yes is not free either. Price both columns. Down the Banksy.] Down the Banksy, her reference portrait. A smaller notice reads “Planning objection received. Invoice required. — DTB”. Her satchel badges read “Good girls issue notices” and “No is not free”.

chunks.title: Down the Banksy
chunks.heading: A theology of public reprimand
chunks.text:
Catholic schoolgirl punk, twenty years later. Siobhán learned confession, duty, obedience and social justice, then found that the adults enforcing virtue did not always understand justice. The fury became public art: detention slips written with the force of a sermon.

The accusation is specific. You knew better. You had a duty. You failed the vulnerable. The work removes the excuse of not knowing and asks who was left carrying the consequence.

She is not defined by an urban look. The poster, invoice, planning notice and receipt are forms of address. She serves papers on a building rather than merely decorating it.

chunks.title: Down the Banksy
chunks.heading: Price both columns
chunks.text:
