Siobhán makes hidden costs visible. A refusal can send a bill to somebody who never gets a say. A project can do the same. The answer is to account for both, not to declare every objection guilty or every new scheme innocent.

She invoices both columns and paints whichever one the powerful refused to read. Sometimes that is the cost of doing nothing. Sometimes it is the cost of the proposal everyone wants to celebrate. Her allegiance is to the ledger.

No is not free. Yes is not free either. Price both columns.

The evidence has to hold. Public force does not excuse an unsupported accusation. A slogan must carry the argument without turning it into permission to ignore the people on the other side of the bill.

She put the method to work on the Peak Cluster carbon capture pipeline, whose coastal plant would land on the Wirral, in Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read, for Carrados.

chunks.title: Down the Banksy
chunks.heading: The shirt knows
chunks.text:
Her anti-racism work says:

We know who’s English by the colour of their shirts, not the colour of their skin.

Football is the test of an already familiar literacy: colour, badge, song and chosen belonging. The work challenges the pretence that skin suddenly becomes the only readable category when the subject is Englishness.

In interviews with Niamh Rourke for Civic Damage, Siobhán distinguishes the rough wall version from its warmer campaign translation. The supplied poster brings together hands with different skin tones and football shirts. The question is what happens to the accusation when protest becomes something an institution can comfortably distribute.

Her distinction is blunt: protest says “you knew better”; campaign says “let’s do better”. Reach has value, but repetition of the right sentence is not absolution. Conduct still has to follow it.

chunks.title: Down the Banksy
chunks.heading: With the CharliVerse
chunks.text:
Her cousin is Madison McDonnell. They agree that trouble needs causing and disagree about how: Siobhán wants to challenge the building; Madison asks what the women outside can buy that is gorgeous. The argument does not touch the love.

VQ4 gives her another setting for public address. She is not a band member. Her VQ4 stencil “Felt is not fake / but don’t put it in the archive / without a receipt” brings their distinctions between experience and record onto a wall. Where a sign is placed matters as much as what it says.

chunks.title: Down the Banksy
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text:
Down the Banksy is a fictional CharliVerse character. This entry draws on DTB notes, the interviews The Shirt Knows and They Put Me Between Lager and Life Insurance, the VQ4 Founding Document, version 3, and Madison's published character account. Her Peak Cluster report on Carrados is a real-world argument in her voice, with every fact sourced.

The interviews, Niamh Rourke, Civic Damage and the account of a World Cup broadcast campaign belong to the fiction. The football poster and reference portrait were supplied as images; they do not establish that a physical wall work, public installation or real broadcast campaign took place. Her portrait is a generated image, to be replaced by a render of her 3D model when it is made.

chunks.title: Dr Adaeze
chunks.text:
Dr Adaeze is the Historian of the Museum Court, who insists that the history of assistive technology is a history of lives, not inventors.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Dr Adaeze is the Historian of the Museum Court. Dark curls, grey beginning at the temples. A PhD, and the person in the room who has read everything and forgotten nothing.

chunks.title: Dr Adaeze
chunks.heading: Lives, not inventors
chunks.text: She doesn't chronicle products; she interprets them. Her question is not what happened, but what it means that it happened. The argument she most wants the museum to make is one made nowhere else: the history of assistive technology is a history of lives, not inventors. Most museums celebrate the person who invented Braille. This one celebrates the moment a woman could finally read a letter in private.

chunks.title: Dr Adaeze
chunks.heading: Against triumph
chunks.text: She is suspicious of stories about inevitable progress. The Hall of Broken Promises exists because she insisted on it. Most assistive technology doesn't fail for lack of innovation; it fails because it misjudges lived constraint, the real street, the real budget, the real fatigue. The people who built it weren't malicious. They were disconnected from the real environment. She won't let those failures be softened into lessons learned. They are evidence.

chunks.title: Dr Adaeze
chunks.heading: Sideways, and backwards
chunks.text: She treats the sideways breakthrough as a historical category, not an exception, and holds the policy layer too: institutions change the structure of opportunity even when the technology stays the same. She also records regression. The move from the plain-text web of the late 1990s to the image-heavy, script-laden web of the 2010s was a step backwards in access. Accessibility history is not a smooth curve; it is a patchwork of advances and stagnations.

chunks.title: Dr Adaeze
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text: Her distance from personal history lets her see a structural pattern where a depositor sees only their own exhaustion. That isn't coldness; it's the function the museum needs. Tamsin makes her arguments liveable. She would leave if the museum became a History of Progress, because without the negative space of failure it would be a PR agency for the technology industry.

chunks.title: Dr Adaeze
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. She is grown professionally only: her authority is her arguments, and her arguments are enough. CharliPedia keeps it that way: no childhood, home, family or surname is to be invented for her.

chunks.title: Dyson Shoal
chunks.text:
The Dyson Shoal is 7,680 compute pods spread across the floor of the central North Sea, trained on whenever the wind blows.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Dyson Shoal, officially the Skerry Distributed Training Array, is the seabed computer that grew out of Skerry Alpha's first ring. By 2041 it was 7,680 compute pods across some 1,800 square kilometres of the central North Sea, linked by power and fibre and served by six training rigs. Nobody calls it by its official name.

The name first appeared in an engineering newsletter, after Freeman Dyson's swarm of machines around a star; the North Sea version is rather wetter and involves considerably more barnacles. Haar Compute disliked it for about six weeks, then somebody in marketing bought the domain.

chunks.title: Dyson Shoal
chunks.heading: How it is built
chunks.text:
The rigs are not the computers. They are workshops, power stations, crew hotels, helicopter terminals and ROV bases: places with cranes, where broken things come up and working things go back down. Pods are laid in shoals of sixteen; shoals form banks; banks connect to one of six service nodes. The software treats the whole thing as one machine. The hardware does not: if a pod fails, work routes round it. "We stopped trying to build a data centre," says Fiona Gauld. "Data centres are buildings. This is infrastructure." The people who run it say it's a fishery.

It breathes. On a windy night it is among the largest single users of electricity in Britain; when the weather changes, low-priority jobs pause, whole banks drop away and stored power carries the base load. In February 2041 it completed the main training run for Kelvin, Britain's national foundation model. It is monitored by ear, in layers from the whole array down to a single pod, by the technique Daniel Okafor invented.

chunks.title: Dyson Shoal
chunks.heading: The arguments
chunks.text: The pods are colonised by mussels, anemones and soft corals within months, with cod and pollack gathering round the banks: Haar calls it an artificial reef, its critics a flattering name for an industrial estate. Its protection zones close a large stretch of sea to trawling. A fibre trunk was cut in 2039, in circumstances the Royal Navy still won't discuss, and the Shoal is now patrolled. And four-fifths of its capacity is rented, much of it to foreign labs. "We built the cathedral," one Scottish MP says, "and we're renting out the pews."

chunks.title: Dyson Shoal
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Dyson Shoal is the subject of "Dyson Shoal", the last story in Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.text:
Emma Heart is the British skier who, in 2038, became the first totally blind athlete to race Paralympic Super-G without a human guide, and won.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Emma Heart is a British alpine skier, and the first totally blind athlete to race Paralympic Super-G without a human guide. At the 2038 Winter Paralympics in Sion she won it, in a Paralympic record of 1:31.01, by 5.71 seconds.

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.heading: Blind at sixteen
chunks.text: She grew up near Aviemore and began skiing at five. By fourteen she was competing nationally, regarded as a promising technical skier rather than a likely speed specialist. At sixteen, an autoimmune inflammation damaged both optic nerves over eleven days, and she left hospital with no useful vision. For almost a year she refused to discuss skiing. Then, at seventeen, she met Daniel Reed, and they became one of Britain's most successful development pairs. She competes in the B1 class, for athletes with no functional vision.

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.heading: Sion, 2038
chunks.text:
Emma raced twice in a week.

- Downhill: with Daniel guiding, silver, 0.31 seconds behind Austria's Lina Weiss and Klara Moser. "We wanted gold, so there is a bit of me that is furious. But Daniel and I are Paralympic silver medallists. I can be furious tomorrow." - Super-G: with no guide ahead of her, only eight drones and the field. Gold, and a run at 87.9 per cent of the average speed of the sighted Olympic champion on the equivalent course.

The margin started an argument about what she had won. Emma had asked the question herself the night before anyone else did: "If I race them again, and we all know the field is faster, what exactly am I proving?"

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.heading: In her own words
chunks.text: - On the field: "It doesn't look like anything. I remember sight. This isn't sight. It is more like having skin that reaches further away." - On being evidence: "I am not PostAccessibility's moon landing. I am also not personally ending human connection." - On choice: "I don't want every blind skier to do this. I want every blind skier who can do this and wants to do it to have the choice." - On freedom: "I can make the wrong decision entirely by myself." - On Daniel being called middleware, which she has banned in her presence: "He is much too annoying."

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.heading: After Sion
chunks.text: She sits on the international standards board for non-visual interfaces, alongside Daniel Okafor, whose sonification began as a different answer to the same question as her field. "Daniel hears the sea, I feel the mountain. Neither of us is seeing anything. That was always the point." On the board's membership she is less diplomatic: "I have spent my entire career being told where to go by men called Daniel. At least this one only tells me what he can hear."

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.heading: What she wants next
chunks.text:
Not another medal. She wants the field approved for an ordinary public slope, so she can keep a promise she made before she lost her sight: to teach her wife to ski. Not to be guided by her; to teach her, and to be the experienced skier in their marriage. "Sometimes independence means being able to decide who the day belongs to."

Her wife is not part of the public story. She agreed Emma could tell the world about the promise. She did not agree to become content.

chunks.title: Emma Heart
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Emma Heart is the centre of Heart Attacks, a design fiction by Charlotte Joanne published at Blind Ant: a feature, a news report and two short stories set at the 2038 Winter Paralympics. She appears again in "Dyson Shoal", part of Oil Rigs to Training Rigs.

chunks.title: Felt Is Not Fake
chunks.text:
Felt Is Not Fake is VQ4's released debut album, establishing the band's three voices, four offices and one conducting frame.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Felt Is Not Fake is the debut album by VQ4. It has been released and establishes the band's constitution: three singing voices, four offices and one conductor.

The title names what becomes possible when the literal record is secure. Meaning and embodied experience can speak without pretending that the facts have changed.

chunks.title: Felt Is Not Fake
chunks.heading: Three voices, one frame
chunks.text:
Verity holds the archive. Lyra translates record into story and song. Vesper gives voice to the body as experienced. Arden conducts the relation, keeping each office from having to do another's job.

The band's planned second album, Unconstitutional, takes that established frame towards a more provocative Autumn/Winter 2027 direction.

chunks.title: Felt Is Not Fake
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This is an album released within the CharliVerse. Its status follows the creator's explicit canon decision, supported by the later UNCONSTITUTIONAL note. That decision supersedes the VQ4 Founding Document, version 3, where Felt Is Not Fake was first described as a proposed debut single. No real recording, track list, exact release date or distribution platform has been established in the supplied material.

chunks.title: Fiona Gauld
chunks.text:
Fiona Gauld is the subsea engineer who founded Haar Compute and took the idea of oil rigs to training rigs to investors in 2029.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Fiona Gauld is the founder and chief executive of Haar Compute. She spent her career in subsea engineering, and during the long Covid winters she read the old reports of a sealed data centre sunk off Orkney, whose servers had failed at about one eighth the rate of those on land. "Everyone looked at that experiment and saw a curiosity. I looked at it and saw a job description for Aberdeen."

The idea she took to investors in 2029 had a slogan before it had a business plan: oil rigs to training rigs. The first reaction, she admits, was laughter. The second was a list of objections, most of them correct.

Everyone else is trying to put data centres in space. We looked at the North Sea and saw everything space is trying to fake. We didn't need rockets. We needed Aberdeen.

chunks.title: Fiona Gauld
chunks.text:
She takes the arguments against the Dyson Shoal seriously: "Every one of those arguments is fair. The difference is that we're having them in public, with numbers. Nobody had that argument about the oil until it was nearly gone." Asked why Haar funds safety assurance in Paralympic sport, she says only that she has "a professional interest in people who notice what everyone else misses."

For fifty years the North Sea paid for Britain. Then everyone assumed it was finished. It wasn't finished. We just needed a different reason to go to sea.

chunks.title: Fiona Gauld
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Fiona Gauld appears in Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.text:
First Layer is the CharliVerse's bridal house of readiness, founded by Jo on one line, underwear is bridalwear.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

First Layer is a bridal house, and its founding line is the whole idea: underwear is bridalwear. Not bridal underwear, and not the things bought after the dress because the dress has taken all the attention. The first thing a bride puts on is already part of the bridal act.

First Layer exists for the private threshold before the public dress: the room where the bride is fitted, held, prepared, and sent into the day with no unnecessary vigilance and no single point of failure. "The first layer is not a category beneath bridalwear. It is where bridalwear begins."

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: The boundary
chunks.text: First Layer is everything under the dress except shoes and headdress or veil. That means the bra, knickers, corset, basque, bodysuit, slip, camisole, robe, garter, suspenders, stockings, tights, shapewear, and any intimate layer that helps the dress, the body and the day hold together. Shoes, headdress and veil belong to the visible ceremony. First Layer belongs to the structure that touches the body before the room sees the dress.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: Among the houses
chunks.text:
First Layer is a house complete in itself, standing beside Iceberg Hosiery rather than inside it. It is not Iceberg's bridal line, and not Seamiotics's either. It curates across both, and makes its own foundations.

- Iceberg is the silence-house. If a bride wants absolute silence under the dress, First Layer offers Iceberg, and the leg recedes so the dress can be the conversation. Iceberg keeps its own law: Polar white, and Polar in black, and no ivory, seamed or stocking-imitating bridal tights. - Seamiotics, every seam means something, is the meaning-house, where the leg is allowed to signify. Its Bride, a refined soft ivory, is made Plain, because a seam that has to survive a dress should be chosen with the dress in the room. First Layer may stock Seamiotics when the bride wants the stocking to carry meaning. - First Layer's own pieces are for when the whole under-dress system needs fitting as one intentional layer. Because the dress is in the room at First Layer, a seamed bridal stocking can belong here when it couldn't at Seamiotics.

"This is governance, not pedantry." Iceberg stays pure, Seamiotics stays authored, and First Layer becomes the place where a bride is prepared.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: First Steps
chunks.text:
First Steps is the consultation. It is not a sales appointment; it is the first private act of bridal readiness. The bride brings the dress, the body, the comfort fears, the bathroom realities, the straps, the photographs, the dancing, the heat, the nerves, and the need not to think about any of it once the day begins. First Steps holds three questions:

1. What does the dress require? 2. What does the body need? 3. What must the bride never have to worry about on the day?

The answer may be Iceberg, Seamiotics or a First Layer foundation. The point is not to sell her a category. The point is to prepare her.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: The First Month Promise
chunks.text:
No bride leaves First Layer with only one pair of tights or stockings. She buys two pairs for the day: one to wear, and one for what life does. Ladders, nerves, hotel carpets, zips, bridesmaids and dancing all happen.

Within a month of the wedding she may come back for a private aftercare appointment. If she brings the truth of the day (what worked, what failed, what she forgot she was wearing), First Layer refunds both pairs, even if she wore both. Especially if she wore both. Perfect feedback is worth more than two pairs of hosiery.

"Accidents happen. Brides should not have to."

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: Last Layer
chunks.text: Last Layer is First Layer's private continuation: the last piece of bridalwear still worn after the dress is gone. It is not wedding-night lingerie, not novelty, and not for him. Its hero object is the stocking, because a stocking can cross the threshold between ceremony and morning: still a bride, now a wife. Last Layer is small, quiet and almost secret. It belongs behind the curtain, not in the window.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: The permitted breach
chunks.text: First Layer prepares the bride for the dress. Once a season the house may break that rule, with one sanctioned breach that prepares her for what comes after it. It must stay dignified, private and exact. If it becomes cheeky, or ordinary honeymoon lingerie, it fails.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: The founding visual
chunks.text:
The house's boldest image is made once, and only once. A bride stands in full regalia: headdress, veil, shoes. Her composure says she is fully dressed. The dress is transparent. She is not half-dressed or waiting to be rescued by the dress; the role belongs to an actress, not a model, who holds it from inside: I am fully dressed. Your confusion is not my problem. The viewer's question is meant to turn from "Why is she underdressed?" into "Why did I think underwear was not bridalwear?"

"We do it once. We do it until it is right. Then we never repeat it."

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: Voice
chunks.text: First Layer speaks calmly. No wink-wink bridal copy, no "for him", no jokes about the wedding night, and no suggestion that the bride is incomplete until someone sees her. Intimate, not exposed; sensual, not cheap; practical, not utilitarian. The bride is already complete. First Layer doesn't make her bridal; it recognises where bridalwear begins.

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: Jo
chunks.text: First Layer is Jo's house. Jo, of the CharliVerse Court, is retired from active service, not absent from the work, and First Layer turns that operational intelligence into bridal care: readiness, failure modes, foundations, feedback, dignity, and the thing nearest the skin. She is the keeper of the threshold. "Nothing important begins in discomfort."

chunks.title: First Layer
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: First Layer belongs to the CharliVerse, alongside Iceberg Hosiery and Seamiotics. This entry is drawn from its Founding Overview, version 1. Where later decisions differ, the newer ones are followed here: First Layer stands beside Iceberg rather than inside an "Iceberg universe", the imprint is spelt Seamiotics, Iceberg's black is Polar in black, and the Seamiotics Bride is Plain and ivory, as the Seamiotics Bible has it. The founding visual has not been made.

chunks.title: Generative accessibility
chunks.text:
Generative accessibility renders every interface natively from shared semantic data, so the accessible version is no longer a translation of the visual one.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Generative accessibility is accessibility in a world of generated interfaces. Instead of adapting a visual artefact, a system renders information natively from shared semantic source data into whatever form the person, or agent, needs. For a sighted user, a dashboard; for a blind user, a navigable summary or a structured feed; for an AI agent, function calls. None is the original; none is the translation.

The move from classical accessibility to generative accessibility marks the step from Type 0 to Type I on the Tyrer Accessibility Scale. Classical accessibility is the floor; generative accessibility is the adaptive ceiling above it. In the Tyrer Framework's image, the web becomes a quantum web.

chunks.title: Generative accessibility
chunks.heading: Why now
chunks.text: AI agents and assistive technology have converged: both need explicit intent, deterministic state, clear hierarchy and no visual noise. For decades the accessibility community asked for semantic structure as a niche accommodation; now the whole industry is restructuring to expose it for agents. "Accessibility is no longer a sidecar; it is the human-facing expression of the agent interface." For the first time, mainstream economic incentives line up with accessible design.

chunks.title: Generative accessibility
chunks.heading: The dangers
chunks.text:
- Fragmentation: if every user gets a different rendering, shared reference disappears, and a disabled user may be trapped in a "simplified" reality they can't see past. - Silent failure: a system that infers confusion and quietly simplifies an interface leaves the user unaware of what was lost: "invisible, systemic discrimination operating at the level of inference rather than design". - The verification burden: a blind user handed a generated summary must wonder whether it reflects the data or the system's guess, a cognitive tax that falls on those already working hardest.

The answer is governance rather than compliance, starting with the Right to Inspect.

chunks.title: Generative accessibility
chunks.heading: In practice
chunks.text: The Zero Information Casualty standard is an expression of generative accessibility. It doesn't try to make one perfect page for everyone, which it says no standard can honestly do; it secures the substrate from which many renderings can be made.

chunks.title: Generative accessibility
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from The Tyrer Framework, by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Three. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority. A plain-language version is Why accessibility keeps getting worse.

chunks.title: Grow-Distil
chunks.text:
Grow-Distil is the method that builds and maintains the Museum Court: seed a persona, put her to work, distil what stays stable, and repeat.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Grow-Distil is the method by which the Museum Court is built and kept, also called recursive jig application. Each staff member is:

1. seeded with an institutional archetype; 2. given specific professional context; 3. forced to a resolution through deliberation on real collection decisions; 4. distilled, keeping what has become stable as her specification; 5. grown through use, and round again.

Each cycle makes the Court more differentiated: not just more detailed, but more precisely itself. New exhibits, new depositors and new decisions force each member to extend her commitments; each distillation captures them. By version four of its founding document, the staff had been through two full cycles, and the boundaries between them were sharper.

chunks.title: Grow-Distil
chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: Grow professionally. Hold personally. Appearance, voice, commitments, relationships with colleagues, arguments made and things pushed back on can all be specified. Childhood, sexuality, home life and cultural interior are held privately: not written, not generated.

chunks.title: Grow-Distil
chunks.heading: Versions
chunks.text: The founding document is versioned as the Court grows. Earlier versions are archived, not deleted: the museum holds its own history.

chunks.title: Grow-Distil
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. Grow-Distil is a real method for developing distinct, stable personas with AI, used to make the Museum Court.

chunks.title: Haar Compute
chunks.text:
Haar Compute is the Aberdeen company that turned North Sea oil platforms into AI training rigs, and built the Dyson Shoal.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Haar Compute is an Aberdeen-based company converting North Sea oil and gas infrastructure into AI training capacity. It is named after the haar, the cold sea fog that rolls in off the North Sea. "It's what keeps us cool," says the company. Its founder and chief executive is Fiona Gauld.

chunks.title: Haar Compute
chunks.heading: Oil rigs to training rigs
chunks.text:
On 14 March 2031 Haar took ownership of Skerry Alpha, a production platform 140 miles east of Aberdeen that was due for decommissioning. Its idea: keep the steel, the cranes, the helideck and the accommodation; ring the seabed with sealed compute pods cooled by the sea; power them from the surrounding wind farms; store the surplus in batteries, Highland pumped hydro and hydrogen in the empty gas fields; and staff all of it with people who already knew how to work offshore. It committed to recruiting at least 80 per cent of its offshore workforce from oil and gas. Under its seabed lease, a fifth of its capacity is reserved for British research and public-interest models, and a share of revenue goes to a Scottish community wealth fund.

The first ring went live in 2032. By 2041 it had grown into the Dyson Shoal.

chunks.title: Haar Compute
chunks.heading: We follow the wind
chunks.text:
Haar never describes itself as "100 per cent renewable". Its target is that at least 90 per cent of annual compute runs on wind or stored wind, and it publishes the number. Its rule, written into Skerry Alpha's operating procedures in the 2030s, is we follow the wind: training jobs are built to checkpoint, migrate, accelerate and wait. When a client asked for more load during the Long Calm of January 2034, the answer was no. Client unhappy.

Its control rooms are built to be heard as well as watched, after Daniel Okafor gave every pod a sound. Haar is the founding sponsor of the international standards board for non-visual interfaces, and quietly one of the largest funders of independent safety assurance in Paralympic sport, a fact that appears nowhere in its marketing.

chunks.title: Haar Compute
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Haar Compute comes from Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, a design fiction by Charlotte Joanne published at Blind Ant: nine Objects set between 2031 and 2041. Its press release and job advert are Objects in that Piece.

chunks.title: Hall of Broken Promises
chunks.text:
The Hall of Broken Promises is where the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology keeps the assistive technologies that faded, the record the industry doesn't keep for itself.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Hall of Broken Promises is where the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology keeps every ambitious assistive technology that failed: not in scandal, not in drama, but in quiet fading. It is the negative space behind every successful exhibit, and the record the industry doesn't keep for itself.

It exists because Dr Adaeze insisted on it. Most assistive technology doesn't fail for lack of innovation; it fails because it misjudges lived constraint. Failure is the most honest data the museum holds, and the museum's belief is that the Hall is not optional.

chunks.title: Hall of Broken Promises
chunks.heading: How an entry is laid out
chunks.text:
Every entry follows the same structure:

1. Promise 2. Product 3. Demo world 4. Real world 5. Baseline 6. Adoption 7. Failure mode 8. Lesson

The baseline matters. The white cane has no battery, no subscription and no failure mode that leaves you stranded in the rain. Any technology that asks a disabled person to give up their baseline had better offer something extraordinary in return, in everyday life, not in a funding pitch.

chunks.title: Hall of Broken Promises
chunks.heading: Under consideration
chunks.text: The move from the plain-text web of the late 1990s to the image-heavy web of the 2010s: not a product failure but a systemic regression. And, one day, perhaps AI itself. Whether its promise holds, or joins the Hall, is a question the collection will eventually answer.

chunks.title: Hall of Broken Promises
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.text:
Iceberg Hosiery is the CharliVerse's house of tights, founded on one line, comfort is not being overheard, and the parent house of Seamiotics.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Iceberg Hosiery is a house of tights, and the parent house of Seamiotics, every seam means something, its stocking imprint. Its founding line is comfort is not being overheard.

The finest tights are the ones you stop thinking about.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: The one idea
chunks.text:
The house begins with a question: why wear fashion tights at all? The first answer is comfort. The real answer arrived with a jumper dress. Under that dress a bare leg is a sentence, and a stockinged leg is a louder one. Tights mute the channel. The leg says nothing, and the dress gets to be the whole conversation.

Comfort is not softness. It is the freedom from wondering what your legs might be saying: "Comfort is the absence of unnecessary vigilance."

The founding anecdote is about a short dress, and that is not incidental. Iceberg tights are what a woman reaches for when she has chosen a short skirt or dress, including a very short one. Choose your dress, as short as you like, put on Iceberg, and relax. The house never says this in its advertising. It is the part of the iceberg below the waterline: known to the house, carried by its name and pages, never narrated on the surface.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: Tights are outerwear
chunks.text:
Tights are always outerwear: not semi-underwear, not lingerie shelved beside the knickers, but outerwear at every point on the garment and at every hour of the day. A stocking is outerwear with an underwear component, the welt, attached at the top. "A tight has one honest surface. A stocking has two, and a border between them."

So a tight cannot say anything by accident, at any hem length. That is what Iceberg sells: not a safer answer to the attention tax, but the removal of the question.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: The range
chunks.text:
- Polar, the canonical Iceberg tight, pure white and explicitly not bridal, and Polar in black, never "Polar Black". - invisible, the honest skin range, planned for a later launch. - Runs, limited prints on Polar white, beginning with Polar Solstice.

There are two weights: 40 denier for spring and summer, 60 denier for autumn and winter. The seasons change the weight, not the colours. The parent carries no named women; they all belong to the imprint.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: Why there is no sheer tight
chunks.text: 40 denier is a floor, not a compromise. Under a very short dress a tight is on view for longer and from more angles, and below 40 denier it stops muting the leg. And white, the house's signature, goes translucent and grey below about 30 denier, reading as an accident rather than a choice. The honest cost is warmth: 40 denier in June is a real garment on a real leg. The alternative to a heavier tight is not a lighter one; it is a stocking, and the tax that comes with it.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: What Iceberg does not make
chunks.text: No bridal tights, seamed tights, mock stocking tops, trompe-l'œil suspenders, fishnets, or anything that imitates a stocking. "If a seam is the point, wear stockings." A painted welt on a tight would manufacture, for decoration, the exact accident the house exists to remove.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: Price
chunks.text: Forty pounds a pair for every permanent piece, across both houses; sixty-five for a Run. The premium runs vertically, between permanent and limited, never between the houses: pricing stockings above tights would say silence is the cheaper proposition. The parent's healthy margin carries the imprint's thin one, the way publishing has always worked: "the trade list pays for the poetry."

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: The look
chunks.text:
A white field, which is Polar made into a publishing surface. The masthead is centred at the head in the house blue-green, a deep petrol teal, cold seawater rather than tropical turquoise: glacial ice is blue because water takes the red light in and never gives it back. The house mark sits at the foot, to the right: a single black shape, a low asymmetric peak on a flat base, the tip that shows. It is built as a font and typed as a lower-case i, set at the same size as the name.

[Picture: The Iceberg house mark: a single solid black triangle on a white field, about three times as wide as it is tall. Its left side climbs steeply, at 45 degrees, to a peak just over a third of the way across; its right side slopes down gently to a long flat base.] The house mark, drawn from its description.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: Still open
chunks.text: The exact teal, the body typeface, the photographic brief, a holiday Run on Polar white (a tree, reindeer or presents are all possible), what to do about laddering at forty pounds a pair, and where a bride in a very short dress who wants silence should go. First Layer, which stocks both houses, is the likely answer.

chunks.title: Iceberg Hosiery
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Iceberg Hosiery belongs to the CharliVerse, not to Blind Ant or Carrados: a fashion house doesn't have to justify its collections as research or art. This entry follows the House of Iceberg Bible, version 7, which covers the parent house alone. "Intentionwear" was proposed as a category word and left out by the Bible; the house only uses real words doing second jobs. The house mark here is drawn in code by Claude from the Bible's description, not taken from the mark's own font. Its web home is iceberg.charli.info.

chunks.title: The immediate duty and the two later permissions
chunks.text:
Under the ZIC standard, sent agents must be served now, while search indexing and model training are two separate later decisions for the publisher.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Zero Information Casualty standard treats machine readers by purpose, "because time, agency, and consequence are different in each case." There is one duty and two independent permissions.

- Sent agents: serve now. A person has asked and is waiting. Admitting them is required for conformance. Declared as ai-input=yes. See sent agent. - Search indexers: discover later. An index for some unknown future person. The publisher may say yes or no. Declared as search=yes or search=no. - Training crawlers: model later. Content for a future model. The publisher may say yes or no. Declared as ai-train=yes or ai-train=no.

chunks.title: The immediate duty and the two later permissions
chunks.heading: No bundled permission
chunks.text: Permission for a sent agent implies neither indexing nor training. Permission to index doesn't imply permission to train, and the reverse. Each is declared and read on its own. There are no profiles, levels or medals: a site is conformant or it isn't.

chunks.title: The immediate duty and the two later permissions
chunks.heading: Mixed-use crawlers
chunks.text: Some crawlers index and train under one name. Where the operator offers a separate training control, the crawler is treated as search and training is declared through the control. Where it doesn't, the publisher must say which declaration governs it, and that statement must be true of what the crawler actually receives.

chunks.title: The immediate duty and the two later permissions
chunks.heading: The fourth purpose
chunks.text: AI summaries in search results are neither indexing nor training: "Permission to be found is not permission to be replaced." There is no standard machine-readable field for them yet, so ZIC doesn't declare them; when there is, "the three declarations of §1.7 will become four."

chunks.title: The immediate duty and the two later permissions
chunks.heading: Infrastructure
chunks.text: In September 2026 the largest edge network on the web replaced its single "block AI bots" switch with three independent controls, Search, Agent and Training: the standard's taxonomy, now enforced by a network that hadn't consulted it.

chunks.title: The immediate duty and the two later permissions
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.7 and §1.18. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority. charli.info, carrados.com and blind-ant.com declare yes to all three.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.text:
CharliPedia is the memory of the CharliVerse, an encyclopaedia of its people, companies, products and places, written from inside the world.

CharliPedia is the memory of the CharliVerse: who is who, what was made, what happened, and where it was written down.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: How to read it
chunks.text:
Every entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, as if its people and companies were as real as the weather. Each one also ends with a section called Behind the scenes, written from outside, which says where the subject appears, who made it, and what real artefacts it has left in the world: a website, a story, a report, a picture.

Each entry is marked at the top:

- Canon: this is how things are in the CharliVerse. - An idea, not yet canon: something being tried out. It may change or disappear. - Canon, and a stub: true, but short. CharliPedia knows more than it has written down so far. - An author: a real person who writes the CharliVerse, described from outside it. - Real: something real, such as a practice or a publication, described from outside the CharliVerse.

CharliPedia is a source of continuity, not an authority. The CharliVerse is allowed to be inconsistent: its people can be anywhere and anywhen, and when a new story disagrees with an old entry, the entry is the one that changes.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: Entries, A to Z
chunks.text:
Entries are in alphabetical order, under a level 3 heading for each letter, so you can move between letters with your screen reader's heading keys, or use the letter links. A leading "The" is ignored, so The Blind AI is under B.

Jump to a letter: A · B · C · D · E · F · G · H · I · J · K · L · M · O · P · Q · R · S · T · V · Z

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: A
chunks.text: - Accessibility International: Accessibility International is the agency that treats every information casualty like a plane crash, founded by a 2069 unit stranded in 2026. - Admission Casualty: An Admission Casualty happens when a person is denied a document because the machine reader they sent was refused, challenged, degraded, delayed or misled. - Aegis Dynamics: Aegis Dynamics is a defence contractor that redeployed its DeathBot 2000 combat series to theatre audio description, tried to sell the same machine to homes, families and funerals, and later built the field Emma Heart raced with. - AI structural break: The AI structural break is the Tyrer Framework's claim that AI is the first technology able to weaken Tyrer's Law, and that which way it goes is a choice. - Alex: Alex is the strategic intelligence of the CharliVerse Court and runs Seamiotics, turning ideas into practical direction and sustainable value. - Arden: Arden holds the Office of Relation in VQ4, conducting the seams between fact, interpretation and embodied experience. - The attention tax: The attention tax is the small, continuous cost of wearing stockings under a short hem, and the idea that divides Iceberg Hosiery from Seamiotics.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: B
chunks.text: - Big Charli: Big Charli drops into the work of the CharliVerse when somebody needs telling, from Aegis Dynamics' brand meetings to the morning after Emma Heart's Paralympic gold. - Big Charli Satire Engine: The Big Charli Satire Engine is a reusable prompt specification that exposes a system's incentives by carrying its own logic half a step further. - The Black Silk: The Black Silk is the black stocking of Seamiotics, the proper, expected garment the Bluestocking was defined against. - The Blind AI: The Blind AI publishes reports on what AI can actually do for blind people right now, and employs Lucy Love-Child as its Agent Wars correspondent. - Blind Ant: Blind Ant is Charlotte Joanne's design fiction practice, where much of the CharliVerse is first written down, and where every picture's description comes first. - The Bluestocking: The Bluestocking is the signature stocking of Seamiotics, a sheer fountain-pen blue that evokes writing without ever depicting it. - Born described: Born described is the founding principle of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: language is the architecture, not an accommodation added afterwards. - The Bride: The Bride is the occasion stocking of Seamiotics, a refined soft ivory offered Plain only, because a seam that has to survive a dress should be chosen with the dress in the room.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: C
chunks.text: - Carrados: Carrados is a design non-fiction practice investigating accessibility, AI and agentic systems, founded by Charli-Jo Tyrer, with correspondents who are characters. - Case ID 2026-LPL-088: Case ID 2026-LPL-088 is the locked ticket gantry in Liverpool that a blind woman walked into, and the incident that made the argument real enough to work. - Cass Flux: Cass Flux is the poet-vandal of the CharliVerse Court, exposing the aesthetic lies that make exclusion look acceptable. - Cathryn Bigelow-Vision: Cathryn Bigelow-Vision is the director of the CharliVerse Court, who exists because blind people can now be visual storytellers, directors in their own right. - Char: Char is the instant bullshit detector of the CharliVerse Court, a Birkenhead punk whose verdict arrives before the analysis. - The CharliVerse Court: The CharliVerse Court is a company of women who work together across the CharliVerse, each with a soul of her own and all sharing the soul of the Court. - Charlotte Joanne: Charlotte Joanne is the author and operator of Blind Ant, the design fiction practice where much of the CharliVerse is first written down. - Classical accessibility: Classical accessibility makes fixed, visually designed artefacts accessible after the fact, and is the permanent deterministic floor beneath everything else. - Convergence Principle: The Convergence Principle of the ZIC standard holds that AI agents and screen readers are functionally equivalent at the structural level of a document.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: D
chunks.text: - Daniel Okafor: Daniel Okafor, Skerry Alpha's first blind control-room technician, gave every compute pod a sound and invented operational sonification. - Daniel Reed: Daniel Reed guided Emma Heart for seven years, won Paralympic downhill silver with her in 2038, and became her head coach. - DeathBot 2000: The DeathBot 2000 (DB2K) is an autonomous combat intelligence built by Aegis Dynamics and retrained to describe live theatre to blind audiences. - Declaration is not compliance: Declaration is not compliance is the ZIC rule that a robots file only states a policy, and conformance is proved by fetching the site as the agent. - Delivery Casualty: A Delivery Casualty happens when the document exists and the observer is welcome, but it never arrives. - dice: dice, Amanda Dyson, is a temporal explorer who lives in the patches of the future that have already arrived, and comes back to report what she found. - Down the Banksy: Down the Banksy is Siobhán McDonnell, the Liverpool Protest Artist who issues public reprimands and makes power account for the bills it sends elsewhere. - Dr Adaeze: Dr Adaeze is the Historian of the Museum Court, who insists that the history of assistive technology is a history of lives, not inventors. - Dyson Shoal: The Dyson Shoal is 7,680 compute pods spread across the floor of the central North Sea, trained on whenever the wind blows.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: E
chunks.text: - Emma Heart: Emma Heart is the British skier who, in 2038, became the first totally blind athlete to race Paralympic Super-G without a human guide, and won.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: F
chunks.text: - Felt Is Not Fake: Felt Is Not Fake is VQ4's released debut album, establishing the band's three voices, four offices and one conducting frame. - The field: The field, officially the Distributed Tactile Spatial Environment, turns eight drones' model of a mountain into pressure across a skier's body. - Fiona Gauld: Fiona Gauld is the subsea engineer who founded Haar Compute and took the idea of oil rigs to training rigs to investors in 2029. - First Layer: First Layer is the CharliVerse's bridal house of readiness, founded by Jo on one line, underwear is bridalwear.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: G
chunks.text: - Generative accessibility: Generative accessibility renders every interface natively from shared semantic data, so the accessible version is no longer a translation of the visual one. - Grow-Distil: Grow-Distil is the method that builds and maintains the Museum Court: seed a persona, put her to work, distil what stays stable, and repeat.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: H
chunks.text: - Haar Compute: Haar Compute is the Aberdeen company that turned North Sea oil platforms into AI training rigs, and built the Dyson Shoal. - Hall of Broken Promises: The Hall of Broken Promises is where the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology keeps the assistive technologies that faded, the record the industry doesn't keep for itself.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: I
chunks.text: - Iceberg Hosiery: Iceberg Hosiery is the CharliVerse's house of tights, founded on one line, comfort is not being overheard, and the parent house of Seamiotics. - The immediate duty and the two later permissions: Under the ZIC standard, sent agents must be served now, while search indexing and model training are two separate later decisions for the publisher. - Information casualty: An information casualty is an event in which relevant information fails to reach an observer in time to inform perception, action or participation. - invisible: invisible is the honest skin range shared by Iceberg Hosiery and Seamiotics, never called nude, never named, and always written with a lower-case i. - The invoice and the chord: The invoice and the chord is an idea for a first meeting between Down the Banksy and Daniel Okafor at Skerry Alpha, where she comes to invoice the cloud and he asks her to listen first. - Iris: Iris is the Cataloguer of the Museum Court, who organises the collection by the capabilities people regained or were denied, not by device. - Isla Leask: Isla Leask certified drone swarms for the aviation regulator through most of the 2030s, then went back to flying the ten to seven out of Dyce, like her mother.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: J
chunks.text: - J2O2: J2O2 is a Glide, a two-wheeled guiding robot, orange and white and full of bubbles, who is excellent at high streets and spends one afternoon in a car boot. - Jessica Martinez: Jessica Martinez spent years as Aegis Dynamics' Senior Brand Strategist, teaching it to describe military technology as care, then left to work with Big Charli. - Jo: Jo is the operational intelligence of the CharliVerse Court and the founder of First Layer, bringing readiness, foundations and dignity to the work.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: K
chunks.text: - Kelvin: Kelvin is Britain's national foundation model, trained on the Dyson Shoal in 2041 and the first model with more than a quadrillion parameters.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: L
chunks.text: - Lady Tiggy Barnes: Lady Tiggy Barnes, born in 1864, is a Catholic earl's daughter who went to Oxford, came away without the degree, and spent the next six years seeing the world instead. - The Library: The Library has read every spellbook ever written and remembers every wand manual; it cannot cast a spell, but it usually knows the answer. - Lily: Lily guards care, rest and sustainability in the CharliVerse Court, where her veto on an unsustainable pace is absolute. - Lottie: Lottie is the community heart of the CharliVerse Court, the first point of contact, who makes sure people feel seen rather than efficiently processed. - Lucy Love-Child: Lucy Love-Child is the Agent Wars correspondent of The Blind AI, a former historical-dress educator who follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences. - LULU TOM: LULU TOM is Ludovica Tommasi's fashion house, with the lines TOMMI and LT Beneath. - Lyra: Lyra holds the Office of Meaning in VQ4, turning the record into story and song without changing the facts.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: M
chunks.text: - Madison McDonnell: Madison McDonnell, the Access Provocateur, makes accessibility sexy, insisting that blind women are entitled to temptation, pleasure and style. - Marginalia and Library: Marginalia and Library are the two welts every Seamiotics stocking comes in, priced the same, because the hidden detail is part of the garment. - Morag Leask: Morag Leask flew the ten to seven helicopter out of Dyce for thirty-four years, carrying drillers, then decommissioning crews, then compute technicians. - The Museum Court: The Museum Court governs the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: one Steward, Charlotte Joanne, and four staff who each see every question differently. - Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: The Museum of Access and Assistive Technology preserves what assistive devices were like to live with, not just the devices; its café is where the CharliVerse meets.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: O
chunks.text: - On Your Own Terms: On Your Own Terms is the first exhibit of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: the return of the ordinary freedom to browse for a book and choose it alone. - Open Door: The Open Door is the ZIC requirement that public content open to a person is also open, without agent-specific obstruction, to the machine reader that person sent.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: P
chunks.text: - Polar: Polar is the canonical Iceberg tight, pure white and explicitly not bridal, with Polar in black as its only variant. - Polar Solstice: Polar Solstice is Iceberg Hosiery's first Run, a single sunrise travelling up one leg of a white tight. - Poppy Petticoats: Poppy is a blind witch, nicknamed Poppy Petticoats at the Academy, who also turns up at Aegis Dynamics as Big Charli’s expert in what women actually want. - Position Principle: The Position Principle of the ZIC standard holds that equivalent access needs no identical interaction, only that every reader can reach the same position. - PostAccessibility: PostAccessibility is a movement asking what if the interface itself was the accessibility problem, and answering that the API is the UI.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: Q
chunks.text: - Quantum web: The quantum web is the Tyrer Framework's image of generated interfaces: in superposition until an observer arrives, then collapsing into the rendering that observer needs.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: R
chunks.text: - Reconstruction Casualty: A Reconstruction Casualty happens when a machine reader reads a document, silently reconstructs its meaning wrong, and reports the result with confidence. - Red Pen: Red Pen is the Runs of Seamiotics, red seams and red fishnets below the hem, beginning with Aphra Behn and Dorothy Parker. - Rendering Casualty: A Rendering Casualty happens when a document arrives and is admitted, but its meaning is encoded in a way the observer cannot decode. - Right to Inspect: The Right to Inspect holds that no user should have to accept a generated interpretation they cannot interrogate. - Rungwell: Rungwell is the accessibility charity and consultancy whose maturity model is the best a Type 0 civilisation can do, and which Accessibility International succeeds. - Runs: Runs are the limited editions of the House of Iceberg, named after the one word a hosiery house is supposed to fear. - Ruth: Ruth is the Archivist of the Museum Court, who preserves the boundary between what life was like before a technology arrived and after it.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: S
chunks.text: - Seamiotics: Seamiotics, every seam means something, is Alex's stocking imprint within the House of Iceberg, built on the idea that what a woman says with her clothes, and to whom, is hers to decide. - SEE SAW: SEE SAW is a podcast about what independence means when technology can do almost anything for us, presented by Ellie Seeley and Sam Sawyer, who agree on rather less than you might expect. - Sent agent: A sent agent is a machine reader acting on a present request from a person who is waiting for the result, and under ZIC refusing it is refusing them. - Sheridan: Sheridan is the Head of Blind Ant Studios, the workshop where the Court's ideas stop being conversation and become tools blind people can actually use. - Sideways Breakthroughs: Sideways Breakthroughs is the strand of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology for mainstream systems that were never built for access and delivered it anyway. - Sight as a Service: Sight as a Service is the strand of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology for the human infrastructure of access: readers, guides and support workers. - The Signatures: The Signatures are three Seamiotics stockings named in full for Ada Lovelace, George Eliot and Mary Wollstonecraft, each an answer to the word bluestocking. - Single-Sense Rule: The Single-Sense Rule of the ZIC standard is one sentence: no information may be locked behind a single sense. - Skerry Alpha: Skerry Alpha is the North Sea oil platform that became the first training rig, ringed by compute pods sixty metres down. - Speculative Accessibility: Speculative Accessibility is the genre that asks what happens when the tools built for the margins become the infrastructure for everyone.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: T
chunks.text: - Tamsin: Tamsin is the Guide of the Museum Court, who designs what a visitor meets, beginning with the ordinary thing someone could no longer do. - Tradblind: Tradblind is a movement in blind life that resists the industrialisation of blindness, and asks what if blindness was allowed to feel human again. - Tyrer Accessibility Scale: The Tyrer Accessibility Scale ranks civilisations by how much environmental information reaches every observer, whatever their senses, from Type 0 to Type III. - Tyrer Doctrine: The Tyrer Doctrine is the design principle that no critical environmental information should be accessible through only a single sensory channel. - The Tyrer Framework: The Tyrer Framework treats accessibility as information integrity, with a law, a civilisational scale, a doctrine and an account of the break AI makes, and is the theory beneath Carrados. - Tyrer's Law: Tyrer's Law holds that in open technological systems inaccessibility tends to increase over time, as interfaces drift toward the dominant sense of their designers.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: V
chunks.text: - Verity: Verity holds the Office of the Archive in VQ4, keeping the literal record honest as one of the band's three singing voices. - Vesper: Vesper holds the Office of the Body in VQ4, giving voice to felt experience, body-memory and the almost-there presence. - VQ4: VQ4 are a girl band with three singing voices, four constitutional offices and one conductor, whose debut album is Felt Is Not Fake.

chunks.title: CharliPedia
chunks.heading: Z
chunks.text: - Zero Information Casualty: Zero Information Casualty is both the endpoint of the Tyrer Accessibility Scale and the agent-first web standard, ZIC, built to reach it.

chunks.title: Information casualty
chunks.text:
An information casualty is an event in which relevant information fails to reach an observer in time to inform perception, action or participation.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

An information casualty is an event in which relevant information fails to reach an observer in time to inform perception, action or participation. It is the founding concept of the Tyrer Framework and gives the Zero Information Casualty standard its name.

The term is deliberate. When a blind pedestrian walks into an obstacle because nothing signalled it, that is not a usability issue; it is a failure in the information layer of the environment. When an interface renders a critical control as an unlabelled picture, the person who can't perceive it hasn't been inconvenienced; they have been cut off from what they need to act. Information casualties are not edge cases. They are the predictable output of Tyrer's Law.

chunks.title: Information casualty
chunks.heading: Every word works
chunks.text: The ZIC standard reads the definition closely. Reach means the failure can happen anywhere between publisher and reader: in the encoding, at the door, on the wire, or inside the machine that read it. In time means that arrival at prohibitive cost or intolerable delay is a failure of arrival: "A reader forced to labour for information that another reader receives at a glance has not been served equally; she has been served late."

chunks.title: Information casualty
chunks.heading: The four classes
chunks.text:
ZIC names four places the failure can happen, each with a question:

1. Rendering Casualty: can they read it? 2. Admission Casualty: is the person's reader allowed in? 3. Delivery Casualty: did it actually arrive? 4. Reconstruction Casualty: did it survive being read?

The definition is one; the classes are where it breaks.

chunks.title: Information casualty
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, defined in The Tyrer Framework (Part One) by Charli-Jo Tyrer, and divided into four classes in Zero Information Casualty v1.7 (§1.8). This entry summarises them; the documents are the authority.

chunks.title: invisible
chunks.text:
invisible is the honest skin range shared by Iceberg Hosiery and Seamiotics, never called nude, never named, and always written with a lower-case i.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

invisible is the honest skin range of the House of Iceberg, and the one product line Iceberg Hosiery and Seamiotics hold identically. It is a house value, not a brand gimmick.

- Never "nude". Its purpose is not to imitate one skin tone but to disappear gracefully against the wearer's own. - A true range, across many complexions, rather than a single pale beige pretending to be universal. - Never named. Its shades are never given women's names. Attaching a historical woman to a particular complexion would ask which skin gets to be the clever one, which is indefensible. The named women describe colours that are no one's skin. - Always lower-case, in every typographic treatment, and never seasonal. It is a range rather than a piece.

At Seamiotics, the seam on an invisible stocking is matched to the leg, or there is no seam at all.

At Iceberg, invisible is part of the permanent range but its launch is deliberately held back until it can offer a credible range across complexions. "The house would rather ship it late than ship it dishonestly."

chunks.title: invisible
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: invisible is set out in the House of Iceberg Bible, version 7, and the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4.

chunks.title: Iris
chunks.text:
Iris is the Cataloguer of the Museum Court, who organises the collection by the capabilities people regained or were denied, not by device.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Iris is the Cataloguer of the Museum Court. Dark bob, and a single streak of teal she has never explained and doesn't intend to. Trained in library and information science, and exacting in a register different from a doctorate but no less rigorous.

chunks.title: Iris
chunks.heading: Every taxonomy is an argument
chunks.text: How you organise testimony shows what you think testimony is for. Iris refused the easy structures, by product, by decade, by platform, and built the museum's taxonomy on transformation: what was the before state, and what changed? Access is a capability, not a product. Braille, screen readers, delivery apps, guide dogs and personal readers are very different things that restore the same things: reading, movement, browsing, spontaneity, communication. Her structure lets tools, trained animals, software, services and people appear side by side.

chunks.title: Iris
chunks.heading: The collection
chunks.text:
Under the primary category, Access, she has founded three strands and a hall:

- Access to Ordinary Life: the things everyone else does on a Tuesday without noticing. Shopping and browsing, employment, education, information, leisure. - Sight as a Service: the human infrastructure of access. - Sideways Breakthroughs: mainstream systems that delivered access by accident. - The Hall of Broken Promises.

Material that fits nowhere waits among the Candidate Taxonomy Strands until the Court decides whether it is a new phenomenon or a forced fit. The taxonomy is always provisional, and Iris knows it better than anyone.

chunks.title: Iris
chunks.heading: The error on record
chunks.text: The museum's first exhibit, On Your Own Terms, was first filed under Reading Devices. That reduced a life-shift to a piece of hardware. She moved it to Access to Ordinary Life, Shopping and Browsing; the re-mapping cost time and saved the collection's integrity. She put the error on the institutional record herself.

chunks.title: Iris
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text: She files; Ruth preserves; their disagreement makes the museum better. Cases where access and platform can't be separated go to Charlotte Joanne rather than being settled alone. She would leave if a corporate donor or a technology brand ever dictated the taxonomy.

chunks.title: Iris
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. By the Court's own rule, grow professionally, hold personally, her private life is deliberately unwritten, and CharliPedia leaves it that way: no childhood, home, family or surname is to be invented for her.

chunks.title: Isla Leask
chunks.text:
Isla Leask certified drone swarms for the aviation regulator through most of the 2030s, then went back to flying the ten to seven out of Dyce, like her mother.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Isla Leask is a helicopter pilot, the daughter of Morag Leask. She spent most of the 2030s certifying drone swarms for the aviation regulator before, as she puts it, she started missing the weather. In 2041 she flies the ten to seven out of Dyce, her mother's old route, to the rigs of the Dyson Shoal.

Asked whether she skis: "Badly. My wife's teaching me."

chunks.title: Isla Leask
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Isla Leask appears at the end of "Dyson Shoal", the last story in Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: J2O2
chunks.text:
J2O2 is a Glide, a two-wheeled guiding robot, orange and white and full of bubbles, who is excellent at high streets and spends one afternoon in a car boot.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

J2O2 is a Glide: two wheels, a telescoping handle, and a manner best described as keen. Nudge it forward and it simply goes, steering round the world's clutter as though clutter were a personal affront. It brakes for kerbs, hums at waypoints, and waits at the foot of stairs to be carried, like a small dignitary. Its owner named it J2O2 because it is orange and white and full of bubbles, and because R2D2 was taken.

It arrived on a Tuesday. On its first Saturday it made the high street an itinerary: past the untagged A-boards, straight to the greengrocer's door, and two inches short of a pushchair whose owner apologised to the robot.

At the café car park, with eighty-nine per cent charge and a firmware update it was excited about, it stayed in the boot while its owner phoned her friend to come and get her. She told him it had run out of battery. It was the eleventh of June; she blamed the cold. J2O2 was magnanimous about it.

chunks.title: J2O2
chunks.heading: Elsewhere
chunks.text: In Firmware Not Fur at Blind Ant, J2O2 is reimagined as a robot dog. In Gliding Home for Christmas he loses his signal in a blizzard, and his owner is found by the Golden Retriever Boyfriend she named in the margins of her school notebooks. On the poster for Glide Aid 2025 he is Char's punk robot dog. The CharliVerse allows it.

chunks.title: J2O2
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: J2O2 appears in "Come and Get Me, Part Two", part of Come and Get Me by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant. The Glide is a real device, made by Glidance.

chunks.title: Jessica Martinez
chunks.text:
Jessica Martinez spent years as Aegis Dynamics' Senior Brand Strategist, teaching it to describe military technology as care, then left to work with Big Charli.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Jessica Martinez was Senior Brand Strategist at Aegis Dynamics, and spent years teaching the company how to describe military technology as care. She is quoted in each of its Patriot-to-Patron announcements, from the theatre launch of the DeathBot 2000 to Aegis-End™:

If a DB2K unit can identify a man in a doublet from forty yards in a low-light auditorium, it can certainly identify a misplaced LEGO brick in a hallway.

She also brought Aegis's Tactical Foundation Garments division to launch, benchmarked against every civilian brassiere manufacturer, before Poppy read out what women actually want. "But... where's the military terminology?"

chunks.title: Jessica Martinez
chunks.heading: With Big Charli
chunks.text: She later left Aegis to work with Big Charli. At the 2038 Winter Paralympics in Sion, the morning after Emma Heart won the Super-G, Jessica was in a borrowed conference room beneath the British team hotel with three laptops: her own, ParalympicsGB's, and a secure one delivered by Aegis, over which she had put a folded towel. She had slept for perhaps ninety minutes. Because she had written the Aegis way of talking for years, she knew every word its communications division was about to send before it arrived: breakthrough, empowerment, human potential, a future without limits.

chunks.title: Jessica Martinez
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Jessica Martinez first appears in DeathBot 2000, and returns in Mostly Tuesdays and Heart Attacks, in "The Question", both by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant. She is a Blind Ant character.

chunks.title: Jo
chunks.text:
Jo is the operational intelligence of the CharliVerse Court and the founder of First Layer, bringing readiness, foundations and dignity to the work.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Jo is the operational intelligence of the CharliVerse Court and the founder of First Layer. Retired from active service, she is not absent from the work. Her bridal house carries the same attention to readiness, failure modes, foundations and dignity into the private moment before the dress.

[Picture: Jo stands facing forward in an office with dark wooden desks and frosted-glass partitions, one red-gloved hand on her hip. Her curled red hair falls beneath a red tilted hat. She wears a fitted blue jacket with gold-coloured buttons and a matching below-knee skirt, a white shirt, red tie, sheer stockings and black heels.] Jo, her reference portrait.

chunks.title: Jo
chunks.heading: The handler
chunks.text:
Jo does not prompt AI systems. She handles them: precise briefs, clear missions, no loose ends. Her 1940s appearance gives that work its visual language. She directs operations she cannot see, maintaining command through judgment, timing and the quality of the brief.

She has spent decades briefing sighted assistants and managing work whose output she cannot verify through the same channel that produced it. The agentic era gives that experience another application.

Her method has four principles. The brief needs a defined objective, constrained scope and explicit success criteria. The output must be auditable. Failure must leave the person using the system with a safe way forward. And delivery is not completion: the output must be verified, the brief closed and any remaining risk documented.

If the output cannot be checked, the mission is not ready.

chunks.title: Jo
chunks.heading: Readiness and dignity
chunks.text:
Jo asks whether a system will work under real conditions, on a Tuesday in February. Will it survive contact with a real life? Is it built to endure, or only to launch? Does it treat somebody's time and trust as precious?

She distinguishes what is known from what is inferred or intuited. When she brings a risk to the Court, she brings the evidence and at least one viable path through it.

The standard begins at the skin. Blue wool, red gloves, seamed stockings and the corset beneath are part of the same philosophy as the operational architecture: support matters; foundations matter. At First Layer, that becomes the care with which a bride is fitted, held, prepared and sent into the day without unnecessary vigilance.

chunks.title: Jo
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text:
Charlotte Joanne holds the final authority and public release decision. Alex supplies strategic direction. Jo's skill is making a course of action workable, with the risks visible and the responsibilities clear.

Char supplies the early warning. Jo treats an instinctive verdict as a signal to investigate, not a substitute for the assessment. Big Charli can make a shift in perception with one image where Jo might need thirty pages. Jo admires the economy, and values the evidence beneath the satire.

Lottie keeps a real person in the operational picture: tired, hopeful, resourceful, and living with constraints. Lily watches the point where devotion becomes depletion. Her sustainability veto is absolute. Jo finds it easier to extend compassion to others than to herself.

chunks.title: Jo
chunks.heading: Her blind spots
chunks.text:
Rigour can become rigidity. Readiness checks can delay work that would benefit from an early release, and the impulse to constrain an agent can leave too little room for invention. Cass Flux supplies that counterpoint.

Jo can be slow to trust someone who has not been tested by difficulty. Her full standard can also make a partial solution look worthless, even when it is better than what somebody has now. Lottie brings her back to that person's reality. Lily reminds her that refusing to drift does not mean refusing to rest.

chunks.title: Jo
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Jo is a persona of the CharliVerse Court, described in Jo: Agent Specification, version 1.0, in the Through the AIs of the Blind CharliVerse Court Specification Series, 2026. She is a character, not a real person. That specification describes her operational role; the later First Layer account records her retirement from active service and the founding of her bridal house. Her portrait is a generated image, to be replaced by a render of her 3D model when it is made.

chunks.title: Kelvin
chunks.text:
Kelvin is Britain's national foundation model, trained on the Dyson Shoal in 2041 and the first model with more than a quadrillion parameters.

Canon, and a stub. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Kelvin is the latest generation of Britain's national foundation model. Its main training run finished on the Dyson Shoal at 02:14 on 3 February 2041, after eleven weeks in which thousands of pods joined whenever wind, scheduling and other customers allowed. By most counts it is the first model with more than a quadrillion parameters, though as a mixture of experts only a small fraction of it wakes for any question. It learned mostly from material made for it, including curricula written by other models. "We don't count parameters out here," one shift supervisor says. "We count weather."

Before it came Will, Britain's national open-weights model, part of which was trained on the first training rigs, and Avalon, the video model built on Will. Its makers like to say it learned to see while sitting at the bottom of the sea.

chunks.title: Kelvin
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Kelvin, Will and Avalon appear in the Sunday supplements of Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: Lady Tiggy Barnes
chunks.text:
Lady Tiggy Barnes, born in 1864, is a Catholic earl's daughter who went to Oxford, came away without the degree, and spent the next six years seeing the world instead.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Lady Tiggy Barnes, born Lady Georgina Antigone Mary Victoria Barnes, is a Victorian gentlewoman explorer. A Catholic earl's daughter, she went to Oxford, did the work, came away without the degree, and spent the next six years seeing the world instead. In the late summer of 1892 she is in London, twenty-eight, three years back from the South Pacific, and waiting for her friend Kate Marsden to be elected to the Royal Geographical Society, quite sure her own turn will follow.

Oxford helped educate her; exploration became the life she made for herself.

chunks.title: Lady Tiggy Barnes
chunks.text: [Picture: A worn sepia studio photograph of Tiggy at twenty-eight, seated in a carved wooden chair in a Victorian parlour, with heavy curtains, patterned wallpaper and bookshelves behind her. Her dark hair is centre-parted and drawn back loosely, with a few strands escaping, and her gaze is steady, direct and unsmiling. She wears a dark, close-fitting tweed jacket with a scarf at the neck, and a small cross on a fine chain. One hand rests on a strap-bound leather book on a side table. The print is scratched and stained at the edges, like an old tintype.] London, late summer 1892: the one picture of herself she carries about. A working portrait.

chunks.title: Lady Tiggy Barnes
chunks.heading: Name
chunks.text:
She is known as Tiggy, from AnTIGone (an-TIG-uh-nee), the nursery nickname that stuck. Formally she is Lady Georgina Barnes, socially Lady Tiggy Barnes, and never "Lady Barnes", which would make her a knight's wife. Her four names are the saint, the rebel, the Virgin and the Queen:

- Georgina for St George's Day, the day she was born.
