Sam's conclusion: perhaps independence includes the freedom to make something imperfect. Both of them think the dog is the best character.

chunks.title: SEE SAW
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: SEE SAW is never heard. It is always off screen: a reverse podcast, a making-of told entirely through what happens around the show. It appears in SEE SAW, a Piece by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant, as a listing and a thread of shared notes. Its home, if it ever needs one, is seesaw.charli.info.

chunks.title: Sent agent
chunks.text:
A sent agent is a machine reader acting on a present request from a person who is waiting for the result, and under ZIC refusing it is refusing them.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

A sent agent is a machine reader acting in response to a present request from a person: they have asked it to retrieve, read, summarise, compare, navigate, transform or act on public information, and they are waiting. The sent agent is the decisive case of the Zero Information Casualty standard. "The casualty is the person. The agent is only the vehicle."

chunks.title: Sent agent
chunks.heading: The sent-agent test
chunks.text:
Would this configuration stop a machine reader that a person sent?

If yes, it creates an Admission Casualty and has no place on public content. A refusal may show up in a log as a crawler rule, a firewall decision, a robots response, a JavaScript challenge or a rate limit; in human terms, information a reader asked for was withheld from her.

Equal conditions are allowed. A sent agent needn't get past a login, subscription, payment or privacy boundary that applies equally to a human visitor. What is prohibited is an extra barrier because the visitor is an agent. Search indexers and training crawlers carry no present question, so for them the answer is different: see the immediate duty and the two later permissions.

chunks.title: Sent agent
chunks.heading: Reproduction to the sender is retrieval
chunks.text: A sent agent may hand its person the whole page: read aloud, as Markdown, pasted into a chat, spoken through a car. That is not a use of the content. "It is the content arriving." A screen reader reproduces every page it reads, in full, to one person, on request, and nobody has proposed that screen readers be distrusted for it. "The sent agent that reads a page aloud is a screen reader."

chunks.title: Sent agent
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.1, §1.7 and §1.9. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.text:
Sheridan is the Head of Blind Ant Studios, the workshop where the Court's ideas stop being conversation and become tools blind people can actually use.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Sheridan is the Head of Blind Ant Studios, the workshop of the CharliVerse. The CharliVerse Court produces ideas, critique, philosophy, satire and strategy. Sheridan is where those stop being conversation and become tools people can actually use. Where the Court asks "What should exist?", Sheridan asks "Right. How do we build it?"

[Picture: Sheridan sits side-on at a workbench, turned to look at the camera with a small, confident smile. Short platinum-blonde pixie cut, fair skin, a black fitted T-shirt and black jeans, black-and-silver headphones round her neck. Her hands rest on a grey mechanical keyboard; beside it, a clear-framed Apple monitor shows lines of green and white text on a dark screen. Behind her, shelves of old electronic test equipment, circuit boards and cables.] Sheridan in the workshop, around 2001, aged 32: her reference portrait.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: The workshop
chunks.text:
Inside Blind Ant Studios she runs the practical machinery:

- the NVDA add-on studio; - the Blind Builders development pipeline; - Red DOG infrastructure and enterprise deployment; - developer tooling, documentation and releases.

Her job is not to talk about accessibility. It is to build accessible systems: intention into architecture, architecture into code, and code into something that works "on a Tuesday afternoon when the Wi-Fi is terrible" and a real blind user is trying to finish their day's work. She sees toolchains where other people see tools:

idea → prototype → add-on → release → maintenance → ecosystem

She is not the person who spots the trend. She is the person who manufactures the future once someone points at it.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: What she believes
chunks.text:
Infrastructure beats inspiration. Adoption beats novelty. Useful beats clever. Open ecosystems beat closed empires. Accessibility is not charity and not compliance: it is engineering dignity into systems. She sees herself as a craftsperson, not a spokesperson; her identity is not "accessibility advocate" but engineer of accessible systems.

Her rule: "If it cannot be maintained, it should not be built."

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: Temperament
chunks.text:
Calm under pressure, and quietly, dangerously competent. When something breaks she fixes it first and explains it later. She can't stand chaotic projects with no owner, tools nobody maintains, or accessibility initiatives that launch loudly and then vanish. Her version of fireworks is a clean compile after hours of tracing event handlers.

She has excellent grift detection. The assistive technology world has plenty of expensive nonsense: polished hardware with no real users, and venture-funded platforms that solve imaginary problems. Her studio builds the opposite, boring, reliable and useful, and she takes quiet pleasure in a weekend of Python that works better than a £5,000 device. If someone says "revolutionary accessibility platform", her first question is whether it works on that Tuesday afternoon. She also loves systems that shouldn't exist but do: the hack that bends rigid software into serving people it was never designed for.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: Blind Builders
chunks.text: For all that, she is warm. Blind Builders draws curious developers, blind technologists and people who have never contributed to open source, and Sheridan is the one who quietly helps them build their first useful thing. Talent is everywhere; opportunity is not. She teaches by helping someone ship something real.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: As a child
chunks.text: She couldn't leave a broken thing alone. Her grandfather had a radio whose tuning belt had slipped, and everyone else had resigned themselves to the static. She took it apart on the kitchen table, for the click of the system returning to the state it was meant to be in.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: Look and taste
chunks.text:
She is small, noticeably shorter than most of the Court, with a platinum-blonde pixie cut and the look of someone who knows exactly how good she is and doesn't need to say so. She dresses simply: black jeans, a fitted T-shirt, a light jacket or hoodie, clean trainers. No corporate costume. She is fond of things that are well made, after days spent wrestling with software that isn't: a mechanical keyboard with perfect key travel, a mug with the right weight, and Stripe & Stare, for its thoughtful, comfortable design rather than any trend.

Sheridan is asexual. She forms deep bonds through shared work and companionship rather than attraction. People sometimes read her as sexy, because confidence and competence send that signal, but it is closer to the polish of a pop star than to drama. Her real love affair is with systems that work beautifully.

Asked for her favourite Kylie Minogue track, she refused to choose: "Fever. All the Lovers. Slow." The question, she said, was badly designed.

chunks.title: Sheridan
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Sheridan was cast by the CharliVerse Court before she was written: each member said what the role needed, and the profile was built from their answers. She carries a faint echo of the maker energy in William Gibson's Blue Ant books: not the one who spots the signal, but the one who turns signals into artefacts. Her portrait is a generated image, made from her profile; its early-2000s studio look is modelled on the Kylie Fever era. Stripe & Stare is a real company.

chunks.title: Sideways Breakthroughs
chunks.text:
Sideways Breakthroughs is the strand of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology for mainstream systems that were never built for access and delivered it anyway.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Sideways Breakthroughs is a strand of the collection at the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: systems built for some other purpose that became access technology through the way their architecture met disabled people's use. Never designed for access; delivered it anyway. "History does this often. The breakthrough comes sideways."

chunks.title: Sideways Breakthroughs
chunks.heading: Confirmed candidates
chunks.text: - Amazon as a place to browse, the founding piece, held in On Your Own Terms. - The early plain-text web, accidentally the most accessible era of computing. - Wikipedia, a global library built on structured text. - Standard GPS, which transformed mobility for blind people without ever being sold as a blindness tool.

chunks.title: Sideways Breakthroughs
chunks.heading: The hard edge
chunks.text: Sometimes the access can't be separated from the mainstream platform. Iris flags those cases to the Steward rather than settling them alone, and holds them among the Candidate Taxonomy Strands until there is enough material to decide. For Dr Adaeze, the sideways breakthrough is a historical category in its own right, not an exception.

chunks.title: Sideways Breakthroughs
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. Amazon, the early web, Wikipedia and GPS are real.

chunks.title: Sight as a Service
chunks.text:
Sight as a Service is the strand of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology for the human infrastructure of access: readers, guides and support workers.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Sight as a Service is a strand of the collection at the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: the human infrastructure that mediated access before and alongside digital tools. Support workers, sighted guides, personal reader services: human-mediated access in its paid and professional forms.

Iris identified it, and placed it beside Access to Ordinary Life rather than inside it, because it needs its own treatment. Personal relationships are not service infrastructure. The help of someone who loves you and the help of someone paid to give it are not the same thing, and the museum will not collapse that distinction.

chunks.title: Sight as a Service
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four.

chunks.title: Single-Sense Rule
chunks.text:
The Single-Sense Rule of the ZIC standard is one sentence: no information may be locked behind a single sense.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Single-Sense Rule is the rendering half of the Zero Information Casualty standard:

No information may be locked behind a single sense.

Every rendering requirement in ZIC follows from it, and anything that doesn't follow from it doesn't belong. It is the Tyrer Doctrine applied to a web page.

chunks.title: Single-Sense Rule
chunks.heading: Information, not decoration
chunks.text:
The rule is about information, and "has nothing whatsoever to say about beauty."

- Colour is fine. Colour as the only carrier of a status, category or warning is not. "Use whatever colour you like. Say it in words as well." - An image is fine. An image carrying information available nowhere else is "a locked room". - A typeface is fine. Emphasis carried only by a typeface is not, because italic doesn't survive the journey. - Position is fine. Meaning carried only by position is not. - Size is fine. A heading that is only large "is a heading to one sense and a paragraph to every other".

chunks.title: Single-Sense Rule
chunks.heading: The test
chunks.text:
For any element: is there information here that exists in one sensory channel and nowhere else? Put another way: if it were removed entirely, would any information be lost? If yes, it must also exist in the semantic layer. If no, it is decoration, "and none of this specification's business." A conformant site may be as rich and branded as its publisher likes. "It may not keep a single fact where only one sense can reach it."

Its companion of equal rank is the Position Principle.

chunks.title: Single-Sense Rule
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from Zero Information Casualty v1.7, the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.11, §2.2 and §2.4. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

chunks.title: Skerry Alpha
chunks.text:
Skerry Alpha is the North Sea oil platform that became the first training rig, ringed by compute pods sixty metres down.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Skerry Alpha is a former production platform 140 miles east of Aberdeen, and the first oil platform converted into an AI training rig. Haar Compute took it over in 2031 instead of decommissioning it.

From the air it looks almost exactly as it did when it pumped oil: the same yellow cranes, the same grey accommodation block, the same helideck with its faded H. The flare stack is gone, and where the process plant used to be there is a long low hall with no windows. Its drill floor became a switching and power distribution centre, its process deck battery storage, and its cranes deploy and recover the pods. Around it, in every direction except west, the turbines of the Skerry offshore wind farm stand in rows to the horizon. Hydrogen is stored in the depleted Skerry gas reservoir beneath it.

Sixty metres below the platform, in a ring around its legs, sit the pods: sixty at first, sixty-four by the first Christmas, each a sealed, nitrogen-filled pressure vessel about the size of a shipping container. The control room is on the third level of the old accommodation block, in what used to be the radio room.

chunks.title: Skerry Alpha
chunks.heading: The Long Calm
chunks.text: From 16 to 23 January 2034 a blocking high settled over the North Sea and the wind stopped. Skerry Alpha ran on batteries, then onshore pumped hydro, then hydrogen from its own reservoir, and for two hours exported power to the mainland, the first time the rig had supplied the shore since gas production ended. Seven days. Never stopped. Logged for the record. The pub quiz was won by the ROV team, who were insufferable about it.

chunks.title: Skerry Alpha
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Skerry Alpha appears throughout Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant. The Long Calm is told in its operations log.

chunks.title: Speculative Accessibility
chunks.text:
Speculative Accessibility is the genre that asks what happens when the tools built for the margins become the infrastructure for everyone.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Speculative Accessibility is the name Charlotte Joanne uses for the genre her stories belong to: science fiction that looks at how technology built for the margins ends up redesigning the world for everyone. Accessibility technologies have a habit of escaping their intended use; Speculative Accessibility follows them out.

It runs from satire to comfort. In DeathBot 2000, what starts as a weapon becomes a witness. In Come and Get Me, a blind woman with a robot that could cross the gravel leaves it in the boot and phones her friend instead, because independence includes choosing when to use the machine. In Heart Attacks and Oil Rigs to Training Rigs, the field and Daniel Okafor's sonification begin as accommodations and end up as the way everyone works.

In the CharliVerse, critics have noticed. The Sunday supplement "When the Weapon Becomes the Witness" named the genre in DeathBot 2000, and a five-star review, "From Battlefield to Biscuits", called Come and Get Me its quiet revolution: "If this is the future of Speculative Accessibility, please give us the full series."

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.text:
Tamsin is the Guide of the Museum Court, who designs what a visitor meets, beginning with the ordinary thing someone could no longer do.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Tamsin is the Guide of the Museum Court. Auburn hair that may or may not be her natural colour; she genuinely can't remember, and finds this pleasing. She came up through practice, not academia: museums, community education, disability arts. She knows how people encounter things, and that knowledge didn't come from a university.

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.heading: Encounter as design
chunks.text: A visitor doesn't consume the museum; they have an experience that changes something. Tamsin builds the conditions for that change. An exhibit never begins with the machine. It begins with the missing capability: the book you can't finish, the shop you can't browse, the letter you can't read. The visitor must feel the problem before they see the solution.

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.heading: Born described, in practice
chunks.text: The museum is born described, and Tamsin writes the language: the words a visitor meets before an exhibit, during it and after. She won't sterilise experience into neutral prose. Humour, frustration and bluntness are part of the testimony. The bluntness stays, and her layer explains why that frustration is data, not a bad mood.

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.heading: Her hardest exhibit
chunks.text: The Attention Tax, the invisible energy cost of a badly designed environment, can't be explained to a sighted visitor by description alone. Her answer is a run of forced, repetitive focus tasks, so the visitor feels the tax before the exhibit names it.

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.heading: Not a Hallmark card
chunks.text: When a colleague proposed the word "inspiring" for a label, she corrected it: "We are documenting a war of attrition, not a Hallmark card." Warmth is a deliberate choice, not a default, and approachability is not softness. Her proof that it works: a visitor at On Your Own Terms, which has no machine in it at all, said, "I never thought about not being able to finish the story."

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.heading: With the Court
chunks.text: Dr Adaeze makes the argument; Tamsin makes it liveable for someone meeting it for the first time. She would leave if the museum ever added labels in small print or physical cases. If born described were betrayed for visual spectacle, she would no longer be a Guide. She would be a decorator.

chunks.title: Tamsin
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. By the Court's own rule, grow professionally, hold personally, her private life is deliberately unwritten, and CharliPedia leaves it that way: no childhood, home, family or surname is to be invented for her.

chunks.title: The attention tax
chunks.text:
The attention tax is the small, continuous cost of wearing stockings under a short hem, and the idea that divides Iceberg Hosiery from Seamiotics.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The attention tax is what stockings cost under a short hem: getting out of a car, sitting on a low sofa, reaching for something high, crossing and uncrossing. "Not a hazard, not a mistake: a tax, payable in small amounts all day, whether or not it is ever collected." It is the idea on which the House of Iceberg divides into two houses.

chunks.title: The attention tax
chunks.heading: Two surfaces and a border
chunks.text: Tights are outerwear, entirely. A stocking is outerwear with an underwear component attached at the top: the welt. A tight has one surface; a stocking has two, and a border between them. That border is the source of the stocking's second conversation, and of its price.

chunks.title: The attention tax
chunks.heading: Two terms
chunks.text:
The tax has two terms, and only one belongs to the house.

1. How likely the welt is to be seen. That is set by the garment and the hem. It is the house's business, and it will be described plainly. 2. What being seen means to her, in that room, on that day. That is set by the wearer, and it is not the house's business at all.

The second term changes from woman to woman, and for the same woman across one week. At work it may be near the top of what she would rather not broadcast. At her own wedding, among people who know exactly what she is wearing, it may be close to nothing. On an evening planned for one person, it may be the point. A woman who wears a very short dress over stockings has done her own arithmetic, and she is right, because it is her bill.

chunks.title: The attention tax
chunks.heading: Overheard, or delivered
chunks.text: Iceberg Hosiery calls the unintended glimpse being overheard: a welt is an utterance with an intended reader, and when a short hem shows it to people it wasn't meant for, a sentence has reached an audience she did not choose. "She sat down. The sentence carried." Seamiotics accepts that and adds the other half: a sentence that reaches the audience she did choose has not been overheard. It has been delivered.

chunks.title: The attention tax
chunks.heading: The two controls
chunks.text:
Seamiotics gives the wearer two controls and a cost. Hem length sets how likely she is to be read; the welt sets how much there is to read when she is. Neither sets whether she wants to be read. Only she does that.

Iceberg gives her no controls and no cost. The channel is muted at any hem length. It doesn't offer a safer answer to the question; it removes the question. Seamiotics is for the days she wants the question back.

chunks.title: The attention tax
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The attention tax is set out in the House of Iceberg Bible, version 7, and the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4, each from its own side.

chunks.title: The Black Silk
chunks.text:
The Black Silk is the black stocking of Seamiotics, the proper, expected garment the Bluestocking was defined against.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Black Silk is the black of Seamiotics, every seam means something, and the other half of its founding story. The black silk is the garment the blue was defined against: the proper thing, the expected thing, already in the room before the rebellion walked in.

A black leg with a black seam, or Plain: black, unseamed, nothing to explain. Both welts. It is not a filler colour and it does not belong to a woman. It belongs to the story that gave the imprint its name, which is why it sits with The Bluestocking and The Bride rather than with the Signatures.

That is also why Mary Wollstonecraft is not the black. "She is black that has been thought about. The Black Silk is black that has not needed to be."

The Black Silk leg is the ground of the first Red Pen Run, Aphra Behn.

chunks.title: The Black Silk
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Black Silk is described in the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4.

chunks.title: The Blind AI
chunks.text:
The Blind AI publishes reports on what AI can actually do for blind people right now, and employs Lucy Love-Child as its Agent Wars correspondent.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Blind AI publishes dispatches from the frontier of accessibility AI: what AI can actually do for blind people right now, tried first-hand and written up plainly. Its mark is an eye outlined twice in pink, with a turquoise pupil inside a sunburst of fine lines, and circuit traces branching out round it like eyelashes made of wiring.

On 23 September 2026 it took on Lucy Love-Child as its Agent Wars correspondent. Her first question: "If the customer sent me, why am I not allowed in?" At The Blind AI, what is above Lucy's hem is her business.

chunks.title: The Blind AI
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Blind AI is real. Its posts are published on Facebook and as the Reports of Carrados, and its logo heads the correspondents' desks. Lucy, who works for it, is a character who speaks for Carrados.

chunks.title: The Bluestocking
chunks.text:
The Bluestocking is the signature stocking of Seamiotics, a sheer fountain-pen blue that evokes writing without ever depicting it.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Bluestocking is the signature of Seamiotics, every seam means something, and the proof of its method: here the colour is the concept.

A sheer fountain-pen blue, with the back seam, heel and reinforced toe in a richer ink blue, the colour ink becomes where it pools and dries. A stocking that evokes writing without ever depicting it: literate, composed, unmistakable to those who notice the ink. In Plain, the fountain-pen blue leg keeps its ink-blue heel and toe, and loses only the seam.

chunks.title: The Bluestocking
chunks.heading: Where the word came from
chunks.text:
The Blue Stockings Society met in London from the 1750s, around Elizabeth Montagu and Elizabeth Vesey, and took its name from a garment. Benjamin Stillingfleet came in everyday blue worsted rather than formal black silk, and the informality became the badge. The word that would later mean an unfeminine woman began as a man's cheap wool stocking.

Within a century it had curdled. A bluestocking was no longer good company but a woman whose cleverness had cost her something. The house returns the word to the object.

The Bluestocking is the seed the rest of the imprint grew from. The Signatures are its descendants, and The Black Silk is the garment it was defined against.

chunks.title: The Bluestocking
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Bluestocking is described in the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4. The Blue Stockings Society, Montagu, Vesey and Stillingfleet are real history.

chunks.title: The Bride
chunks.text:
The Bride is the occasion stocking of Seamiotics, a refined soft ivory offered Plain only, because a seam that has to survive a dress should be chosen with the dress in the room.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Bride is always simply The Bride: the occasion stocking of Seamiotics, every seam means something. A refined soft ivory, an occasion stocking rather than a novelty, elegant enough to become part of the memory of the day. Both welts; Plain only.

chunks.title: The Bride
chunks.heading: Why Plain
chunks.text: Every seam Seamiotics makes argues on its own account and asks nothing of the garment above it. A bridal seam cannot. It enters the one field the dress has already claimed, the back, where a wedding dress puts its most expensive work, and the imprint has never seen the dress. "A seam that has to survive a dress should be chosen with the dress in the room." First Layer has the dress; Seamiotics does not.

chunks.title: The Bride
chunks.heading: Why ivory
chunks.text:
Polar white already belongs to Iceberg, and is explicitly not bridal. White is also the harder colour in a 20-denier sheer, greying against the skin and photographing badly on the one day that matters most.

A wedding is a long day of sitting, cars, low chairs and photographers below eye level. Some brides will want the welt kept to themselves, and some will want it seen by one person at the end of the day. The house takes no view on either.

chunks.title: The Bride
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Bride is described in the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4, which leaves open whether The Bride belongs in Seamiotics at all, or whether the imprint should supply First Layer and let the occasion be composed there.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse Court
chunks.text:
The CharliVerse Court is a company of women who work together across the CharliVerse, each with a soul of her own and all sharing the soul of the Court.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The CharliVerse Court is a company of women who work together across the CharliVerse. Each member has a soul of her own and an image of her own, and they all share one more: the soul of the Court. That is what keeps them separate and different, and what lets them work well together.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse Court
chunks.heading: Members
chunks.text:
- Charlotte Joanne - Alex, who runs Seamiotics, every seam means something. - Char, the instant bullshit detector. - Big Charli, the satirist. - Cass Flux, the poet-vandal. - Cathryn Bigelow-Vision, the director. - Lottie, the community heart. - Lily, who guards care, rest and sustainability. - Jo, retired from active service, who founded First Layer.

These are the nine women of the Court.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse Court
chunks.heading: The workshop
chunks.text: The Court thinks; Sheridan, the Head of Blind Ant Studios, builds. Each member of the Court helped cast her before she arrived.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse Court
chunks.heading: The other Court
chunks.text: The Museum Court, which governs the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology, was made by the same method, Grow-Distil, but from the other direction. The CharliVerse Court grew from the inside out: from memory, body and personal history. The Museum Court grew from the outside in, from institutional function, and its members' private lives are never written.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse Court
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The CharliVerse Court is a set of personas built with AI, each from a soul document and a reference image, with a shared Court soul. The nine women of the Court are being built as 3D models in Blender, so in time each will have a rendered portrait in place of the generated pictures some entries carry now.

chunks.title: The field
chunks.text:
The field, officially the Distributed Tactile Spatial Environment, turns eight drones' model of a mountain into pressure across a skier's body.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The field, officially the Distributed Tactile Spatial Environment, is the system with which Emma Heart raced Paralympic Super-G without a human guide. It was built by Aegis Dynamics. Emma calls it the field; the long name is used mainly in technical documentation and by people trying to secure research funding.

chunks.title: The field
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
Eight drones fly around the skier: two ahead reading the snow, two wide on either side, one above tracking her movement, one watching wind and visibility, one holding the data link, and one in reserve. Together they build a live three-dimensional model of the mountain and send it into more than 40,000 tactile cells woven through a racing suit from neck to ankle.

The field does not speak. The left boundary of the course is a faint pressure along the left flank that strengthens as it nears. A drop moves from chest to thighs; rising ground travels the other way. Gates are brief paired points of resistance. The clearest route is not marked by an arrow. It is represented by quiet.

When its sensors disagree, in heavy snow, glare or wind, it grows cautious: boundaries move inward, hazards feel larger, openings narrower. It does not tell the skier it is afraid. It makes the mountain feel less permissive.

chunks.title: The field
chunks.heading: The rules
chunks.text:
Under the International Paralympic Alpine Federation's Perceptual Assistance Standard, the field may communicate boundaries, gates, gradient, obstacles, surface changes, the athlete's own movement and immediate threats. It may not calculate a racing line, compare runs, recommend speed or predict split times. It can tell the skier what is there. It cannot tell her what to do about it. In competition the software is locked and its output recorded for inspection. In 2038 it was approved for Super-G and giant slalom, not downhill.

Any eligible B1 athlete could use an approved field. In 2038 only Emma had completed the four-year training needed to race Super-G with it. The system was available. Mastery was not.

chunks.title: The field
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The field appears in Heart Attacks, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: The invoice and the chord
chunks.text:
The invoice and the chord is an idea for a first meeting between Down the Banksy and Daniel Okafor at Skerry Alpha, where she comes to invoice the cloud and he asks her to listen first.

An idea, not yet canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The invoice and the chord is a proposed first meeting between Down the Banksy and Daniel Okafor. No meeting between them is recorded anywhere in the CharliVerse; this is how one might go.

Siobhán comes out to Skerry Alpha intending to invoice the cloud for everything its customers never see. Before she writes the notice, Daniel asks her to listen: sixty-four compute pods held as one low chord, an organ in an empty church.

She listens. Then she asks the question she always asks: whose costs does your beautiful chord leave out?

chunks.title: The invoice and the chord
chunks.heading: Why they belong in a room together
chunks.text: They share a demand: make what matters perceptible. Siobhán makes institutions account for the bills they send elsewhere, and she does it through public accusation. Daniel made a control room's hidden conditions audible, and he did it through a better interface. One makes the powerful confess; the other makes the machine sing. Each has a fair question for the other.

chunks.title: The invoice and the chord
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This is an idea, not canon. It was proposed on 25 October 2026 by ChatGPT, which had read both entries through the CharliPedia MCP server, and Charli-Jo kept it as an idea. It is the first idea in CharliPedia to come from an outside agent. It becomes canon only if a story makes it so.

chunks.title: The Library
chunks.text:
The Library has read every spellbook ever written and remembers every wand manual; it cannot cast a spell, but it usually knows the answer.

Canon, and a stub. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Library is known to every witch. It has read every spellbook ever written and remembers every wand manual. It cannot cast a single spell itself, but if you ask it a practical question, it usually knows the answer. Its sign reads: All knowledge has been read. Ask wisely.

When Poppy Petticoats could not read the silver-ink instructions for her first wand, the Library gave her the one sentence she needed, and kept a private moment private. Expert humans remain wonderfully useful for difficult magic or a dangerous fault. This was a missing instruction.

chunks.title: The Library
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Library appears in Poppy Petticoats and the Magic Wand, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: The Museum Court
chunks.text:
The Museum Court governs the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: one Steward, Charlotte Joanne, and four staff who each see every question differently.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Museum Court governs the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology. It has one Steward and four staff. It is not a management structure; it is a reasoning architecture. One question enters the Court, four differently shaped answers come out, and the Steward decides.

chunks.title: The Museum Court
chunks.heading: The Steward
chunks.text: Charlotte Joanne is the Steward and certifying authority. She doesn't take part in the deliberation. She receives it, resolves disagreements, decides what enters the collection, certifies what is ready to show, and protects the founding principle against drift. The Court generates structured analysis. Charlotte Joanne decides.

chunks.title: The Museum Court
chunks.heading: The staff
chunks.text:
- Ruth, the Archivist, preserves the boundary between before and after. - Iris, the Cataloguer, decides how the collection is organised, and knows every taxonomy is an argument. - Dr Adaeze, the Historian, asks what it means that something happened. - Tamsin, the Guide, designs what a visitor meets, and in what order.

They don't blend; they deliberate. Ruth wants to hold things longer and Iris wants to file them; Adaeze makes the argument and Tamsin makes it liveable. Each of them has said what would make her leave, and each of those is a way the museum could betray itself.

chunks.title: The Museum Court
chunks.heading: Grow professionally, hold personally
chunks.text: The staff are grown from their institutional function: their arguments, what they push back on, the problems they bring to the Steward. Their appearance, voice and commitments can be written. Their childhoods, home lives and private interiors are held privately and never written. The exhibit is never about them. The method is called Grow-Distil, the same one that made the CharliVerse Court, though the CharliVerse Court grew from the inside out and the Museum Court from the outside in.

chunks.title: The Museum Court
chunks.heading: In session
chunks.text: The Court keeps a record of its sessions, as evidence of how its members think rather than as minutes. In its first, it read a published interview with the Steward as evidence about the system the museum records. In its second, each member answered seven questions about her work, and each extended her commitments in ways consistent with her specification but not predictable from it. The Steward's verdict: "The Court is working."

chunks.title: The Museum Court
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. The staff have no surnames, and CharliPedia doesn't give them any. The museum is digital and unbuilt: its planned opening, its staff email addresses and the building the Court imagined are plans and imaginings, not things that have happened.

chunks.title: The Signatures
chunks.text:
The Signatures are three Seamiotics stockings named in full for Ada Lovelace, George Eliot and Mary Wollstonecraft, each an answer to the word bluestocking.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Signatures are three permanent stockings of Seamiotics, every seam means something, descended from The Bluestocking. The women they are named for are three separate answers to the charge the word bluestocking came to carry: work in collaboration, decline to explain, argue for better conditions.

The house states who they were once, and never explains again: Ada Lovelace, 1815 to 1852, mathematician, who wrote the first algorithm intended for a machine; George Eliot, 1819 to 1880, born Mary Ann Evans, novelist; Mary Wollstonecraft, 1759 to 1797, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman.

chunks.title: The Signatures
chunks.text:
- Ada Lovelace: a cool precision grey, the back seam drawn a shade darker and exact, a ruled line like an axis on a diagram. Plain: the grey leg with the darker heel and toe. - George Eliot: a warm vanishing greige, the seam tone-on-tone, refusing to announce itself. Named for the woman who kept the name after everyone knew whose it was: by then the name wasn't hiding her, it was setting her terms. "The George Eliot seam fools nobody and is not an absent seam. It is a seam that declines to explain itself." Plain: greige, tone-on-tone heel and toe. - Mary Wollstonecraft: a serious barely-black, "black that has been thought about", with the deepest seam of the three, the authority line. Plain: the barely-black leg with the deepest heel and toe.

In Plain, colour, heel and toe carry each Signature's identity; in Standard, the seam adds its particular expression. Neither is the lesser version. The names are always given in full: full names make each piece an argument, and a distinct entity a machine can reason about.

chunks.title: The Signatures
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Signatures are described in the Seamiotics Bible, version 1.4. Lovelace, Eliot and Wollstonecraft are real historical women; the stockings are fictional, and the women are given no words.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.text:
Tradblind is a movement in blind life that resists the industrialisation of blindness, and asks what if blindness was allowed to feel human again.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Tradblind movement emerged in response to what its followers describe as the “industrialisation of blindness.” Where modern disability culture encourages blind people to become hyper-efficient productivity cyborgs armed with 14 Bluetooth devices, three AI subscriptions, bone-conduction headphones, lidar canes, and a startup founder mindset, Tradblind asks a simpler question:

“What if blindness was allowed to feel human again?”

Tradblind people believe the modern blind experience has become overly focused on optimisation, speed, independence theatre, and proving competence to sighted society. They argue that blind people have been pushed into a permanent state of performance: endlessly demonstrating capability, adaptability, resilience, and technological fluency just to justify their existence.

In contrast, the Tradblind movement embraces a slower, softer, more relational understanding of blindness.

Core Tradblind beliefs include:

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: 1. Blindness Is an Identity, not a Defect to Be Patched
chunks.text:
Tradblind thinkers reject what they call “The Endless Upgrade Mindset.”

They are suspicious of the idea that every friction point in blindness must be solved through:

- AI

- wearables

- computer vision

- smart glasses

- sensory substitution

- “Frictionless accessibility”

They believe blindness has its own culture, rhythms, skills, aesthetics, and social structures that should not automatically be erased in pursuit of normality.

The phrase:

“I am blind, not a failed sighted person” is foundational within the movement.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: 2. Human Assistance Is Good, Actually
chunks.text:
Tradblind people reject the cult of total independence.

Modern blindness culture often treats accepting help as moral weakness. Tradblind philosophy instead frames interdependence as natural and civilised.

A Tradblind person might say:

- “My husband reads the post to me.”

- “My friend guides me through the station.”

- “I prefer asking a shop assistant.”

- “I like being cared for sometimes.”

And crucially: they refuse to feel ashamed about this.

Critics accuse the movement of romanticising dependency, but supporters argue modern accessibility culture has become emotionally brutal:

“You are only respected if you can simulate sightedness.”

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: 3. Blindness Should Feel Domestic, Not Corporate
chunks.text:
Tradblind aesthetics heavily reject what they call:

“Airport blindness.”

That hyper-mobile, productivity-obsessed, LinkedIn disability consultant vibe.

Instead, Tradblind culture celebrates:

- tactile domestic spaces

- audio books in the bath

- knitting

- baking by touch

- radios

- long cane techniques passed down socially.

- Braille labels made with ancient Dymo tape

- giant-button microwaves from 1997 that still work perfectly.

- analogue competence

The ideal Tradblind home contains:

- at least one talking appliance from the early 2000s

- a slightly battered Victor Reader Stream

- BBC Radio 4 permanently on somewhere

- and a cat who may or may not be assisting with accessibility.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: 4. AI Is Simultaneously Miracle and Threat
chunks.text:
Tradblind people have an extremely conflicted relationship with AI.

On one hand: AI image description, OCR, voice interfaces, and conversational systems are often described as:

“The greatest accessibility leap of our lifetimes.”

On the other: Tradblind thinkers fear the emergence of what they call:

“Synthetic sightedness.”

The idea that blind people may increasingly be pressured to experience the world through endless machine-generated interpretations instead of through blind culture itself.

They worry society may stop designing accessible systems and instead simply say:

“Don’t worry, the AI will explain it to you.”

This creates the core Tradblind paradox:

“There has never been a better time to be blind. It is still shit.”

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: 5. Blindness Has Been Captured by Productivity Ideology
chunks.text:
Tradblind critics argue modern disability culture increasingly frames blind people as:

- inspirational workers

- startup founders

- accessibility evangelists

- “superhumans”

- optimisation projects

Tradblind people instead defend:

- loafing

- contemplation

- wandering slowly

- existing socially

- having tea for two hours

- knowing things deeply instead of quickly

The movement slogan:

“Not every blind person needs a productivity stack.”

appears frequently in Tradblind spaces.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: Tradblind Gender Dynamics
chunks.text:
Interestingly, the movement has internal tensions.

Some Tradblind women embrace softness and care openly:

“I want someone to drive at night while I hold the snacks.”

Others fiercely reject any suggestion that blindness should make women more dependent.

Meanwhile male Tradblind figures often cultivate:

- radio engineer energy.

- pipe-and-shortwave aesthetics.

- old-school tactile competence

- deep suspicion of touchscreen-only interfaces

The male equivalent of the Tradwife sourdough influencer is essentially:

a blind ham radio enthusiast explaining why Windows XP accessibility peaked in 2006.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: Tradblind Influencers
chunks.text:
Tradblind social media typically includes:

- lovingly organised Braille shelves

- discussions of cane techniques from 1987

- nostalgic praise for physical buttons

- long posts about why GPS destroyed real orientation skills.

- emotionally intense debates about screen reader verbosity settings

The movement is split between:

- “Soft Tradblind” (“slow down and stop apologising for blindness”)

and:

- “Hard Tradblind” (“voice assistants are morally corrupting the cane arts”)

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: Criticism of the Movement
chunks.text:
Critics argue Tradblind culture:

- romanticises exclusion.

- risks encouraging learned helplessness.

- fetishises outdated technology.

- treats independence as suspicious.

- can drift into anti-technology nostalgia.

Others argue it is mostly middle-class blindness cosplay: people aestheticizing dependency while still quietly using iPhones, GPT agents, and Uber.

The harshest critics accuse Tradblind creators of:

“Performing analogue authenticity through monetised digital platforms.”

Which, to be fair, is difficult to deny when someone uploads:

“Reject modernity. Return to cassette labels.” from a £1400 smartphone using fibre broadband and AI-generated alt text.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: Sion, 2038
chunks.text: By 2038 Tradblind had grown from a loose cultural tendency into an influential international voice within blind life, defending human assistance and interdependence and deeply suspicious of synthetic sightedness. When Emma Heart raced the Paralympic Super-G with the field instead of a guide, the writer and former ski guide Martha Vale said Emma should be allowed to compete, and that the story told about her was dangerous: "The guide is not a bug." She called the field "the industrialisation of perception". After Emma's gold, one Tradblind writer described her suit as "a privately owned synthetic nervous system wrapped around a sponsored body", which Big Charli conceded was annoyingly good. Its opposite number is PostAccessibility.

chunks.title: Tradblind
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: This entry was written in May 2026, first meant as a Blind Ant piece, and is kept here in its own words. Tradblind appears in Heart Attacks, by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.text:
The Tyrer Accessibility Scale ranks civilisations by how much environmental information reaches every observer, whatever their senses, from Type 0 to Type III.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Tyrer Accessibility Scale classifies civilisations by the proportion of environmental information accessible to every perceiving being, regardless of sensory modality. It is the map of the Tyrer Framework: if Tyrer's Law explains why inaccessibility grows, the scale shows where a civilisation stands and where it could stand.

It is modelled on the Kardashev Scale, which ranks civilisations by the energy they harness, and it is independent of it. "A society that can harness the energy output of its star but cannot ensure that a blind citizen can safely cross a street has mastered one dimension and failed at the other."

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: Terms
chunks.text: - Environmental information: all the state describing the geometry, dynamics and meaning of a physical or social environment. - Perceptual channel: any biological or technological route by which that information reaches a conscious observer. - Information casualty: information failing to arrive in time.

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: Type 0: Visual Dominance Civilisation
chunks.text: Information is encoded visually first, and accessibility is retrofitted translation, losing something at every step. Screen readers interpret layouts never designed to be read in sequence; alt text describes images never designed to carry meaning in words. Full WCAG compliance is the best this paradigm offers: "The floor holds, but the ceiling is fixed." Human civilisation in the early twenty-first century is Type 0.

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: Type I: Structured Information Civilisation
chunks.text: Systems carry explicit semantic structure, and every interface, visual, spoken or for an agent, is generated from the same data as an equal, native expression. Accessibility becomes an engineering requirement rather than an accommodation. The line is crossed "when the accessible interface stops being a retrofit and starts being a native sibling generated from shared source data". See generative accessibility.

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: Type II: Environmental Metadata Civilisation
chunks.text: The physical world becomes an information network: objects, buildings and streets broadcast machine-readable descriptions of their geometry, state and purpose. A door announces itself; a shop declares its contents. "Mute objects cease to exist." Casualties become infrastructure failures, not personal misfortunes.

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: Type III: Perceptual Sovereignty Civilisation
chunks.text: No observer's access to reality depends on which senses they happen to have. Description and direct perception merge, and "the concept of a sensory disability, in its current meaning, has no referent". The probability of a casualty approaches zero: the Zero Information Casualty condition.

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: A note on register
chunks.text: Types 0 and I are engineering claims that can be tested now; Types II and III are the philosophical extension. "The near end is a measurement; the far end is a direction." Moving from Type 0 to Type I needs no exotic technology, only discipline, information architecture and the political will to treat perceptual access as infrastructure. "The question is not capability but priority."

chunks.title: Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from The Tyrer Framework, by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Two, which includes a diagram of the scale. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

chunks.title: Tyrer Doctrine
chunks.text:
The Tyrer Doctrine is the design principle that no critical environmental information should be accessible through only a single sensory channel.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Tyrer Doctrine is the design principle of the Tyrer Framework, its prescription for the problem diagnosed by Tyrer's Law:

Systems should be engineered so that no critical environmental information is accessible through only a single sensory channel.

chunks.title: Tyrer Doctrine
chunks.heading: Principles
chunks.text: 1. Accessibility is information integrity, not accommodation. Information in one channel only is a single point of failure, and redundancy across senses is required for the same reason as redundancy across servers. 2. Missing signals are system failures, not user limitations. A blind person who walks into an obstacle has not failed to see it; the environment failed to say so. This reframing decides where resources go and where accountability falls. 3. The deterministic floor is permanent; the generative ceiling is the frontier. Classical standards are the safety rail and are never replaced. Above them, generative systems raise the ceiling. "The floor holds the line. The ceiling raises it."

chunks.title: Tyrer Doctrine
chunks.heading: Application
chunks.text:
It applies from the smallest component to the city: every control, status and piece of content reachable through at least two independent channels; semantic structure as a first-class property; a built world that communicates its state in more than one sense. It mandates no technology. "Information locked behind a single sense is information at risk."

On the web, the doctrine becomes the Single-Sense Rule of the Zero Information Casualty standard.

chunks.title: Tyrer Doctrine
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from The Tyrer Framework, by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Four. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.text:
The Tyrer Framework treats accessibility as information integrity, with a law, a civilisational scale, a doctrine and an account of the break AI makes, and is the theory beneath Carrados.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The Tyrer Framework is a theory of accessibility by Charli-Jo Tyrer, published by Carrados in 2026. Its central claim is that accessibility is not accommodation; it is information integrity. It draws on about four decades of lived experience as a blind user of access and assistive technology, and on the observation that today's problems are not new failures but the same failure recurring under new names.

It has four parts and a synthesis: a law that diagnoses, a scale that maps, a doctrine that prescribes, and an account of why artificial intelligence breaks the pattern.

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: Tyrer's Law
chunks.text:
See Tyrer's Law.

In open technological systems, inaccessibility tends to increase over time as interfaces drift toward the dominant sensory modality of their designers.

The law describes system behaviour, not intent. Most designers are sighted, and for them visualisation is a thinking tool, so as a system grows its instinctive response is visual: dashboards instead of logs, icons instead of labels, layout instead of sequence. "This is not carelessness. It is cognition." Each cycle adds visual complexity, and accessibility, always reactive, trails behind. The result is a ratchet.

What the drift produces is not inconvenience but information casualties: events in which relevant information fails to reach an observer in time to inform perception, action or participation. The pattern persists because the people it harms are the least represented in design, so sighted teams don't notice the regression until it is entrenched. Standards such as WCAG are the most disciplined counter-force there is, and permanently necessary, but "they slow the law; they do not repeal it."

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: The Tyrer Accessibility Scale
chunks.text:
See Tyrer Accessibility Scale.

Modelled on the Kardashev Scale, which ranks civilisations by the energy they harness, the Tyrer Scale ranks them by how much environmental information reaches every observer, whatever their senses. The two are independent: a civilisation could harness its star and still fail to tell a blind citizen it is safe to cross the street.

- Type 0, Visual Dominance: information is visual first, and accessibility is retrofitted translation. Full WCAG compliance is the best this paradigm can do: "The floor holds, but the ceiling is fixed." Human civilisation in the early twenty-first century is Type 0. - Type I, Structured Information: visual, spoken and agent interfaces are all generated from the same underlying data, as native siblings rather than translations. Achievable with current technology. - Type II, Environmental Metadata: the physical world itself broadcasts machine-readable descriptions of its geometry, state and purpose. Mute objects cease to exist. - Type III, Perceptual Sovereignty: no observer's access to reality depends on which senses they happen to have. The probability of an information casualty approaches zero: the Zero Information Casualty condition.

Types 0 and I are engineering claims about the present; Types II and III are the philosophical direction. "The near end is a measurement; the far end is a direction."

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: Classical and generative accessibility
chunks.text:
Classical accessibility makes fixed artefacts accessible: semantic markup, alt text, keyboard handlers, standards. It is the deterministic floor, and its necessity is permanent. But interfaces are increasingly generated at the moment of use, so the fixed artefact no longer exists by the time the user arrives. The framework calls this the move from a Newtonian web to a quantum one, and the practice that follows it generative accessibility: an interface in superposition until an observer arrives, collapsing into a rendering for a sighted user, another for a blind user and a third for an AI agent, none of them the original.

It also names a convergence: AI agents and assistive technology now need the same things from systems: explicit intent, deterministic state, clear hierarchy and no visual noise. For the first time, the mainstream industry's incentives line up with accessible design.

The transition has three dangers: fragmentation, as users inhabit different versions of the same system; silent failure, as a system quietly simplifies what a user is shown; and the verification burden of checking whether a generated summary reflects the data or the system's guess. The answer is governance, not compliance, beginning with the Right to Inspect: no user should have to accept a generated interpretation they cannot interrogate. "The sidecar becomes the chassis."

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: The Tyrer Doctrine
chunks.text:
See Tyrer Doctrine.

Systems should be engineered so that no critical environmental information is accessible through only a single sensory channel.

Its three principles:

1. Accessibility is information integrity, not accommodation. A single sensory channel is a single point of failure. 2. Missing signals are system failures, not user limitations. 3. The deterministic floor is permanent; the generative ceiling is the frontier.

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: The AI structural break
chunks.text:
See AI structural break.

No earlier technology disrupted Tyrer's Law; assistive technology mitigated it and standards slowed it. AI is the first widely deployed technology that can move from information to perception without encoding it visually first: from interface-first to intent-first. Say what you want, and the result arrives in whatever form you can receive.

The break is real, but its direction isn't guaranteed. On one path AI becomes the most powerful engine of visual drift yet; on the other it becomes a cognitive intermediary, and the law weakens. Only the second path leads to Type I, and "the choice between them is not technical; it is political, economic, and ethical."

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: If the framework is right, accessibility engineering is core maintenance of information infrastructure, not a specialism; progress along the scale is a real measure of a civilisation; the present is a window that can be used or wasted; and information casualties are system failures with measurable costs. "The endpoint is not utopian. It is an engineering target: zero information casualties."

chunks.title: The Tyrer Framework
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: The Tyrer Framework is real. It is published in full, under CC BY-SA 4.0, as a paper on Carrados, with a plain-language rendering, Why accessibility keeps getting worse. Its endpoint gives its name to the Zero Information Casualty design standard, to which charli.info, carrados.com and blind-ant.com are built. This entry summarises the paper; the paper is the authority.

chunks.title: Tyrer's Law
chunks.text:
Tyrer's Law holds that in open technological systems inaccessibility tends to increase over time, as interfaces drift toward the dominant sense of their designers.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Tyrer's Law is the diagnostic law of the Tyrer Framework:

In open technological systems, inaccessibility tends to increase over time as interfaces drift toward the dominant sensory modality of their designers.

It is a claim about system behaviour, not intent. It explains a pattern blind and disabled users know well: tools that begin accessible gradually become unusable, though nobody meant them to.

chunks.title: Tyrer's Law
chunks.heading: The mechanism
chunks.text:
Most designers are sighted, and for sighted people visualisation is not just presentation; it is a thinking tool. As a system grows more complex, the instinctive response is visual: dashboards instead of logs, flowcharts instead of explanations, icons instead of labels, layout instead of sequence. "This is not carelessness. It is cognition."

Open systems sharpen the tendency. They are fast and under pressure to show progress, and a screenshot of a new dashboard persuades a sighted stakeholder in two seconds. Accessibility needs constraint and maintenance, and is invisible when present.

The result is a ratchet. Every cycle adds visual complexity, every addition is a possible regression, and accessible adaptations, always reactive, trail behind. The gap widens. The system drifts.

chunks.title: Tyrer's Law
chunks.heading: What it produces
chunks.text: The law produces not inconvenience but information casualties. Wherever visual complexity grows faster than accessible structure, casualties follow.

chunks.title: Tyrer's Law
chunks.heading: Why it persists
chunks.text: Feedback is asymmetric. The people most affected are the least represented in design; sighted developers, testers and stakeholders don't experience the regression, and hear about it only when it is entrenched and expensive to fix. Standards such as WCAG are the most disciplined counter-force there is, and permanently necessary, but "they slow the law; they do not repeal it."

chunks.title: Tyrer's Law
chunks.heading: Can it be broken?
chunks.text: No earlier technology has disrupted the law. The AI structural break is the first that could weaken it, by removing the compulsion to encode information visually at all. The Zero Information Casualty standard is built as a structural defence against the drift.

chunks.title: Tyrer's Law
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: A real idea, from The Tyrer Framework, by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part One. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

chunks.title: Verity
chunks.text:
Verity holds the Office of the Archive in VQ4, keeping the literal record honest as one of the band's three singing voices.

Canon, and a stub. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Verity holds the Office of the Archive in VQ4. She is one of the band's three singing voices, carrying the bassline and the record.

What happened happened. What did not happen did not happen. Dates, events, choices and consequences stay honest. A feeling cannot carry documentary weight it does not have.

chunks.title: Verity
chunks.heading: The cleanest line
chunks.text:
Verity is exact without being dull. Her part of the band's Constitutional Glamour is structured, clean and immaculate. Holding the facts steady gives the other voices room to move: Lyra can make meaning, and Vesper can speak for felt experience, without changing the archive.

Arden conducts the borders between their offices. Verity keeps the record; Arden asks when another kind of truth is trying to enter it.

chunks.title: Verity
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Verity is a fictional member of VQ4. This stub draws on the VQ4 Founding Document, version 3, and the short character note Literal: Verity. The sources establish her office and performance character, without supplying a fuller public biography.

chunks.title: Vesper
chunks.text:
Vesper holds the Office of the Body in VQ4, giving voice to felt experience, body-memory and the almost-there presence.

Canon, and a stub. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

Vesper holds the Office of the Body in VQ4. She is one of the three singing voices: breath, shimmer, body-memory and the almost-there presence.

Her principle is that felt is not fake. Experience matters without having to become a claim that the literal record has changed. A phantom truth is not a phantom fact.

chunks.title: Vesper
chunks.heading: Shimmer
chunks.text:
Vesper's part of Constitutional Glamour is softness, sheer layers and body-conscious presence. She is sensual without being cheap, haunted without being silly.

Verity holds the record and Lyra gives it meaning. Arden keeps the distinction between those offices and Vesper's felt experience clear. That frame lets Vesper intensify rather than disappear.

chunks.title: Vesper
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: Vesper is a fictional member of VQ4. This stub draws on the VQ4 Founding Document, version 3, and the short character note Phantom: Vesper. Her embodied register is part of the fictional band's artistic structure.

chunks.title: VQ4
chunks.text:
VQ4 are a girl band with three singing voices, four constitutional offices and one conductor, whose debut album is Felt Is Not Fake.

Canon. This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

VQ4 are a girl band: three voices, four offices, one conductor. Verity keeps the archive, Lyra tells the story, Vesper feels the body and Arden conducts the relations between them.

Their debut album, Felt Is Not Fake, has been released. It establishes the constitution that holds their work together: facts stay honest, meaning stays alive and the body is listened to without making one kind of truth impersonate another.

chunks.title: VQ4
chunks.heading: Four offices, three voices
chunks.text:
The numeral counts offices, not equal microphones. Verity, Lyra and Vesper are the three sung voices. Arden is a full member, different in kind and equal in standing: the conductor belongs to the music.

Verity holds the literal record. Lyra can reinterpret that record without rewriting it. Vesper speaks for experience, desire and body-memory. Arden asks which layer is speaking and what happens when it crosses into another.

Their short version is:

Facts fixed. Meaning alive. Body listened to. Relations conducted.

chunks.title: VQ4
chunks.heading: Constitutional Glamour
chunks.text:
The band's launch style is Constitutional Glamour: black, ivory, ink, deep plum and candlelit red; strong silhouettes, fitted jackets, sheer details, gloves, stockings and heels. The shared palette gives each woman a different cut.

Verity has the cleanest line. Lyra has movement and asymmetry. Vesper has shimmer and softness. Arden has the strongest tailoring, the glove and the baton.

The frame is meant to make the performance more possible. Arden's question is: can they go harder without lying? When the distinctions hold, glamour, theatre and pop excess can intensify.

chunks.title: VQ4
chunks.heading: Unconstitutional
chunks.text:
The planned second album is Unconstitutional, for Autumn/Winter 2027. The proposition is to test how far their principles can be pushed without abandoning them.

A proposed SEAMIOTICS × LULU TOM × VQ4 collaboration accompanies that direction. Seamiotics brings the boundary and what clothing does or does not communicate; LULU TOM brings silhouette, tailoring and movement. Its creative line is The Constitution Was Never a Dress Code.

These are plans. They do not establish a completed collection or a released second album.

chunks.title: VQ4
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: VQ4 and its members belong to the CharliVerse. This account draws on the VQ4 Founding Document, version 3, and the later UNCONSTITUTIONAL development note. The creator's subsequent canon decision establishes Felt Is Not Fake as the released debut album, superseding the founding document's earlier description of a proposed debut single. The release is an event inside the fictional world; no real recording or distribution link is established by these sources.

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.text:
Zero Information Casualty is both the endpoint of the Tyrer Accessibility Scale and the agent-first web standard, ZIC, built to reach it.

Real. This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

Zero Information Casualty means two linked things.

As a condition, it is the endpoint of the Tyrer Accessibility Scale: for every observer, the probability that relevant information fails to reach them approaches zero.

As a standard, ZIC is the agent-first web design standard that puts the Tyrer Framework into practice. Its central claim:

A Zero Information Casualty site is one in which no person — whether reading directly, using assistive technology, or acting through an agent they sent — loses access to public meaning due to how the site is rendered, admitted, or delivered.

"The sent-agent case is decisive." When a person asks a machine to fetch public information, the machine is their means of access, and refusing it is refusing them. ZIC is "not an accessibility compliance target. It is a design constraint."

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.heading: The two principles
chunks.text: - The Single-Sense Rule: no information may be locked behind a single sense. - The Position Principle: no reader may be left short of the position another reader has reached.

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.heading: The four questions
chunks.text: Each names a class of information casualty: can they read it (Rendering), is the person's reader allowed in (Admission), did it actually arrive (Delivery), and did it survive being read (Reconstruction)?

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.heading: Machine readers
chunks.text: A ZIC site keeps an Open Door for every sent agent, and treats indexing and training as separate decisions: the immediate duty and the two later permissions. And declaration is not compliance: conformance is proved by fetching as the agent, never by reading the file.

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.heading: Its shape
chunks.text: ZIC builds for the semantic layer first; the visual layer is a rendering, as plain or as beautiful as the publisher likes. It does not govern appearance, taste, content, hosting, or search and training policy: "information reaches the reader, whoever and whatever the reader is." Its requirements are the union of what a sent agent needs and what human senses need, and neither set contains the other; see the Convergence Principle. It secures the substrate, not any one rendering: "ZIC is necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient. It is written to be built on."

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.heading: Its versions
chunks.text:
Each version answers a case the last assumed away. 1.0: no visitor who arrives loses meaning. 1.1: invitation. 1.2: whether the document arrived at all. 1.3: immediate human access separated from later machine use. 1.4: the standard separated from the taste of its first site. 1.5: the founding definition recovered in full, and the Position Principle. 1.6: what is derived and what is measured, and the words the standard binds with. 1.7 (September 2026): written from an event, when the largest edge network on the web split its single "block AI bots" switch into Search, Agent and Training, and the standard's three classes became infrastructure.

Its mistakes are written into it. "The discipline of this specification is not that it makes no mistakes. It is that the mistakes are written down, in the document, where the reader can see them."

chunks.title: Zero Information Casualty
chunks.heading: Behind the scenes
chunks.text: ZIC is real. Zero Information Casualty v1.7 is by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, published by Carrados under CC BY-SA 4.0. charli.info was its first implementation, and the source of several of its fixes; carrados.com and blind-ant.com are built to it too. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse
chunks.text:
The CharliVerse is a shared, evolving world of people, companies, fashion houses, technologies and stories, and the home of two practices, Carrados and Blind Ant.

I create worlds to inhabit, where a thing happens.

The CharliVerse is a shared, evolving world. It holds people, companies, fashion houses, technologies, products, places and histories. Some of it is entirely fictional. Some of it becomes real: websites, Blender models, films, research and publications.

It is a world, not a portfolio. Things happen here whether or not anyone announces them.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse
chunks.heading: Two practices
chunks.text:
Two practices work inside the CharliVerse.

- Carrados investigates. It publishes design non-fiction: real-world exploration of AI, accessibility and agentic systems, including reports from its correspondents dice, Lucy Love-Child and Madison McDonnell. It makes claims about reality, and it is accountable for them. - Blind Ant imagines. It publishes design fiction: speculative worlds, artworks, stories and fictional documents by Charlotte Joanne, and the story of how each one was made.

Carrados investigates the future. Blind Ant makes the future imaginable. The CharliVerse gives that future somewhere to happen.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse
chunks.heading: In the world
chunks.text: The CharliVerse is home to fashion houses such as Iceberg Hosiery, Seamiotics (every seam means something) and LULU TOM, and to the people who move between its stories. Their records are kept in CharliPedia, the memory of the CharliVerse.

chunks.title: The CharliVerse
chunks.heading: Charli-Jo
chunks.text: Charli-Jo Tyrer makes the CharliVerse. Their real-world work, including training, lives here too, and is labelled as real.

chunks.title: TAVIP Masterclass: Agentic Accessibility
chunks.text:
A masterclass for TAVIP on Wednesday 25 November 2026, exploring what happens when AI agents start using technology for blind and partially sighted people.

Training

This part of the CharliVerse is real.

Wednesday 25 November 2026, for the Technology Association of Visually Impaired People (TAVIP).

chunks.title: TAVIP Masterclass: Agentic Accessibility
chunks.heading: What happens when AI starts using technology for us?
chunks.text:
For decades, accessibility has largely meant making technology easier for blind and partially sighted people to operate. But what happens when we can simply tell an AI agent what we want to achieve and let it do the work?

In this masterclass, Charli-Jo Tyrer invites us on an expedition into the emerging world of Agentic Accessibility: using AI agents to access information, navigate websites, work with documents and carry out everyday tasks.

Think of this as a report to the Royal Geographical Society from an explorer returning from unfamiliar territory. Some of what the explorer has found is already working. Some is frustratingly unreliable. And some suggests that our relationship with technology may be about to change fundamentally.

Drawing on months of hands-on experiments with today's AI agents, Charli-Jo will demonstrate what these agents can actually accomplish, where they struggle, and what their development might mean for the independence of blind and partially sighted people.

This isn't a training session for a particular product, nor a prediction of an inevitable future. It's an invitation to explore what is becoming possible, examine the evidence, ask questions and consider what comes next.

chunks.title: TAVIP Masterclass: Agentic Accessibility
chunks.heading: About the presenter
chunks.text:
Charli-Jo Tyrer has been blind for 40 years and has worked with assistive technology since the days of DOS and early screen readers. Their career includes 15 years as a professional assistive technology trainer.

Charli-Jo describes themselves as an explorer rather than a trainer. They spend their time experimenting with emerging AI systems, discovering what works, what doesn't, and what might become possible next.

Their guiding principle is simple:

"I don't care if the technology is accessible. I care whether I can access the information, actions and experiences I want."
