The course that came before this masterclass is Confident with AI.

Every module is a self-contained page with a learning outcome, activity and checkpoint. Each ends with previous, contents and next links.

chunks.title: Confident with AI
chunks.heading: What the course assumes
chunks.text:
You need an internet connection and access to a general AI assistant for the practical activities. The course is device-neutral: it does not assume Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, JAWS, NVDA or VoiceOver. It describes goals and interactions rather than platform-specific keystrokes.

If a service does not work with your device or access method, choose another service. The durable lessons do not depend on one product.

chunks.title: 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Go to www.chat.com and ask your first question.

We use ChatGPT for this first exercise because it provides a simple starting point. In the next module, you can choose a different assistant.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will have asked an assistant for something useful and improved its first answer.

Before you begin: Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information during this exercise.

chunks.title: 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
An AI assistant is a service you can talk to by typing or speaking. It generates a response based on your request.

Treat its answer as a draft or estimate, not proof.

You can ask follow-up questions: the conversation is part of the tool.

Notice that you do not need to start again. Your second instruction changes the answer within the same conversation.

chunks.title: 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text:
Open www.chat.com. Find the message box and ask the assistant to explain something you already understand.

If you cannot think of a subject, ask: “Explain why we have seasons.”

When it replies, say:

Make that shorter and give me one example.

chunks.title: 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI
chunks.heading: If you get stuck
chunks.text: You may be asked to sign in or create an account, and the service may work differently in different places. If you cannot reach the message box, use the General AI Assistants Tool Card to find another way to continue.

chunks.title: 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You received an answer, asked for one change and can explain how the second response was more useful.

chunks.title: 2. Choose an AI Assistant
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Begin with the service that is easiest to access on your device.

Free access is enough for this course. Do not subscribe merely to complete it.

Assistant names, prices and features change, so current product comparisons belong in Tool Cards.

See the General AI Assistants Tool Card for services you can try.

chunks.title: 2. Choose an AI Assistant
chunks.heading: What to check
chunks.text: - Can you create an account and sign in? - Can you find the message box and send a message? - Can you read and navigate the response comfortably? - Are the features you need available without payment?

chunks.title: 2. Choose an AI Assistant
chunks.heading: Worked example
chunks.text:
Priya tries two assistants. Both let her send messages, but one presents long answers more cleanly with her screen reader.

She chooses that assistant for now. She has not decided it is the best assistant—only that it is the easiest place to begin.

chunks.title: 2. Choose an AI Assistant
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Use the General AI Assistants Tool Card to choose one or two services to try. Check that you can sign in if necessary, find the message box, send a message and read the response with your preferred access method. Check that the features you need are available without payment.

chunks.title: 2. Choose an AI Assistant
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can name the assistant you will use for now, confirm that basic conversation is accessible and explain why you can change later.

chunks.title: 3. Have Your First Useful Conversation
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will be able to improve an answer through follow-up rather than starting again.

Before you begin: Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information. Keep this first task low-risk.

chunks.title: 3. Have Your First Useful Conversation
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Purpose means what you are trying to accomplish.

Context is information that materially changes the answer.

Form means how you want the answer presented, such as steps, a short explanation, a comparison or a draft.

Correct the assistant and continue the same conversation.

chunks.title: 3. Have Your First Useful Conversation
chunks.heading: Worked example
chunks.text:
Weak request: “Write an email.”

Better request: “Write a friendly, concise email declining an invitation because I already have plans. Keep it warm and leave open the possibility of meeting another time.”

Follow-up: “Make it less formal and remove the apology.”

chunks.title: 3. Have Your First Useful Conversation
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text:
Ask for help with a real low-stakes task. Add your purpose, one relevant detail and the form you want. Then request one revision.

If you need a task, send these messages one at a time in the same conversation:

1. “Help me plan three simple evening meals.” 2. “They need to be vegetarian.” 3. “Give me the result as a shopping list followed by three short recipes.” 4. “Make the recipes suitable for one person.”

chunks.title: 3. Have Your First Useful Conversation
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
The revised response is more useful to you, and you can identify which extra instruction improved it.

chunks.title: 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will have matched a real task to an appropriate kind of AI help.

Before you begin: Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information. Keep your first task low-risk.

chunks.title: 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
AI can help you begin, organise or understand a task while you retain responsibility for checking and deciding.

A useful answer should reduce work or open access, not create more checking than it saves.

chunks.title: 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do
chunks.heading: Match the task to the kind of help
chunks.text: | If you need to… | Ask AI to… | |------------------------|---------------------------------------------------| | Understand something | Explain it in simpler language or with an example | | Reduce a long text | Summarise its main points | | Begin writing | Produce a first draft | | Consider alternatives | Compare them using stated criteria | | Organise a task | Suggest a plan or checklist | | Generate possibilities | Brainstorm several ideas |

chunks.title: 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do
chunks.heading: Worked example
chunks.text:
A learner asks AI to draft questions for a broadband provider. AI helps organise the questions, but the learner checks the prices and decides which provider to use.

The assistant helped prepare for the decision; it did not make the decision.

chunks.title: 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text:
Choose one row from the table and use it for a small, low-risk task you might otherwise postpone. Ask for a useful result, then check or edit it yourself.

Fallback prompt:

1. “Give me a five-step plan for clearing and organising one kitchen cupboard.”

chunks.title: 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You matched one task to an appropriate kind of AI help, produced something usable and can say what checking or decision remained yours.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.text:
Recognise a useful AI response without mistaking polish or confidence for proof.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will separate observations, interpretations, estimates and unsupported claims.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
AI produces language with the shape of an answer. Clear, fluent wording does not prove that the claim is true.

An estimate can still provide valuable access to a subject.

Your purpose, context and judgement remain essential.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.heading: Listen to the kind of claim
chunks.text:
A description may mix literal details with interpretation. “A red cover with white lettering” is presented as observation. “A luxurious and romantic design” is judgement. Both may be useful, but they are not the same evidence.

- Visible: the image itself may establish it. - Contextual: it comes from a caption, filename or surrounding page. - Inferred: it is an interpretation, not directly visible. - Uncertain: the system cannot establish it confidently.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.heading: Confidence belongs to the wording
chunks.text: A calm, definite sentence can still be wrong. Treat confidence as a feature of the answer’s style, not proof of its evidence.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Choose one confident AI answer, preferably an image description. Label its important statements as visible, contextual, inferred or uncertain.

chunks.title: 5. Know What You Are Holding
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can explain why the answer is useful while identifying which statements are not established facts.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will match the consequences of a mistake to an appropriate checking level.

Before you begin: For red tasks, use an authoritative source or appropriately qualified human. A person who can see information is not automatically qualified to interpret it.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Do not ask whether AI is trustworthy in general. Ask how much trust this answer needs for this purpose, now.

Most everyday uses are low stakes. The skill is noticing the smaller number where an error matters.

Checking should rise with both the chance of error and the harm it could cause.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: Green: good enough
chunks.text: Use one everyday AI answer when a mistake would cost little or nothing, such as understanding a social photograph, meme or book-cover mood.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: Amber: want it right
chunks.text: Use an independent source or second model when you are learning, may repeat the information or would be embarrassed by an avoidable error.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: Red: need it right
chunks.text: Use a qualified person, authoritative source or human visual-assistance service when an error could affect health, medication, food safety, money, safety, identity, an official decision or professional reputation.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Classify three tasks as green, amber or red. State what could happen if each answer were wrong and what checking is proportionate.

chunks.title: 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
Your checking effort increases with the consequences, and you can explain why.

chunks.title: 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will verify the most consequential part of an answer without checking every sentence.

chunks.title: 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Ask for sources, then open them: a citation is a lead, not verification.

Check that the source supports the exact claim and is current enough.

Use independent sources or qualified help when the stakes demand it.

chunks.title: 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert
chunks.heading: Concentrate on fragile details
chunks.text: - Names and identities. - Prices, dates, doses, telephone numbers and serial codes. - Counts, positions, chart values, axes and units. - Claims carrying your name or professional reputation.

chunks.title: 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert
chunks.heading: Use accessible context
chunks.text: Cross-check the filename, existing alt text, caption, page title, nearby text and link destination. Ask whether a claim came from that context or from the item itself.

chunks.title: 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Choose one factual claim. Find the original or authoritative source, check its date and write one sentence explaining exactly what it supports.

chunks.title: 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can show what the source confirms and distinguish it from what remains uncertain.

chunks.title: 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will choose a tool category from the information, privacy and certainty involved.

Before you begin: Do not upload sensitive material merely to test a service. Check its current privacy terms first.

chunks.title: 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
There is no single best visual AI service. Build a small toolkit rather than an allegiance.

Product names and features change. Choosing the right category is the durable skill.

Cloud services may offer stronger models; on-device services may offer greater privacy, offline use or control.

chunks.title: 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool
chunks.heading: Five useful categories
chunks.text: - Conversational image describers for photographs, objects and scenes. - Text and document recognition for exact wording, forms and structure. - Multiple-model comparison for stronger evidence than one description. - Private or on-device processing for sensitive material or offline access. - Human visual assistance when accuracy, judgement or consequences require it.

chunks.title: 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool
chunks.heading: Choose according to the job
chunks.text: - Do you need an overview, exact text, structure or judgement? - How sensitive is the image? - What would happen if the answer were wrong? - Can you operate the service comfortably with your access method?

chunks.title: 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: For a social photograph, bank letter and medicine label, choose a tool category and explain why. Then use the Tool Cards to compare current services.

chunks.title: 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
Your choice changes when exact text, privacy, accessibility or consequences change.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will request two meaningfully different descriptions of the same image.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Begin with purpose: identification, navigation, appreciation, publication or checking.

Narrow questions direct attention to the information you need.

Request literal facts before mood or interpretation when accuracy matters.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: Useful requests
chunks.text: - Give me a brief overview of the whole image. - Describe only what is literally visible; do not infer identities or intentions. - Read every visible word exactly as it appears. - Describe the layout and positions of the main elements. - What is unclear, small, obscured or uncertain? - Describe the atmosphere and identify the details that create that impression.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: Separate different jobs
chunks.text: An overview, transcription, layout description and interpretation answer different questions. Asking separately makes omissions and guesses easier to notice.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: Worked example
chunks.text: For a book cover, request the background, illustration, title, author and layout. Ask separately for all text verbatim. Then ask what mood the design suggests, treating that answer as interpretation.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Use one non-sensitive image. Request a brief overview, then a detailed literal account including layout, all visible text and uncertainty.

chunks.title: 9. Ask for the Description You Need
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
The descriptions differ in useful ways because each request states a distinct purpose.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will classify one important claim, judge whether it needs checking and choose a proportionate response.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Verification without sight means using narrower questions, independent evidence and human help where needed.

Use four categories consistently: visible, contextual, inferred and unsupported. Uncertainty is a property a claim can acknowledge, not a separate evidence category.

A model may present an inference or unsupported guess with the texture of visible fact.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Classify the claim before relying on it
chunks.text: - Visible: the image itself supplies the evidence, such as printed words, colours or objects. - Contextual: the evidence comes from a caption, filename, surrounding page or other source rather than the image alone. - Inferred: the claim interprets visible evidence, such as mood, genre, relationship or intention. - Unsupported: the available image and context do not justify the claim, even if it is stated confidently.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Ask how likely the detail is to be wrong
chunks.text: - Could the image establish the claimed name, relationship or location? - Is exact text small, stylised, curved or obscured? - Does the answer depend on counting or left and right? - Is an inference being presented as visible fact? - Does the wording acknowledge appropriate uncertainty?

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Decide what is proportionate
chunks.text: Check a claim when being wrong could cost money, affect safety, require an apology or cause a public correction. A decorative detail with no effect on meaning may not need checking. Use the green, amber and red risk bands from Module 6 when the decision is unclear.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Ways to verify without sight
chunks.text: - Ask a narrower question about the disputed detail. - Ask whether the evidence came from the image, context or inference. - Request an independent description. - For exact text, compare the answer with optical character recognition, or OCR. - Check captions, filenames and surrounding content. - Use human assistance or an authoritative source when the consequences justify it.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Agreement, disagreement and no verdict
chunks.text:
Agreement increases confidence but does not prove correctness. If two descriptions disagree, a third independent reading may help, but it does not automatically settle a consequential dispute. Escalate important unresolved details to an authoritative source or person.

If verification is not possible, either omit the claim or carry it forward with its provenance and uncertainty attached. For example: “One image-description model reported a red logo, but I could not verify that detail independently.” Do not repeat it as established fact.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Worked example
chunks.text:
Return to the book cover from Module 9. “The title reads The Stranger Times” is a visible-text claim, but stylised lettering makes the transcription fragile. “C. K. McDonnell” is visible printed text; confirming that it names the correct author and edition requires contextual or authoritative evidence. “The cover suggests comic fantasy” is inferred. A confidently reported quotation that cannot be read in the image or supported by context is unsupported.

Whether to verify each claim depends on purpose. A casual impression of the cover may need no further check. Reproducing the title, author or quotation in published work does.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Take the description you produced in Module 9, or another non-sensitive description. Label its important claims as visible, contextual, inferred or unsupported. Choose one claim, explain what would happen if it were wrong and decide whether to accept it, verify it or carry it forward with an explicit qualification.

chunks.title: 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can name the claim and category, explain its fragility and consequences, and justify the proportionate response you chose.

Recover exact text, reading order and structure without hiding uncertainty.

Recover exact text, reading order and structure without hiding uncertainty.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will request transcription, structure and uncertainty as separate outputs.

Before you begin: Use an authoritative source or human verification for consequential figures and official documents.

chunks.title: 11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Ask for verbatim text before a summary.

Request headings, labels, fields, checked states and reading order.

Exact characters matter: prices, dates, doses, reference numbers and telephone numbers deserve special checking.

chunks.title: 11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots
chunks.heading: Use three passes
chunks.text: - Transcription: read every visible character exactly as it appears. - Structure: identify headings, sections, columns, fields, selected states and reading order. - Uncertainty: list every character, word or field that is unclear, cropped, handwritten or partly obscured.

chunks.title: 11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots
chunks.heading: Do not silently repair the document
chunks.text: A plausible correction can conceal an error. Ask the system to mark uncertainty explicitly rather than guessing. Compare conversational output with a dedicated recognition mode when exact text matters.

chunks.title: 11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Use a non-sensitive document image. Ask for exact text, then a structural outline, then a list of uncertain characters or fields.

chunks.title: 11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can reconstruct the document without silently treating uncertain text as exact.

Recover structure, labels, order and values before asking for interpretation.

Confident with AI course contents

Recover structure, labels, order and values before asking for interpretation.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will request a structured representation and trace conclusions back to its values.

chunks.title: 12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
A fluent summary may capture a chart’s general shape while getting the underlying data wrong.

For tables, request column headings and each row in a consistent order.

For slides, preserve slide order, headings, body text and the distinction between printed content and interpretation.

chunks.title: 12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides
chunks.heading: For charts
chunks.text: - Title and chart type. - Horizontal and vertical axes. - Units, scale and range. - Legend categories and colours or patterns. - Exact labelled values or clearly marked estimates. - Trend or conclusion only after the data account.

chunks.title: 12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides
chunks.heading: Prefer the source data
chunks.text: When values matter, obtain the accessible source table or data file if one exists. Treat an image-based reconstruction as an intermediate access route, not automatically as the authoritative dataset.

chunks.title: 12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Take one non-sensitive table, chart or slide. Ask first for structure and values, then for a short interpretation that identifies uncertainty.

chunks.title: 12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can trace every important conclusion back to a label or value in the structured account.

chunks.text:
Write a brief, generate an image, describe it back and make one deliberate revision.

Confident with AI course contents

Part Four: Create Visual Media

Write a brief, generate an image, describe it back and make one deliberate revision.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will complete a create, describe, compare and revise cycle.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Begin with what the visual must do, not only how it should look.

Keep the original brief: it records your intention and becomes the standard for review.

Generate alternatives when useful, then have a describing model examine the selected result.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: Write the brief
chunks.text: - Purpose and intended audience. - Where the image will appear. - Subject, setting and action. - Composition and visual hierarchy. - Mood, style and colour preferences. - Required wording and elements that must not appear. - What would count as failure.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: Describe the result back
chunks.text: - Describe the complete image literally. - Read every word exactly. - List anything malformed, duplicated or inconsistent. - Compare the image with every requirement in the brief. - Explain what a sighted viewer might misunderstand.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: Revise deliberately
chunks.text: Do not request “better”. Name the change: remove an object, correct wording, simplify the background, emphasise the subject, preserve a logo or change the emotional tone.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Create a low-stakes image from a plain-language brief. Obtain a fresh description, compare it with the brief and make one specific revision.

chunks.title: 13. Create Your First Image
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
You can name the mismatch and explain how the revision addressed it.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.text:
Use intention, hierarchy and proportionate review to remain the author.

Confident with AI course contents

Part Four: Create Visual Media

Use intention, hierarchy and proportionate review to remain the author.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will separate authorship from pixel-by-pixel inspection and define your review standard.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
A blind creator can control the concept, constraints, revisions, sound and publication choices without certifying every pixel.

Descriptions, comparison and selective human review are instruments; they do not become the author.

Spend verification on details carrying meaning, harm or reputational risk.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.heading: Control the process
chunks.text: - Develop the idea in words. - Define essential and forbidden elements. - Generate and request a literal description. - Compare the account with the brief. - Make named revisions rather than vague improvements. - Escalate checking as audience, stakes and permanence increase.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.heading: Choose a finish line
chunks.text: A personal experiment may be finished when it delights you. Public work carrying your name may need an independent second review. Commercial, sensitive or safety-related work may require a designer, intended audience member or qualified human reviewer.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Write a five-line visual brief stating purpose, audience, essential elements, forbidden elements and the test for success. Add whether the work is green, amber or red and what that means for review.

chunks.title: 14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
Another person or tool could review the result against your criteria without guessing your intention.

- Previous: 13. Create Your First Image - Course contents - Next: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story

chunks.text:
Plan story beats, panels, dialogue and continuity, then check reading order.

Confident with AI course contents

Part Four: Create Visual Media

Plan story beats, panels, dialogue and continuity, then check reading order.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will create a panel plan that can be checked independently of finished artwork.

chunks.title: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Write the purpose and action of every panel before generating artwork.

Use a stable character description and repeated visual anchors.

Request a panel-by-panel account rather than one general summary.

chunks.title: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story
chunks.heading: Check the finished comic
chunks.text: - Are panels presented in the intended reading order? - Are characters consistent across panels and pages? - Does each panel show its intended story beat? - Are speech bubbles attributed to the correct speaker? - Is every word spelled correctly? - Do props, positions or actions contradict the script?

chunks.title: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story
chunks.heading: Worked example
chunks.text: A six-page comic about theatrical crime-fighting cats was generated from a written story and visual prompt. One model described each page; a second checked spelling and continuity and found two spelling errors. The second review turned “Does it look all right?” into specific, actionable information.

chunks.title: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Draft a three-panel story as numbered beats. Generate it, then request a panel-by-panel description with every piece of text transcribed. Use a second check for spelling and continuity.

chunks.title: 15. Create a Comic or Visual Story
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
The described sequence tells the intended story in the intended order, and you have recorded any uncertainty.

Confident with AI course contents

Part Four: Create Visual Media

Plan movement, dialogue, music and sound as one accessible time-based sequence.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will specify and check a short sequence using both visual description and audio evidence.

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Describe what changes over time, not only the starting frame.

Sound is both creative material and directly accessible evidence about speech, mood and timing.

Request a shot-by-shot or time-coded account to catch unexpected changes.

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: Plan the whole sequence
chunks.text: - Starting frame and intended movement. - Character or object continuity. - Spoken words and who says them. - Music, sound effects and silence. - Timing of each action and transition. - The final frame or end state.

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: Check the result
chunks.text: - Does movement follow naturally from the starting image? - Do characters or objects change unexpectedly? - Is every spoken word correct? - Do voice, music and effects match the intended tone? - Is important visual information unavailable through sound? - Are captions, a transcript or audio description required?

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: Examples of the pipeline
chunks.text: A comic scene can become an animated curtain call with dialogue and music. A branded still image can become a promotional race video. A static cover can become a short title ident combining motion, a spoken name and sound. Each begins with intention and ends with proportionate review.

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Write a ten-second sequence with timestamps for action, speech, music and sound effects. Ask for a time-coded account of the generated result.

chunks.title: 16. Create Animation and Video
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
The timing and story can be understood from the combined visual description and audio plan.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.text:
Define finished, check proportionately and publish an equivalent accessible experience.

Confident with AI course contents

Part Four: Create Visual Media

Define finished, check proportionately and publish an equivalent accessible experience.

Estimated time: 10 minutes. Last reviewed: 11 August 2026.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: What you need to know
chunks.text:
This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Learning outcome: By the end, you will choose and write the accessible alternative appropriate to one visual work.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: The lesson
chunks.text:
Accessibility is part of the work, not an apology added after it.

Check spelling, identity, continuity, composition and essential meaning before publication.

Choose alt text, an extended description, captions, a transcript or audio description according to purpose.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: Quality checks by medium
chunks.text: - Still image: subject, prominence, embedded text, anatomy, mood and unwanted symbolism. - Comic: reading order, character continuity, dialogue ownership, spelling and contradictions. - Video: movement, continuity, spoken wording, audio, captions and visually essential information. - Branding: name, logo, colours, symbols, unintended associations and audience expectations.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: Write for the work’s purpose
chunks.text: Concise alt text should communicate the image’s purpose and essential information without repeating nearby text. Use an extended description when detail, relationships or a visual story cannot fit concisely. Time-based work may need captions, a transcript and audio description because these serve different access needs.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: Do not overclaim checking
chunks.text: Record which checks were actually performed. A model description is evidence, not a visual guarantee. If no screen-reader, intended-audience or professional design review took place, do not imply that it did.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Write alt text for one finished image. If concise text cannot carry its purpose and essential detail, add an extended description. For a video, also identify whether captions, transcript or audio description are needed.

chunks.title: 17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly
chunks.heading: Checkpoint
chunks.text:
A person who cannot see the work receives its purpose and essential information without redundant filler.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.text:
A TAVIP handbook introducing ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini and Grok, written by Charli-Jo Tyrer.

Session 1: Getting Useful Answers from AI

Written by Charli-Jo Tyrer for TAVIP, July 2026

This handbook is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. You may copy, share, adapt and use it for any purpose, including commercially, provided that you credit the author.

Suggested attribution: AI Assistants, written by Charli-Jo Tyrer for TAVIP, July 2026. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Welcome
chunks.text: This handbook accompanies the Confident with AI course.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is an AI assistant?
chunks.text:
For this course, when we say AI, we mean AI assistants: computer programs you can have a conversation with using ordinary language.

The five assistants covered are:

- ChatGPT - Claude - Copilot - Gemini - Grok

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: How do I choose one?
chunks.text: There is no single best assistant. Choose the one that feels easiest for you to use. The skills in this course transfer between all five.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Things all AI assistants can do
chunks.text: - Answer questions - Explain - Summarise - Write - Brainstorm - Describe images - Help plan

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Things all AI assistants get wrong
chunks.text:
Every AI assistant can:

- misunderstand you - invent facts - be out of date - sound confident while being wrong

Always use your own judgement and check important information.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is it?
chunks.text:
ChatGPT is an AI assistant. You can ask it questions, have conversations, and ask it to write, explain, summarise, plan, translate or help solve problems.

Think of it as someone you can ask for a first draft, an explanation or another way of thinking about a problem.

ChatGPT uses artificial intelligence to generate its responses. Like all AI assistants, it can be extremely useful, but you should still use your own judgement and check important information.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Who makes it?
chunks.text: ChatGPT is made by OpenAI, an AI company.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What does ChatGPT mean?
chunks.text:
The name has two parts.

Chat refers to the way you can have a conversation with it.

GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

You do not need to understand what a Transformer is to use ChatGPT. It is simply the name of the type of AI model that powers the assistant.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Where do I use it?
chunks.text:
You can use ChatGPT:

- on the web at chatgpt.com - on an iPhone or iPad using the ChatGPT app - on Android using the ChatGPT app - on Windows or Mac using the desktop app or a web browser

You can create a free OpenAI account. ChatGPT also allows limited use without signing in.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Does it cost anything?
chunks.text:
There is a free version, which is suitable for most people getting started.

Paid subscriptions are also available. These provide higher usage limits and additional features.

For this course, the free version is perfectly adequate.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is ChatGPT good at?
chunks.text:
Many people use ChatGPT to:

- write emails and letters - explain difficult topics - summarise long documents - brainstorm ideas - improve writing - help with planning - describe and create images - answer questions - compare options - support everyday decision-making

ChatGPT is widely used and offers a broad range of features. Because so many people use it, there are also plenty of guides, examples and sources of help available.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What should I be careful about?
chunks.text:
Do not assume ChatGPT is always right.

It can misunderstand your question, invent facts, provide incomplete or out-of-date information, and sound confident while being wrong.

Always check important information, particularly when making medical, legal or financial decisions.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Should I choose ChatGPT?
chunks.text:
ChatGPT is an excellent place to start if you have never used an AI assistant before. It is widely available, relatively easy to begin using, and has become the assistant many people first think of when they hear the term AI.

You do not need to choose the perfect AI assistant. The best place to start is often whichever one feels easiest for you to use.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Remember
chunks.text:
ChatGPT is one AI assistant. The others discussed during this course are Claude, Copilot, Gemini and Grok.

The skills you learn in this course transfer between all of them.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is it?
chunks.text:
Claude is an AI assistant. You can ask it questions, have conversations, and ask it to write, explain, summarise, plan, translate or help solve problems.

Think of it as someone you can ask for a first draft, an explanation or another way of thinking about a problem.

Claude uses artificial intelligence to generate its responses. Like all AI assistants, it can be extremely useful, but you should still use your own judgement and check important information.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Who makes it?
chunks.text: Claude is made by Anthropic, an AI company that places particular emphasis on making its systems helpful, honest and safe.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What does Claude mean?
chunks.text:
Claude is not an acronym and does not stand for anything technical.

The name is widely understood as a reference to Claude Shannon, one of the founders of modern information theory. You do not need to know anything about him to use Claude.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Where do I use it?
chunks.text:
You can use Claude:

- on the web at claude.ai - on an iPhone or iPad using the Claude app - on Android using the Claude app - on Windows or Mac using the desktop app or a web browser

You sign in using a free Anthropic account.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Does it cost anything?
chunks.text:
There is a free version, which is suitable for most people getting started. Paid subscriptions are also available. These provide higher usage limits and additional features.

For this course, the free version is perfectly adequate.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is Claude good at?
chunks.text:
Many people use Claude to write emails and letters, explain difficult topics, summarise long documents, brainstorm ideas, improve writing, help with planning, describe and create images, answer questions, compare options and support everyday decision-making.

Claude is often praised for careful, natural writing and for working steadily with long or complicated documents.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What should I be careful about?
chunks.text:
Do not assume Claude is always right. It can misunderstand your question, invent facts, provide incomplete or out-of-date information, and sound confident while being wrong.

Always check important information, particularly when making medical, legal or financial decisions.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Should I choose Claude?
chunks.text:
Claude is an excellent choice if you value thoughtful, natural writing or regularly work with longer documents. Many people find its tone calm, clear and easy to work with.

You do not need to choose the perfect AI assistant. The best place to start is often whichever one feels easiest for you to use.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Remember
chunks.text:
Claude is one AI assistant. The others discussed during this course are ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Grok.

The skills you learn in this course transfer between all of them.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is it?
chunks.text:
Copilot is an AI assistant. You can ask it questions, have conversations, and ask it to write, explain, summarise, plan, translate or help solve problems.

Think of it as someone you can ask for a first draft, an explanation or another way of thinking about a problem.

Copilot uses artificial intelligence to generate its responses. Like all AI assistants, it can be extremely useful, but you should still use your own judgement and check important information.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Who makes it?
chunks.text:
Copilot is made by Microsoft.

Microsoft uses the Copilot name for several AI products. This course is discussing the general Microsoft Copilot assistant, rather than GitHub Copilot for computer programmers or Microsoft 365 Copilot for workplaces.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What does Copilot mean?
chunks.text:
A co-pilot is the second pilot in an aircraft, who works alongside the person in command.

Microsoft chose the name to suggest an assistant that works alongside you. You remain in control and responsible for checking the result.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Where do I use it?
chunks.text:
You can use Copilot:

- on the web at copilot.com - on an iPhone or iPad using the Microsoft Copilot app - on Android using the Microsoft Copilot app - on Windows or Mac using the Copilot app or a web browser

You can sign in using a free Microsoft account.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Does it cost anything?
chunks.text:
There is a free version, which is suitable for most people getting started. Paid Microsoft subscriptions are also available. These can provide higher usage limits, additional features or Copilot inside Microsoft 365 apps such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.

For this course, the free version is perfectly adequate.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is Copilot good at?
chunks.text:
Many people use Copilot to write emails and letters, explain difficult topics, summarise information, brainstorm ideas, improve writing, help with planning, describe and create images, answer questions using current information from the web, compare options and support everyday decision-making.

Copilot may be particularly useful if you already use Windows, Microsoft Edge or Microsoft 365.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What should I be careful about?
chunks.text:
Do not assume Copilot is always right. It can misunderstand your question, invent facts, provide incomplete or out-of-date information, and sound confident while being wrong.

Always check important information, particularly when making medical, legal or financial decisions.

Microsoft has several products with Copilot in their names. Check which Copilot you are using and whether it can access information from your personal, work or school account.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Should I choose Copilot?
chunks.text:
Copilot is an excellent choice if you already use Microsoft products such as Windows, Edge, Word, Outlook or Microsoft 365. Its web search can also make it useful when you want help finding and understanding current information.

You do not need to choose the perfect AI assistant. The best place to start is often whichever one feels easiest for you to use.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Remember
chunks.text:
Copilot is one AI assistant. The others discussed during this course are ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok.

The skills you learn in this course transfer between all of them.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is it?
chunks.text:
Gemini is an AI assistant. You can ask it questions, have conversations, and ask it to write, explain, summarise, plan, translate or help solve problems.

Think of it as someone you can ask for a first draft, an explanation or another way of thinking about a problem.

Gemini uses artificial intelligence to generate its responses. Like all AI assistants, it can be extremely useful, but you should still use your own judgement and check important information.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Who makes it?
chunks.text:
Gemini is made by Google.

It can work with some Google services, including Gmail, Drive, Maps and other Google apps, when those connections are available and you choose to enable them.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What does Gemini mean?
chunks.text:
Gemini is the Latin word for twins and is also the name of a constellation.

Google chose Gemini as the name for its family of AI models and its AI assistant. You do not need to know anything technical about the name to use it.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Where do I use it?
chunks.text:
You can use Gemini:

- on the web at gemini.google.com - on an iPhone or iPad using the Gemini app - on Android using the Gemini app - on Windows or Mac using a web browser

You sign in using a free Google Account.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Does it cost anything?
chunks.text:
There is a free version, which is suitable for most people getting started. Paid Google AI plans are also available. These provide higher usage limits and additional features.

For this course, the free version is perfectly adequate.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is Gemini good at?
chunks.text:
Many people use Gemini to write emails and letters, explain difficult topics, summarise long documents, brainstorm ideas, improve writing, help with planning, describe and create images, answer questions, compare options and support everyday decision-making.

Gemini may be particularly useful if you already use Google services. It can use current information from the web for some questions and may be able to work with information from your Google apps when you choose to enable those connections.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What should I be careful about?
chunks.text:
Do not assume Gemini is always right. It can misunderstand your question, invent facts, provide incomplete or out-of-date information, and sound confident while being wrong.

Always check important information, particularly when making medical, legal or financial decisions.

Be especially careful before allowing any AI assistant to access personal information stored in your email, documents or other accounts.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Should I choose Gemini?
chunks.text:
Gemini is an excellent choice if you already use Google services such as Gmail, Google Drive, Google Maps or Android.

You do not need to choose the perfect AI assistant. The best place to start is often whichever one feels easiest for you to use.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Remember
chunks.text:
Gemini is one AI assistant. The others discussed during this course are ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and Grok.

The skills you learn in this course transfer between all of them.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is it?
chunks.text:
Grok is an AI assistant. You can ask it questions, have conversations, and ask it to write, explain, summarise, plan, translate or help solve problems.

Think of it as someone you can ask for a first draft, an explanation or another way of thinking about a problem.

Grok uses artificial intelligence to generate its responses. Like all AI assistants, it can be extremely useful, but you should still use your own judgement and check important information.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Who makes it?
chunks.text:
Grok is made by xAI, the artificial intelligence company founded by Elon Musk. The company now describes itself as SpaceXAI.

Grok is closely connected with X, formerly called Twitter, but you do not have to use it inside X.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What does Grok mean?
chunks.text:
The word grok comes from Robert A. Heinlein’s science-fiction novel Stranger in a Strange Land.

It means to understand something deeply and intuitively, rather than merely knowing facts about it.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Where do I use it?
chunks.text:
You can use Grok:

- on the web at grok.com - on an iPhone or iPad using the Grok app, or inside the X app - on Android using the Grok app, or inside the X app - on Windows or Mac using a web browser

You can sign in using an X account or an email address.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Does it cost anything?
chunks.text:
There is a free version, which is suitable for most people getting started. Paid subscriptions are also available. These provide higher usage limits and additional features.

For this course, the free version is perfectly adequate.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What is Grok good at?
chunks.text:
Many people use Grok to write emails and letters, explain difficult topics, summarise long documents, brainstorm ideas, improve writing, help with planning, describe and create images, answer questions, compare options and support everyday decision-making.

Grok can search the web and public posts on X. This may make it particularly useful for recent news, live events and current discussions.

It is designed to have a more humorous, playful and sometimes rebellious personality than many other AI assistants.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What should I be careful about?
chunks.text:
Do not assume Grok is always right. It can misunderstand your question, invent facts, provide incomplete or out-of-date information, sound confident while being wrong, and treat rumours or unreliable posts on X as useful evidence.

Always check important information, particularly when making medical, legal or financial decisions.

If you use Grok through X, check the data-sharing and personalisation settings. X says your public data and your interactions with Grok may be used to train and improve its AI unless you opt out.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Should I choose Grok?
chunks.text:
Grok is an excellent choice if you already use X, want help exploring current discussions, or enjoy a more playful and irreverent style.

It may be less suitable if you dislike X, prefer a more restrained tone, or do not want to spend time checking information drawn from social media.

You do not need to choose the perfect AI assistant. The best place to start is often whichever one feels easiest for you to use.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Remember
chunks.text:
Grok is one AI assistant. The others discussed during this course are ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and Gemini.

The skills you learn in this course transfer between all of them.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: AI assistants, models and the wild frontier
chunks.text:
So far, this handbook has treated ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini and Grok as five AI assistants. That is the most useful way to begin. Underneath each assistant, however, is one or more AI models: the systems that generate the answers.

An assistant is the service you use. A model is the engine inside it. The same assistant may use a fast model for an everyday question, a reasoning model for a difficult problem and a specialist model for voice or images. The provider may choose automatically, or may let you choose. This is why an assistant can change noticeably even though its name and app remain the same.

The following is a snapshot from 21 July 2026. Model names and availability change extremely quickly.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: ChatGPT: the GPT family
chunks.text: ChatGPT is powered by OpenAI’s GPT models. The current frontier generation is GPT-5.6, with Sol, Terra and Luna variants offering different balances of capability, speed and cost. ChatGPT can route a request to an appropriate model, while some paid plans and specialist OpenAI products provide more choice. OpenAI also develops models for coding, voice, images and other particular forms of work.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Claude: the Claude family
chunks.text: Claude is powered by Anthropic’s Claude models. Sonnet 5 is the everyday default for many users and is designed for writing, coding, tool use and multi-step work. Opus 4.8 remains a more powerful option for demanding work. Fable 5 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model, while the closely related Mythos 5 has restricted access because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. The older Haiku, Sonnet and Opus names originally formed a simple fast-to-powerful ladder; the newer family is less tidy, which is itself a sign of how quickly the frontier is moving.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Copilot: a multi-model assistant
chunks.text: Copilot is different because Microsoft does not present it as the product of one permanent model family. Microsoft’s consumer and workplace assistants have traditionally relied heavily on OpenAI models, and GPT-5.6 is the preferred model in Microsoft 365 Copilot as of July 2026. Microsoft now describes Copilot as model-diverse, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and open models available in different products and settings. The name Copilot therefore tells you more about the Microsoft service around the model than about the particular model answering.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Gemini: the Gemini family
chunks.text: Gemini is both the name of Google’s assistant and its main model family. The current range includes Gemini 3.1 Pro for complex work, Gemini 3.1 Deep Think for difficult scientific and reasoning problems, Gemini 3.5 Flash for fast multimodal and agentic work, and Flash-Lite for efficient high-volume use. Gemini models are designed to work across text, images, audio and video rather than treating those as entirely separate worlds. Google also has specialist families for images, video, music and robotics.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Grok: the Grok family
chunks.text: Grok is powered by models developed by SpaceXAI, formerly xAI. Grok 4.5 is the current leading general model, with particular emphasis on coding, tool use and work carried out by AI agents. The wider family includes faster coding models and separate Grok Imagine models for images and video. Grok’s close connection with X and real-time search remains part of the assistant’s identity, but the models can also be used through Grok’s own apps and by developers.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Beyond the five
chunks.text: The five assistants are prominent consumer services, not the whole AI world. Developers, companies and technically confident individuals can choose from hundreds of other models. Some are available through their maker’s website or an independent assistant. Others can be downloaded and run on a company’s own servers or, when small enough, on a personal computer.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Open-weight models
chunks.text: A closed model is normally used through its maker’s app or online service; its internal parameters are not released. With an open-weight model, the trained numerical weights can be downloaded, adapted and run elsewhere. This can offer more privacy, control and independence, but it requires hardware and technical knowledge. Open-weight does not always mean completely open source: the training data, full development process or licence may still impose limits.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Chinese model families
chunks.text: China is now one of the two main centres of frontier model development. DeepSeek’s V4 family combines long context, reasoning and agentic work at comparatively low cost. Alibaba’s Qwen family includes both very large services and smaller downloadable multimodal models. Z.ai’s GLM-5 family concentrates on coding and long-running agent tasks. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, released in July 2026, is a very large open-weight multimodal model aimed at long-context coding and agentic work. These families are not curiosities at the edge of the market: they compete with leading American models and are especially influential in the open-weight world. Users should still consider where their information is processed, the provider’s privacy terms and any restrictions that apply in their country or workplace.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: American open-weight models
chunks.text: The United States also has an important open-weight ecosystem. Meta’s Llama family helped popularise downloadable general-purpose models. OpenAI’s gpt-oss models provide open-weight reasoning and tool use in sizes intended for servers and powerful personal hardware. Google’s Gemma models offer smaller open models related to its Gemini research, while NVIDIA’s Nemotron family is designed particularly for efficient, long-running AI agents. Many smaller assistants and business systems are built from these families rather than from the closed models their users may recognise.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: Mistral and the European alternative
chunks.text: Mistral AI is very much still going. The French company offers the Le Chat assistant, commercial services and a continuing range of open-weight models. Mistral 3 includes Large 3, a powerful mixture-of-experts model, alongside smaller models that are easier to deploy locally. Mistral also develops specialist families for reasoning, coding, documents, audio and speech. Its importance is not only technical: it provides a significant European alternative to an AI landscape dominated by American and Chinese companies.

chunks.title: AI Assistants
chunks.heading: What should an ordinary user do with this?
chunks.text: Probably nothing—unless you are curious. You do not need to follow model rankings or understand parameter counts to use an AI assistant well. Choose an assistant that is accessible, affordable and useful to you. The deeper lesson is simply that the name on the app is not the whole system. Models will be replaced, combined and specialised, while the skills you are learning—asking clearly, providing context, checking important answers and using your own judgement—will travel with you across all of them.
